50f4c76f-0aeb-4b3d-8f9d-f6ad6c803079.text: How does Shakespeare use the extended metaphor in “Our revels now are ended” to explore the relationship between illusion and reality?
50f4c76f-0aeb-4b3d-8f9d-f6ad6c803079.marks:
Upper band (3-4): Detailed analysis of the three-level metaphor (masque, life, theatre). Discusses “the great globe itself” as both the world and the Globe Theatre, “rounded with a sleep” as death/oblivion, and the metatheatrical implications for Shakespeare’s own art. Links to the play’s wider theme of illusion.
Lower band (1-2): Basic identification that Prospero compares life to a dream.

50f4c76f-0aeb-4b3d-8f9d-f6ad6c803079.text: Read Act 5, Scene 1 from “Your charm so strongly works ’em” to “The rarer action is / In virtue than in vengeance.” How does Shakespeare present the moment when Prospero decides to forgive his enemies?
50f4c76f-0aeb-4b3d-8f9d-f6ad6c803079.marks:
Top band (7-8): Sophisticated analysis of Ariel’s compassion as the catalyst, the irony that a non-human spirit feels more empathy than Prospero, the significance of “rarer” (harder and more admirable), and how this choice transforms the play from potential tragedy into romance. Links to the genre of late romance and the theme of forgiveness.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Clear analysis with several features and thematic understanding.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Some relevant points.
Lower band (1-2): Simple comments.

50f4c76f-0aeb-4b3d-8f9d-f6ad6c803079.text: Read Act 5, Scene 1 from “I have bedimmed / The noontide sun” to “I’ll drown my book.” How does Shakespeare use language and imagery in this extract to present Prospero’s renunciation of magic?
50f4c76f-0aeb-4b3d-8f9d-f6ad6c803079.marks:
Top band (7-8): Sophisticated analysis of the imagery of power (controlling sun, winds, lightning), the physicality of breaking the staff and drowning the book, the verb “abjure” as a formal rejection, and the metatheatrical reading of Shakespeare abandoning his craft. Discusses the paradox of the speech itself being powerfully poetic even as it renounces power.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Clear analysis with relevant imagery discussion.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Some relevant points with limited analysis.
Lower band (1-2): Simple identification that Prospero gives up magic.

50f4c76f-0aeb-4b3d-8f9d-f6ad6c803079.text: Explore how Shakespeare uses the epilogue to reverse the power dynamic between Prospero and the audience. How does this relate to the play’s themes of power and freedom?
50f4c76f-0aeb-4b3d-8f9d-f6ad6c803079.marks:
Top band (11-12) Convincing analysis of the power reversal: Prospero moves from absolute control to total dependence on the audience. Discusses “indulgence” as both applause and religious pardon, the connection to Ariel’s freedom, the metatheatrical dimension (Shakespeare addressing playgoers), and how the epilogue enacts the play’s theme that true freedom requires giving up control. Precise quotations.
Upper band (9-10) Thoughtful analysis with clear thematic links.
Top band (7-8): Clear understanding with relevant evidence.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Some understanding with basic points.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Limited response.
Lower band (1-2): Simple statements.

50f4c76f-0aeb-4b3d-8f9d-f6ad6c803079.text: Starting with Act 5, Scene 1 (“This thing of darkness I / Acknowledge mine”), explore how Shakespeare presents the theme of forgiveness in The Tempest. Write about: how Shakespeare presents forgiveness in this extract, and how Shakespeare presents forgiveness in the play as a whole.
50f4c76f-0aeb-4b3d-8f9d-f6ad6c803079.marks:
Top band (25–30 marks + 4 spelling/grammar)Critical, exploratory response. Analyses the ambiguity of “This thing of darkness I acknowledge mine” (responsibility vs ownership vs self-recognition). Discusses Prospero’s cold forgiveness of Antonio, warm reunion with Alonso, the role of Ariel’s compassion in prompting mercy, and the epilogue’s plea for the audience’s own forgiveness. Considers whether the play’s forgiveness is complete or conditional. Embeds genre context (late romance). Well-structured with precise quotation analysis.

Upper band (19–24 marks + 3 spelling/grammar)Thoughtful response with clear evidence and context.

Upper-mid band (13–18 marks + 2 spelling/grammar)Clear response with some analysis.

Mid band (7–12 marks + 2 spelling/grammar)Some understanding.

Lower-mid band (3–6 marks + 1 spelling/grammar)Limited response.

Lower band (1–2 marks + 1 spelling/grammar)Simple, brief response.

50f4c76f-0aeb-4b3d-8f9d-f6ad6c803079.text: Analyse how Shakespeare uses Prospero’s line “This thing of darkness I acknowledge mine” to present ideas about responsibility and power in Act 5, Scene 1.
50f4c76f-0aeb-4b3d-8f9d-f6ad6c803079.marks:
Upper band (3-4): Detailed analysis of the multiple meanings: “thing” as dehumanising, “darkness” as moral/colonial metaphor, “acknowledge” as admission of responsibility vs claim of ownership, “mine” as possession. Links to the colonial dynamic and Prospero’s possible recognition of his own darker impulses. Considers the ambiguity Shakespeare deliberately leaves.
Lower band (1-2): Basic identification that Prospero accepts Caliban.

8f02e52e-c13c-4098-8802-5d8df7cc82ad.text: Identify two main ideas the writer presents in lines 1 to 12 of the 19th-century text.
8f02e52e-c13c-4098-8802-5d8df7cc82ad.marks: 1 mark per valid main idea identified, up to 2 marks. Must be drawn from the specified lines.

8f02e52e-c13c-4098-8802-5d8df7cc82ad.text: Summarise what the modern writer tells you about the effects of social media on young people. Use evidence from lines 5 to 18.
8f02e52e-c13c-4098-8802-5d8df7cc82ad.marks:
Upper band (3-4): Clear, concise summary of the main points with brief supporting evidence. Uses own words rather than copying.
Lower band (1-2): Some relevant points with limited clarity or accuracy.

8f02e52e-c13c-4098-8802-5d8df7cc82ad.text: Analyse how the 19th-century writer uses language to present their view of the natural world. Use specific evidence from the text.
8f02e52e-c13c-4098-8802-5d8df7cc82ad.marks:
Top band (7-8): Perceptive analysis with well-chosen evidence and precise terminology.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Clear analysis with relevant evidence.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Some relevant comments.
Lower band (1-2): Simple identification.

8f02e52e-c13c-4098-8802-5d8df7cc82ad.text: Using information from both texts, summarise the different attitudes the writers have towards progress and change.
8f02e52e-c13c-4098-8802-5d8df7cc82ad.marks:
Top band (10-12): Perceptive synthesis drawing from both texts. Identifies key similarities and differences in attitudes with well-integrated evidence.
Upper-mid band (7-9): Clear synthesis with relevant evidence from both texts.
Lower-mid band (4-6): Some comparison with evidence from at least one text.
Lower band (1-3): Simple statements.

8f02e52e-c13c-4098-8802-5d8df7cc82ad.text: Write a speech to be delivered at a community meeting in which you argue that a local park should be preserved rather than developed for housing.
8f02e52e-c13c-4098-8802-5d8df7cc82ad.marks:
Content and Organisation (24 marks):
Top band (19–24) Compelling, convincing argument.
Upper-mid band (13–18) Clearly communicated.
Lower-mid band (7–12) Some success.
Lower band (1–6) Simple.

Technical Accuracy (16 marks):
Top band (13–16) Highly accurate.
Upper-mid band (9–12) Mostly accurate.
Lower-mid band (5–8) Some.
Lower band (1–4) Limited.

8f02e52e-c13c-4098-8802-5d8df7cc82ad.text: How do both writers present the idea that education is important? Synthesise information from both texts in your answer.
8f02e52e-c13c-4098-8802-5d8df7cc82ad.marks:
Upper band (3-4): Draws from both texts and identifies a connection or contrast. Uses brief evidence from each text.
Lower band (1-2): References one or both texts with limited synthesis.

0b59cacc-7a82-448a-8a30-0951d22c3d61.text: Identify two relevant features from the specified lines.
0b59cacc-7a82-448a-8a30-0951d22c3d61.marks: 1 mark per valid feature identified with brief evidence, up to 2 marks.

0b59cacc-7a82-448a-8a30-0951d22c3d61.text: Explain how the writer uses language to create a specific effect. Use evidence from the text.
0b59cacc-7a82-448a-8a30-0951d22c3d61.marks:
Upper band (3-4): Clear explanation with relevant evidence and analysis of effect.
Lower band (1-2): Some identification with limited comment.

0b59cacc-7a82-448a-8a30-0951d22c3d61.text: Analyse how the writer uses language and/or structure to achieve their purpose. Use subject terminology.
0b59cacc-7a82-448a-8a30-0951d22c3d61.marks:
Top band (7-8): Perceptive analysis with precise terminology.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Clear analysis.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Some relevant comments.
Lower band (1-2): Simple identification.

0b59cacc-7a82-448a-8a30-0951d22c3d61.text: Compare how the two writers convey their perspectives. Consider ideas and methods.
0b59cacc-7a82-448a-8a30-0951d22c3d61.marks:
Top band (10-12): Perceptive comparison with well-integrated evidence.
Upper-mid band (7-9): Clear comparison.
Lower-mid band (4-6): Some comparison.
Lower band (1-3): Simple statements.

0b59cacc-7a82-448a-8a30-0951d22c3d61.text: Write a piece of non-fiction for a specified audience and purpose.
0b59cacc-7a82-448a-8a30-0951d22c3d61.marks:
Content and Organisation (24 marks):
Top band (19–24) Compelling communication.
Upper-mid band (13–18) Clearly communicated.
Lower-mid band (7–12) Some success.
Lower band (1–6) Simple.

Technical Accuracy (16 marks):
Top band (13–16) Highly accurate.
Upper-mid band (9–12) Mostly accurate.
Lower-mid band (5–8) Some accuracy.
Lower band (1–4) Limited accuracy.

0b59cacc-7a82-448a-8a30-0951d22c3d61.text: Explain how a specific word or phrase affects the reader's understanding.
0b59cacc-7a82-448a-8a30-0951d22c3d61.marks:
Upper band (3-4): Analyses connotations and effect with evidence.
Lower band (1-2): Basic comment.

6f651859-36d1-4753-b77f-9abe0c05d8f9.text: Identify two language techniques the writer uses in lines 6 to 14.
6f651859-36d1-4753-b77f-9abe0c05d8f9.marks: 1 mark per valid technique identified with brief evidence, up to 2 marks.

6f651859-36d1-4753-b77f-9abe0c05d8f9.text: Explain how the writer uses metaphor in lines 10 to 16 to convey the devastation of the flood.
6f651859-36d1-4753-b77f-9abe0c05d8f9.marks:
Upper band (3-4): Analyses the metaphor with specific evidence, exploring connotations and effects on the reader.
Lower band (1-2): Identifies the metaphor with limited analysis.

6f651859-36d1-4753-b77f-9abe0c05d8f9.text: Analyse how the writer uses language techniques to present the beauty of the landscape. Use subject terminology to support your analysis.
6f651859-36d1-4753-b77f-9abe0c05d8f9.marks:
Top band (7-8): Perceptive analysis using precise terminology with detailed exploration of effects.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Clear analysis with appropriate terminology.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Some relevant comments.
Lower band (1-2): Simple identification.

6f651859-36d1-4753-b77f-9abe0c05d8f9.text: Compare how both writers use rhetorical techniques to engage their audiences. Use terminology to support your answer.
6f651859-36d1-4753-b77f-9abe0c05d8f9.marks:
Top band (10-12): Perceptive comparison of techniques and effects with precise terminology.
Upper-mid band (7-9): Clear comparison.
Lower-mid band (4-6): Some comparison.
Lower band (1-3): Simple statements.

6f651859-36d1-4753-b77f-9abe0c05d8f9.text: Write a speech for your year group in which you persuade them to support a charity event.
6f651859-36d1-4753-b77f-9abe0c05d8f9.marks:
Content and Organisation (24 marks):
Top band (19–24) Compelling communication.
Upper-mid band (13–18) Clear.
Lower-mid band (7–12) Some.
Lower band (1–6) Simple.

Technical Accuracy (16 marks):
Top band (13–16) Highly accurate.
Upper-mid band (9–12) Mostly.
Lower-mid band (5–8) Some.
Lower band (1–4) Limited.

6f651859-36d1-4753-b77f-9abe0c05d8f9.text: How does the writer's use of antithesis in the final paragraph strengthen their argument?
6f651859-36d1-4753-b77f-9abe0c05d8f9.marks:
Upper band (3-4): Explains how contrasting ideas in a parallel structure create emphasis and clarity, making the argument memorable.
Lower band (1-2): Basic identification of contrast.

b3e9f051-a4d9-4d22-ad48-2b26fb29f855.marks: An independent clause is a group of words that contains a subject and a verb and can stand alone as a complete sentence (1 mark).

b3e9f051-a4d9-4d22-ad48-2b26fb29f855.text: Describe two effects a semicolon can create in creative writing.
b3e9f051-a4d9-4d22-ad48-2b26fb29f855.marks:
1 marks for each effect, up to 2 marks. Possible answers:
• It can create contrast/juxtaposition by placing two opposing ideas side by side (1)
• It can extend a description by adding a second layer of detail (1)
• It can build tension or suspense by linking stillness with action (1)
• It can control pace by creating a pause shorter than a full stop (1)

b3e9f051-a4d9-4d22-ad48-2b26fb29f855.text: Explain why the following sentence uses the semicolon incorrectly: 'He ran through the forest; gasping for air.' Write a corrected version.
b3e9f051-a4d9-4d22-ad48-2b26fb29f855.marks:
Award up to 4 marks:
• Identifies that 'gasping for air' is not a complete/independent clause (1)
• Explains that both sides of a semicolon must be able to stand alone as sentences (1)
• Explains that 'gasping for air' is a fragment/phrase without a subject and main verb (1)
• Provides a correct version, e.g. 'He ran through the forest; his lungs burned with every breath' (1)

b3e9f051-a4d9-4d22-ad48-2b26fb29f855.text: Explain how a writer could use semicolons alongside other sentence structures (such as short sentences) to create a varied and effective piece of descriptive writing. Use examples in your answer.
b3e9f051-a4d9-4d22-ad48-2b26fb29f855.marks:
Award up to 6 marks across these areas:
• Explains that short sentences create sharp, punchy effects such as tension or shock (1)
• Explains that semicolons create longer, flowing sentences that can develop or contrast ideas (1)
• Explains that varying between short and semicolon-linked sentences shows control of pace (1)
• Provides an effective example of a short sentence used for impact (1)
• Provides an effective example of a semicolon sentence used for contrast, description, or suspense (1)
• Links this variation to the AO6 requirement for a range of sentence structures and punctuation (1)

b3e9f051-a4d9-4d22-ad48-2b26fb29f855.text:
Read the following extract from a student's creative writing:

'The house stood at the end of the lane. It was old. The windows were dark. The garden was overgrown. Nobody had lived there for years.'

Evaluate this extract and rewrite it to include at least one semicolon, explaining how your changes improve the writing.
b3e9f051-a4d9-4d22-ad48-2b26fb29f855.marks:
Award marks across two areas:

Evaluation of the original (up to 4 marks):
• Identifies that the original uses only simple/short sentences with full stops (1)
• Comments that this creates a repetitive, monotonous rhythm (1)
• Notes the lack of punctuation range limits the technical accuracy mark (1)
• Recognises that while short sentences can create tension, using only short sentences loses impact (1)

Rewrite and explanation (up to 5 marks):
• Rewrites with at least one correctly used semicolon (both halves are independent clauses) (1)
• Explains the effect of the semicolon (e.g. contrast, extension, tension) (1)
• Shows variation in sentence structure beyond just the semicolon (1)
• Explains how the rewrite demonstrates a wider range of punctuation for AO6 (1)
• Quality and sophistication of the rewritten passage (1)

b3e9f051-a4d9-4d22-ad48-2b26fb29f855.text:
Write a description suggested by the following image: a narrow street at night, lit by a single lamp.

In your writing, you must use at least two semicolons correctly and demonstrate a range of punctuation.

(24 marks for content and organisation, 16 marks for technical accuracy)
b3e9f051-a4d9-4d22-ad48-2b26fb29f855.marks:
AO5 Content and Organisation (24 marks) — assessed using AQA Level 1–4 descriptors:
• Top band (19–24) Compelling, convincing communication. Varied and inventive structural features. Extensive vocabulary with sustained crafting of linguistic devices.
• Upper-mid band (13–18) Consistently clear communication. Effective structural features. Increasingly sophisticated vocabulary chosen for effect.
• Lower-mid band (7–12) Some successful communication. Some use of structural features. Conscious use of vocabulary.
• Lower band (1–6) Simple, limited communication. Simple vocabulary and structural features.

AO6 Technical Accuracy (16 marks) — assessed using AQA Level 1–4 descriptors:
• Top band (13–16) Wide range of punctuation with high accuracy. Full range of sentence forms. Secure control of complex grammar. High accuracy in spelling.
• Upper-mid band (9–12) Range of punctuation mostly used with success. Variety of sentence forms. Generally accurate spelling.
• Lower-mid band (5–8) Some control of punctuation. Attempts variety of sentence forms. Some accurate spelling.
• Lower band (1–4) Some evidence of conscious punctuation. Simple sentence forms. Accurate basic spelling.

For this question, look specifically for:
• At least two correctly used semicolons (both halves must be independent clauses)
• Semicolons used for deliberate effect (contrast, extension, or tension)
• Range of other punctuation (commas, colons, dashes, ellipses, exclamation marks)
• Variation in sentence length and structure

e0ea09ff-1dc2-4afb-9c88-020747161d16.text: Write a letter to a newspaper editor arguing that the government should do more to support young people's mental health. Focus on using precise vocabulary and varied sentence structures.
e0ea09ff-1dc2-4afb-9c88-020747161d16.marks:
Content and Organisation (24 marks):
Top band (19–24) Extensive, ambitious vocabulary with sustained crafting. Varied, effective structural features with fluently linked ideas.
Upper-mid band (13–18) Chosen vocabulary with a range of successful linguistic devices.
Lower-mid band (7–12) Some appropriate vocabulary.
Lower band (1–6) Simple vocabulary.

Technical Accuracy (16 marks):
Top band (13–16) Wide range of punctuation used accurately, extensive ambitious vocabulary, varied sentence structures.
Upper-mid band (9–12) Range of punctuation mostly used accurately, increasingly sophisticated vocabulary.
Lower-mid band (5–8) Some controlled use of punctuation, varied vocabulary.
Lower band (1–4) Some evidence of punctuation, simple vocabulary.

e0ea09ff-1dc2-4afb-9c88-020747161d16.text: Rewrite the following sentence to make it more effective for an argument about climate change: 'Climate change is bad and we should do something about it.'
e0ea09ff-1dc2-4afb-9c88-020747161d16.marks:
Upper band (3-4): Demonstrates clear improvement with precise vocabulary, varied sentence structure, and explanation of why the revision is more effective (e.g. specificity, authority, impact).
Lower band (1-2): Some improvement but limited explanation.

e0ea09ff-1dc2-4afb-9c88-020747161d16.text: Identify two types of sentence structure that create different effects in non-fiction writing.
e0ea09ff-1dc2-4afb-9c88-020747161d16.marks: 1 mark per valid structure with its effect, up to 2 marks. Accept: short/simple for impact/emphasis, complex for development/sophistication, rhetorical question for engagement, exclamatory for emotion, etc.

e0ea09ff-1dc2-4afb-9c88-020747161d16.text: Explain how a writer's vocabulary choices should differ when writing for a broadsheet newspaper audience compared to a school magazine audience.
e0ea09ff-1dc2-4afb-9c88-020747161d16.marks:
Upper band (3-4): Clear explanation with examples showing how formality, complexity, and specialist terminology differ between audiences, with comment on why this matters.
Lower band (1-2): Some comment with limited examples.

e0ea09ff-1dc2-4afb-9c88-020747161d16.text: Analyse how using a variety of punctuation (semicolons, colons, dashes) can improve the quality of non-fiction writing.
e0ea09ff-1dc2-4afb-9c88-020747161d16.marks:
Top band (7-8): Perceptive analysis of how each punctuation mark creates specific effects (semicolons link related ideas, colons introduce explanations, dashes create dramatic parenthetical asides) with examples.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Clear analysis.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Some relevant comments.
Lower band (1-2): Simple identification.

e0ea09ff-1dc2-4afb-9c88-020747161d16.text: Evaluate the statement: 'The most effective non-fiction writing always uses the longest, most complex vocabulary possible.'
e0ea09ff-1dc2-4afb-9c88-020747161d16.marks:
Top band (10-12): Perceptive evaluation arguing that precision matters more than length, that overwriting alienates readers, and that the best vocabulary is suited to audience and purpose. Uses examples of effective simple and complex vocabulary.
Upper-mid band (7-9): Clear evaluation.
Lower-mid band (4-6): Some evaluation.
Lower band (1-3): Simple statements.

ff53b3d5-01ab-42e4-99dc-6e5c9954ed87.text: Identify two features of 19th-century fiction that make it different from modern writing.
ff53b3d5-01ab-42e4-99dc-6e5c9954ed87.marks: Any two from: longer sentences / more formal vocabulary / elaborate descriptions / serial publication format / archaic language / complex sentence structures. 1 mark for each correct feature identified.

ff53b3d5-01ab-42e4-99dc-6e5c9954ed87.text: Select one genre of 19th-century fiction and explain how you would recognise it in an unseen extract.
ff53b3d5-01ab-42e4-99dc-6e5c9954ed87.marks: 1 mark for identifying a genre (e.g. Gothic fiction, social realism, adventure, romance). 1 mark for a clear explanation of how to recognise it (e.g. Gothic fiction uses dark settings, supernatural elements, and a sense of fear or suspense).

ff53b3d5-01ab-42e4-99dc-6e5c9954ed87.text: Summarise the key Assessment Objectives tested in Paper 1 Section A and explain how they connect to the reading questions.
ff53b3d5-01ab-42e4-99dc-6e5c9954ed87.marks: identify and interpret explicit and implicit information (1 mark). analyse how writers use language and structure to achieve effects (1 mark). evaluate texts critically with textual references (1 mark). Connection: early questions focus on AO1 (identification), later questions on AO2 (analysis) and AO4 (evaluation) (1 mark). All three overlap — inference skills from AO1 feed into analysis and evaluation (1 mark).

ff53b3d5-01ab-42e4-99dc-6e5c9954ed87.text:
Read the following extract:

'The room was dark, save for the feeble glow of a single tallow candle. Its light flickered against the damp stone walls, casting shadows that seemed to move of their own accord. Somewhere above, a door creaked.'

Analyse how the writer uses language to create a particular atmosphere in this extract.
ff53b3d5-01ab-42e4-99dc-6e5c9954ed87.marks:
Top band (8–10) Perceptive analysis of language with well-integrated evidence. Shows detailed understanding of effects.
Upper-mid band (5–7) Clear analysis with appropriate evidence and some understanding of effects.
Lower-mid band (3–4) Some relevant comments on language with limited evidence.
Lower band (1–2) Simple identification of language features.

Expected points: 'feeble glow' suggests weakness and vulnerability; 'single tallow candle' implies poverty or isolation; 'flickered' connotes instability and uncertainty; 'damp stone walls' creates a cold, prison-like setting; 'seemed to move of their own accord' personifies shadows, suggesting the supernatural; 'creaked' is onomatopoeia creating suspense. Overall Gothic atmosphere of menace and unease.

ff53b3d5-01ab-42e4-99dc-6e5c9954ed87.text: A student said: 'Students who read the extract only once before answering are at a disadvantage.' To what extent do you agree? Use evidence from your understanding of the exam format to support your answer.
ff53b3d5-01ab-42e4-99dc-6e5c9954ed87.marks:
Top band (12–15) Perceptive evaluation with convincing reasoning.
Upper-mid band (8–11) Clear evaluation with relevant reasoning.
Lower-mid band (4–7) Some evaluation with basic reasoning.
Lower band (1–3) Simple response with limited reasoning.

Students may argue: agree — first read gives only surface meaning; second read allows annotation and deeper understanding of implicit meaning; questions test AO2 and AO4 which require close analysis that one read cannot provide. Partial agreement — strong readers may grasp enough on one read for lower-mark questions but still need re-reading for evaluation questions. Disagree — time pressure means some students prefer to read once and use question-directed re-reading instead.

ff53b3d5-01ab-42e4-99dc-6e5c9954ed87.text: You are given an unseen 19th-century fiction extract about a character arriving at a new place. Write a short imaginative description (approximately 150 words) that continues the scene, using at least two techniques commonly found in 19th-century fiction.
ff53b3d5-01ab-42e4-99dc-6e5c9954ed87.marks:
Content and Organisation (24 marks):
Top band (19–24) Compelling writing with sophisticated control of ideas and effective structural features.
Upper-mid band (13–18) Engaging writing with clear structure and well-chosen language.
Lower-mid band (7–12) Some successful writing with some structure.
Lower band (1–6) Simple writing with limited structure.

Technical Accuracy (16 marks):
Top band (13–16) Wide range of accurate sentence structures, spelling, and punctuation.
Upper-mid band (9–12) Mostly accurate with varied sentence structures.
Lower-mid band (5–8) Some accuracy with simple sentence structures.
Lower band (1–4) Limited accuracy.

Expected techniques: elaborate descriptions, longer complex sentences, formal register, vivid sensory detail, pathetic fallacy, symbolism.

15e1a8bc-2929-4595-bc93-f05d3f14b593.text: Starting with Act 1, Scene 3 (“Signor Antonio, many a time and oft”), explore how Shakespeare presents Shylock as a complex character. Write about the extract and the play as a whole.
15e1a8bc-2929-4595-bc93-f05d3f14b593.marks:
Top band (25–30 + 4 spelling/grammar)Analyses Shylock’s rhetoric in the extract (listing of abuses, the gaberdine, rhetorical questions), then tracks his complexity across the play: the bond, “Hath not a Jew eyes,” Jessica’s elopement, the trial, forced conversion. Explores victim vs villain duality. Embeds context: anti-Semitism, Elizabethan vs modern readings. Word-level analysis of key quotations.

Upper band (19–24 + 3)Thoughtful.
Upper-mid band (13–18 + 2)Clear.
Mid band (7–12 + 2)Some understanding.
Lower-mid band (3–6 + 1)Limited.

15e1a8bc-2929-4595-bc93-f05d3f14b593.text: Analyse Antonio’s metaphor “I am a tainted wether of the flock, / Meetest for death” (Act 4, Scene 1). What does it reveal about his character?
15e1a8bc-2929-4595-bc93-f05d3f14b593.marks:
Upper band (3-4): A wether is a castrated sheep — Antonio compares himself to something damaged and expendable. “Tainted” suggests corruption or impurity. “Meetest for death” shows he accepts death willingly, even eagerly. The metaphor is self-pitying and sacrificial, linking to his unexplained melancholy in Act 1. Some critics read this as Antonio’s desire for martyrdom to prove his love for Bassanio.
Lower band (1-2): Basic comment about Antonio accepting death.

15e1a8bc-2929-4595-bc93-f05d3f14b593.text: How does Shakespeare present the relationship between Bassanio and money throughout the play?
15e1a8bc-2929-4595-bc93-f05d3f14b593.marks:
Top band (7-8): Bassanio describes Portia’s wealth first (“richly left”), borrows from Antonio/Shylock to woo her, chooses lead (rejecting gold/silver = materialism), but gives away Portia’s ring carelessly. His quest depends on other people’s money. Shakespeare creates tension between his idealism (the casket choice) and his financial dependence. Links to the play’s wider theme: everyone is entangled in financial relationships.
Top band (5–6) Clear analysis.
Mid band (3–4) Some points.
Lower band (1–2) Simple.

15e1a8bc-2929-4595-bc93-f05d3f14b593.text: Explore how Shakespeare presents Jessica’s journey from Shylock’s daughter to Lorenzo’s wife. Is she liberated or diminished?
15e1a8bc-2929-4595-bc93-f05d3f14b593.marks:
Top band (7-8): Jessica gains a Christian husband and wealth but loses her identity, faith, and family. She trades Leah’s ring carelessly (internalised contempt for Jewish culture). In Act 5, she is “never merry” — not fully accepted in Christian society. Shakespeare presents her as caught between worlds: liberated from her father’s household but displaced and melancholic.
Top band (5–6) Clear analysis.
Mid band (3–4) Some points.
Lower band (1–2) Simple.

15e1a8bc-2929-4595-bc93-f05d3f14b593.text: Analyse why Shakespeare makes Shylock and Antonio mirror each other. What does this structural choice achieve?
15e1a8bc-2929-4595-bc93-f05d3f14b593.marks:
Upper band (3-4): Both are outsiders (Shylock as Jew, Antonio as melancholic bachelor). Both define themselves through money. Both suffer loss (Shylock: daughter, faith; Antonio: wealth, Bassanio). The mirroring prevents the audience from seeing one as purely good and the other as purely evil. It reinforces the theme of appearance vs reality: the Christian and the Jew are more alike than either would admit.
Lower band (1-2): Basic comment about similarities.

Top band (17-20) Sophisticated analysis. Discusses the symbolism of meeting at the ‘ruined place’, Estella’s metaphor ‘bent and broken’ into a better shape, the ambiguity of ‘I saw no shadow of another parting from her.’ Analyses the shift from decay to open space as they leave. Notes the contrast with earlier Satis House scenes.
Upper band (13-16) Developed analysis.
Top band (9-12): Some analytical comments.
Upper-mid band (5-8): Basic.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Surface-level.
Lower band (1-2): Minimal.

02133c93-0327-4b90-bb65-58048e6f710e.text: Explore how Dickens presents Joe Gargery as the moral heart of Great Expectations.
02133c93-0327-4b90-bb65-58048e6f710e.marks:
Top band (17-20) Critical exploration across the whole text. Analyses Joe’s consistent goodness: protecting Pip from Mrs Joe, being ‘ever the best of friends’, dignified withdrawal from London, nursing Pip during illness, paying his debts. Contrasts Joe’s unchanging loyalty with Pip’s fluctuating moral character. Discusses what Joe represents: that true gentility is moral, not social.
Upper band (13-16) Thoughtful with evidence.
Top band (9-12): Clear with some analysis.
Upper-mid band (5-8): Basic.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Limited.
Lower band (1-2): Simple.

02133c93-0327-4b90-bb65-58048e6f710e.text: Read the following extract from Chapter 57, in which Pip wakes from his fever to find Joe at his bedside. How does Dickens use language to present Joe’s kindness and Pip’s emotional response?
02133c93-0327-4b90-bb65-58048e6f710e.marks:
Top band (17-20) Perceptive analysis. Discusses Joe calling Pip ‘old chap’ (return to childhood intimacy), the tenderness of the nursing, Pip’s tears of gratitude. Analyses the structural parallel: Joe nursed Pip as a child and does so again now, bookending the novel. Explores the pathos of Joe slipping away and calling Pip ‘Sir’ as he recovers.
Upper band (13-16) Developed analysis.
Top band (9-12): Clear points.
Upper-mid band (5-8): Some understanding.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Limited.
Lower band (1-2): Minimal.

02133c93-0327-4b90-bb65-58048e6f710e.text: Explore how Dickens uses the two endings of Great Expectations to present different views of Pip’s future. Which ending do you find more convincing?
02133c93-0327-4b90-bb65-58048e6f710e.marks:
Top band (17-20) Convincing personal response. Compares both endings: original (bleak, realistic, consistent with themes) versus revised (ambiguous, hopeful, Estella transformed by suffering). Analyses key language from the revised ending. Offers a personal judgement supported by evidence. Discusses the novel’s themes to argue which ending is more appropriate.
Upper band (13-16) Thoughtful comparison with evidence.
Top band (9-12): Clear response addressing both endings.
Upper-mid band (5-8): Some understanding of the difference.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Limited.
Lower band (1-2): Brief.

fafab0d7-c6e1-4d77-aa35-ba2796413028.marks:
Top band (17-20) Perceptive analysis. Explores the dual meaning of ‘made me’ (created/manufactured). Analyses Estella’s cold, precise language as a product of her upbringing. Discusses how Dickens presents Miss Havisham’s dawning horror. Links to the theme of nurture versus nature: Estella’s cruelty is taught, not inherent.
Upper band (13-16) Developed with evidence.
Top band (9-12): Clear understanding.
Upper-mid band (5-8): Basic points.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Limited.

Top band (17-20) Critical exploration across the novel. Traces Magwitch from terrifying convict (Chapter 1) to sympathetic benefactor (Chapter 39) to loving father figure (Chapter 56). Analyses key quotations (‘what the Devil was I to do?’, ‘I lived rough’). Compares Magwitch with Compeyson to show the gentleman is the true villain. Links to Victorian attitudes to crime and class.
Upper band (13-16) Thoughtful with evidence.
Top band (9-12): Clear response.

Analyses Joe’s actions (protecting, nurturing, forgiving) as evidence of genuine goodness. Explores the irony that the uneducated blacksmith is morally superior to every ‘gentleman’ in the novel.

Top band (17-20) Convincing exploration. Discusses her backstory (jilted by Compeyson), her frozen grief, her use of Estella as revenge. Analyses her genuine remorse (‘What have I done!’) alongside the irreversible damage she caused. Explores the fire as symbolic destruction. Argues that Dickens presents her as a victim who became a perpetrator.
Upper band (13-16) Thoughtful response.

fafab0d7-c6e1-4d77-aa35-ba2796413028.text: Read the following extract in which the older Pip reflects on his younger self’s behaviour. How does Dickens use narrative voice to present Pip’s self-criticism?
fafab0d7-c6e1-4d77-aa35-ba2796413028.marks:
Top band (17-20) Critical analysis of narrative technique. Discusses the dual perspective: young Pip’s actions versus older Pip’s judgement. Analyses the confessional tone, the use of direct address, and the self-condemnation in ‘too cowardly to do what I knew to be right.’ Explores how retrospective narration creates sympathy and moral awareness simultaneously.
Upper band (13-16) Developed with evidence.

Upper-mid band (5-8): Some understanding.

fafab0d7-c6e1-4d77-aa35-ba2796413028.text: Explore how Dickens uses the characters of Biddy and Herbert Pocket to present alternatives to Pip’s version of the good life.

8a10c6c4-3fdf-4a37-8b45-ba12c594905f.text: Explore how Dickens uses the quotation “I am as light as a feather, I am as happy as an angel, I am as merry as a schoolboy” to present Scrooge’s transformation.
8a10c6c4-3fdf-4a37-8b45-ba12c594905f.marks:
Upper band (3-4): Detailed analysis linking similes to transformation. E.g. ‘Light as a feather’ suggests Scrooge’s burden of guilt has been lifted. ‘Happy as an angel’ implies spiritual joy and moral purity. ‘Merry as a schoolboy’ links to recovered innocence — the child he was in Stave 2. These directly contrast the Stave 1 similes (‘hard as flint’, ‘solitary as an oyster’), showing the completeness of his change.
Lower band (1-2): Basic comment on the similes with limited analysis. E.g. These show Scrooge is now happy.

8a10c6c4-3fdf-4a37-8b45-ba12c594905f.text:
Read the following extract from Stave 5:

“He dressed himself ‘all in his best,’ and at last got out into the streets. The people were by this time pouring forth, as he had seen them with the Ghost of Christmas Present; and walking with his hands behind him, Scrooge regarded every one with a delighted smile. He looked so irresistibly pleasant, in a word, that three or four good-humoured fellows said, ‘Good morning, sir! A merry Christmas to you!’”

Starting with this extract, explore how Dickens presents Scrooge’s transformation and its effect on the people around him.
8a10c6c4-3fdf-4a37-8b45-ba12c594905f.marks:
Top band (7-8): Perceptive analysis of language and structure. Contrasts with Stave 1 where ‘nobody ever stopped him in the street’ and ‘even the blind men’s dogs’ avoided him. ‘Irresistibly pleasant’ suggests his inner change is visible externally. ‘Delighted smile’ shows genuine joy, not performance. Links to Dickens’s message: when individuals change, their community responds positively. The cyclical structure means the reader measures this against Stave 1.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Clear analysis with relevant textual contrast.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Supported comments with some comparison to Stave 1.
Lower band (1-2): Simple comments about Scrooge being happy.

8a10c6c4-3fdf-4a37-8b45-ba12c594905f.text:
Read the following extract from the end of Stave 5:

“Scrooge was better than his word. He did it all, and infinitely more; and to Tiny Tim, who did NOT die, he was a second father. He became as good a friend, as good a master, and as good a man, as the good old city knew.”

Starting with this extract, explore how Dickens presents the theme of redemption in A Christmas Carol.
8a10c6c4-3fdf-4a37-8b45-ba12c594905f.marks:
Top band (7-8): Perceptive analysis of language, structure, and context. Explores the repetition of ‘good’ (five times) as emphasising completeness of change. ‘Better than his word’ means actions exceeded promises. ‘Second father’ to Tiny Tim shows Scrooge accepting social responsibility — the key message of the novella. ‘Did NOT die’ (Dickens’s emphasis) is the emotional reward for both Scrooge and the reader. Links to Victorian context: Dickens arguing that wealthy people can save lives through generosity.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Clear analysis with relevant references and some context.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Supported comments with some language analysis.
Lower band (1-2): Simple comments about redemption.

8a10c6c4-3fdf-4a37-8b45-ba12c594905f.text: How does Dickens use the cyclical structure of A Christmas Carol to reinforce his message about the possibility of change?
8a10c6c4-3fdf-4a37-8b45-ba12c594905f.marks:
Top band (26-30): Convincing analysis exploring how Stave 5 mirrors Stave 1 in setting (weather), characters (carol singer, charity collector, Fred, Bob), and tone. Discusses how the cyclical structure allows the reader to measure transformation precisely. Analyses specific contrasts: ‘cold, bleak, biting’ becomes ‘Golden sunlight; Heavenly sky’; rejection of charity becomes generous donation; cruelty to Bob becomes ‘I’ll raise your salary.’ Links to Dickens’s purpose: the structure is optimistic — wrongs can be put right, people can change.
Upper band (21-25): Thoughtful, developed response with well-chosen references and clear analysis of language, form and structure.
Upper-mid band (16-20): Clear analysis with relevant structural comparisons.
Mid band (11-15): Some explained comments with relevant references and limited analysis of methods.
Lower-mid band (6-10): Supported comments with some structural awareness.
Lower band (1-5): Simple statements about the beginning and ending.

8a10c6c4-3fdf-4a37-8b45-ba12c594905f.text:
Starting with the following extract from Stave 5, explore how Dickens presents the importance of generosity and social responsibility in A Christmas Carol.

“‘My dear sir,’ said Scrooge, quickening his pace, and taking the old gentleman by both his hands. ‘How do you do? I hope you succeeded yesterday. It was very kind of you. A merry Christmas to you, sir!’”

Write about:
• how Dickens presents generosity in this extract
• how Dickens presents generosity and social responsibility in the novella as a whole.
[30 marks]
8a10c6c4-3fdf-4a37-8b45-ba12c594905f.marks:
Top band (26-30) Convincing, critical response. Analyses ‘quickening his pace’ as urgency to do good — contrasting his former reluctance. ‘Both his hands’ shows warmth and physical connection vs Stave 1 isolation. ‘Back-payments’ implies acknowledgement of years of neglect. Explores generosity across the novella: Fezziwig’s party (costs little, gives much), the Cratchits (generous in spirit despite poverty), Fred (offers love despite rejection). Links to Dickens’s social purpose: the novella as a call to wealthy Victorians to take responsibility for poverty. References Malthus, the Poor Law, and Dickens’s own experience of poverty.
Upper band (21-25) Thoughtful response with clear analysis and contextual links.
Top band (16-20): Clear understanding with explained comments.
Upper-mid band (11-15): Some explained comments with references.
Lower-mid band (6-10): Supported comments with some textual reference.
Lower band (1-5): Simple comments with limited reference.

8a10c6c4-3fdf-4a37-8b45-ba12c594905f.text: Explore how Dickens uses the character of Scrooge in Stave 5 to show that redemption is possible for everyone. Refer to specific moments in the text.
8a10c6c4-3fdf-4a37-8b45-ba12c594905f.marks:
Top band (26-30): Convincing analysis. Explores Scrooge’s emotional awakening (‘laughing and crying in the same breath’), his declaration to live in ‘Past, Present, and Future’, and his concrete actions (turkey, donation, Fred’s dinner, Bob’s raise). Analyses the narrator’s comment that ‘some people laughed to see the alteration in him, but he let them laugh’ — showing resilience in his new life. Links to Dickens’s message: redemption requires action, not just feeling. References the Victorian context of social reform.
Upper band (21-25): Thoughtful, developed response with well-chosen references and clear analysis of language, form and structure.
Upper-mid band (16-20): Clear analysis with relevant examples.
Mid band (11-15): Some explained comments with relevant references and limited analysis of methods.
Lower-mid band (6-10): Supported comments with some textual reference.
Lower band (1-5): Simple statements about Scrooge changing.

0872ff4f-b3c3-45ea-9ba2-85d14976c3bf.text: Read the following extract from Chapter 23, beginning ‘Do you think, because I am poor, obscure, plain, and little, I am soulless and heartless?’ Explore how Brontë uses language to present Jane’s feelings about class and equality in this extract.
0872ff4f-b3c3-45ea-9ba2-85d14976c3bf.marks:
Top band (17-20) Judicious, well-chosen references integrated into a sophisticated analysis. Examines: the rhetorical question directly challenging Rochester and the reader, the listing of ‘poor, obscure, plain, and little’ as Jane reclaiming these as strengths rather than weaknesses, the shift to the assertive ‘I am’ construction. 2ce4c909-c966-44a5-92b3-87702c31c401.text: Analyse the significance of Don John’s line “I am a plain-dealing villain” (Act 1, Scene 3). What does it reveal about his role in the play?
2ce4c909-c966-44a5-92b3-87702c31c401.marks:
Upper band (3-4): “Plain-dealing” is ironic: Don John deals in deception, not honesty. The oxymoron of an honest villain signals his function as the play’s catalyst. Shakespeare does not develop his psychology — he exists to test other characters. His self-awareness (“I am”) contrasts with characters who lack self-knowledge. Elizabethan audience: a stock villain; modern audience: an underdeveloped motivation.
Lower band (1-2): Basic comment about Don John being the villain.

2ce4c909-c966-44a5-92b3-87702c31c401.text: How does Shakespeare use the ‘haggard’ metaphor in Beatrice’s gulling scene (Act 3, Scene 1) to explore ideas about gender?
2ce4c909-c966-44a5-92b3-87702c31c401.marks:
Top band (7-8): A haggard is a wild female hawk that needs taming. Hero uses it to criticise Beatrice’s independence as excessive. This reflects patriarchal assumptions: female independence is a problem to be corrected. But Beatrice’s response (“Taming my wild heart to thy loving hand”) shows she internalises the metaphor willingly. Tension: does love tame her or does she choose to change? Context: the shrew-taming tradition in Elizabethan literature.
Top band (5–6) Clear.
Mid band (3–4) Some.
Lower band (1–2) Simple.

2ce4c909-c966-44a5-92b3-87702c31c401.text: Explore how Shakespeare uses the parallel structure of benevolent and malicious deceptions to develop the theme of ‘noting’ in Much Ado About Nothing.
2ce4c909-c966-44a5-92b3-87702c31c401.marks:

Don John’s trick: Claudio sees the window scene and believes it because his trust is shallow. Same mechanism, opposite outcomes. Shakespeare questions the reliability of observation. Links to the title’s “noting/nothing” pun. The play suggests interpretation, not truth, determines outcomes.
Top band (5–6) Clear.
Mid band (3–4) Some.
Lower band (1–2) Simple.

The exclamation marks and formal structure (“farewelladieu”) give the moment ceremonial weight — she is publicly renouncing her old self.

ca408a9a-327d-4627-9ffe-55f5b713545d.text: Read the following quotation: 'for the time being, certainly, it had been found necessary to make a readjustment of rations.' How does Orwell use language to present the pigs' manipulation in this quotation?
ca408a9a-327d-4627-9ffe-55f5b713545d.marks:
Upper band (3-4): Detailed analysis. E.g. 'Readjustment' is a euphemism for 'reduction' — Squealer uses bureaucratic language to disguise suffering. 'For the time being' implies the cut is temporary, when it is clearly permanent. 'Had been found necessary' uses passive voice to avoid attributing the decision to anyone — nobody is responsible. The phrase 'certainly' adds false confidence, as though the decision is beyond question. Orwell uses this understated language to mirror totalitarian propaganda: making terrible decisions sound reasonable.
Lower band (1-2): Basic comments. E.g. The pigs are reducing food but using nice words to make it sound better.

Top band (7-8): Perceptive, detailed analysis. The lettering on the van — 'Horse Slaughterer and Glue Boiler' — is blunt and brutal, contrasting with Squealer's gentle lie about a 'hospital.' Boxer's inability to kick his way out ('his strength had left him') is heartbreaking: the strongest animal on the farm is now powerless. Clover's desperate scream creates pathos. This betrayal is the culmination of a pattern: the pigs have been betraying the animals since they took the milk in Chapter Two. Each betrayal is larger: milk → beds → executions → Boxer's murder. The revolution itself is a betrayal of Old Major's vision. Context: parallels the Soviet state's abandonment of workers who had built the nation.

ca408a9a-327d-4627-9ffe-55f5b713545d.text: How far does Orwell present Boxer as a sympathetic character in Animal Farm? Write about: what Boxer says and does, and how far Orwell presents Boxer as a sympathetic character.
ca408a9a-327d-4627-9ffe-55f5b713545d.marks:
Top band (26–30 marks + up to 4 spelling/grammar)Critical, exploratory response. Boxer is Orwell's most sympathetic creation. His physical strength ('equal to that of all the rest of the animals put together'), his selfless mottos ('I will work harder'), and his genuine belief in the revolution's ideals make him deeply admirable. His collapse while hauling stone and his innocent hope for retirement create powerful pathos. The scene at the knacker's van is devastating precisely because the reader has grown to love Boxer. HOWEVER — Orwell also invites criticism. Boxer's second motto, 'Napoleon is always right', represents the danger of blind loyalty. His refusal to think critically enables the pigs' tyranny. When Boxer accepts Squealer's lies about Snowball despite his own memories, he surrenders his moral agency. Orwell creates sympathy to make a political point: the exploitation of loyal, uncritical workers is one of totalitarianism's greatest crimes. Context: Boxer parallels Stakhanovite workers — praised as heroes but ultimately expendable.

ca408a9a-327d-4627-9ffe-55f5b713545d.text: Starting with the moment when Squealer explains that Boxer died peacefully in hospital and the animals are 'enormously relieved', explore how Orwell presents lies and deception in Animal Farm. Squealer's claim that the van 'had previously belonged to a knacker' and the vet 'had not yet painted over the old name' is an absurdly transparent lie — yet the animals are 'enormously relieved.' Their relief reveals how desperate they are to believe the lie rather than face the truth. This mirrors a pattern: the animals have been accepting increasingly outrageous lies throughout the novel (Snowball as traitor, changed commandments). Orwell's flat, understated narration forces the reader to supply the outrage. ca408a9a-327d-4627-9ffe-55f5b713545d.text: How does Orwell use the character of Benjamin to explore ideas about political responsibility in Animal Farm?
ca408a9a-327d-4627-9ffe-55f5b713545d.marks:
Top band (11-12) Critical, exploratory response. Benjamin is one of the most complex characters in Animal Farm. He represents the educated cynic who sees through propaganda but refuses to act. His cynicism ('Donkeys live a long time') masks a deeper despair about the possibility of change. Unlike Boxer, Benjamin can read and think critically — but he wastes these gifts through inaction. His scream of 'Fools! Fools!' at the knacker's van is the novel's most tragic moment of self-awareness: he finally acts, but too late. Orwell suggests that Benjamin's silence was as harmful as Squealer's lies — both enable tyranny, one actively and one passively. This is a warning to the reader: political apathy has consequences.

ca408a9a-327d-4627-9ffe-55f5b713545d.text: How does Orwell use the pigs' increasing privileges in Chapter Nine to develop the theme of inequality in Animal Farm?
ca408a9a-327d-4627-9ffe-55f5b713545d.marks:
Top band (11-12) Critical, exploratory response. Chapter Nine catalogues the pigs' privileges with devastating precision: beer rations, separate schooling for piglets, green ribbons on Sundays. Napoleon drinks from the 'Crown Derby soup tureen' — an object associated with human luxury. The 'Republic' with a single candidate is Orwell's most pointed political satire. Each privilege directly contradicts a principle of Animalism: equality is replaced by hierarchy, communal living by class separation. The 'spontaneous demonstrations' are involuntary celebrations of their own oppression. Orwell shows that revolution does not eliminate inequality — it merely replaces one elite with another. f8b7c82c-cfa0-4f3b-8a46-87a845392f30.text: 'Orwell creates a shocking and unexpected ending to Animal Farm.' How far do you agree with this statement? Write about: what happens towards the end of the novel, and how Orwell presents the ending.
f8b7c82c-cfa0-4f3b-8a46-87a845392f30.marks:
Top band (26–30 marks + up to 4 spelling/grammar)Critical, exploratory response. Students should argue BOTH sides. The ending IS shocking: the image of pigs walking on hind legs, carrying whips, and drinking with humans is viscerally disturbing. The final line ('impossible to say which was which') delivers a powerful emotional punch. HOWEVER, the ending is arguably NOT unexpected — Orwell foreshadows it throughout: the pigs take the milk (Ch.2), move into the farmhouse (Ch.6), walk upright is foreshadowed by the gradual humanisation of the pigs. The fable structure means the moral is inevitable. Orwell's use of dramatic irony means the reader has seen the corruption building — it is the ANIMALS for whom the ending is shocking, not the reader. The real shock is how completely the revolution has failed — the farm is worse than under Jones ('the lower animals did more work and received less food'). Context: Orwell is critiquing Stalinism specifically — the ending mirrors how the USSR under Stalin became as oppressive as the Tsarist regime it replaced.

f8b7c82c-cfa0-4f3b-8a46-87a845392f30.text: Starting with the final chapter, explore how Orwell presents the failure of the rebellion in Animal Farm. Write about: the ways the rebellion fails, and how Orwell presents the failure of the rebellion.
f8b7c82c-cfa0-4f3b-8a46-87a845392f30.marks:

Chapter Ten presents the failure as total: commandments reduced to a paradox, the farm renamed 'Manor Farm', pigs walking upright with whips, Pilkington praising the 'lower animals' for working harder for less food. The word 'revolution' literally means 'a complete turn' — the farm has turned full circle. Orwell traces the failure through structural choices: from Old Major's utopian vision (Ch.1) through gradual corruption to complete reversal (Ch.10). The rebellion fails because: no democratic accountability, no free press, no education for the masses, and blind loyalty (Boxer's 'Napoleon is always right'). Context: Orwell believed the Russian Revolution's ideals were sound but were betrayed by Stalinist totalitarianism.

f8b7c82c-cfa0-4f3b-8a46-87a845392f30.text: How does Orwell use what happens to the Seven Commandments to explore ideas about the revolution? Write about: what happens to the Seven Commandments, and how Orwell uses the Seven Commandments to explore ideas about the revolution.
f8b7c82c-cfa0-4f3b-8a46-87a845392f30.marks:
Top band (26–30 marks + up to 4 spelling/grammar)Critical, exploratory response. The commandments function as a barometer of the revolution's health. Initially, they represent Old Major's vision of equality and freedom — no beds, no alcohol, no killing, all animals equal. Each alteration represents a specific betrayal: 'with sheets' allows the pigs to enjoy human luxuries; 'without cause' permits political murder; 'to excess' permits drinking. The animals cannot challenge the changes because they cannot read — Orwell's point about the importance of education. The final paradox ('some animals are more equal than others') is the logical endpoint: a statement that means the exact opposite of the original principle. Structurally, the commandments provide the novel's framework — from seven principles of equality to one statement of inequality. Context: parallels the Soviet Constitution of 1936, which promised rights that were never honoured.

f8b7c82c-cfa0-4f3b-8a46-87a845392f30.text: Starting with the scene where Napoleon carries a whip and the sheep chant 'Four legs good, two legs better,' explore how Orwell presents the theme of power and control in Animal Farm. f8b7c82c-cfa0-4f3b-8a46-87a845392f30.marks:

The whip is the most powerful symbol in the novel — it was Jones's tool of oppression and now Napoleon carries it, completing his transformation into a human tyrant. The sheep's chant has been inverted: 'two legs better' replaces 'two legs bad,' showing how propaganda can make people support the exact opposite of their original beliefs. The sheep have been retrained by Squealer — their mindless repetition drowns out dissent, just as it did in earlier chapters. Across the novel, power is maintained through three methods: propaganda (Squealer), violence (the dogs), and the suppression of education (the animals cannot read). The ending shows all three working in combination.

Lower band (1-2): Simple comments.

f8b7c82c-cfa0-4f3b-8a46-87a845392f30.text: How does Orwell use events in Animal Farm to explore ideas about revolution? Write about: some of the events in the book, and how Orwell uses these events to explore ideas about revolution.
f8b7c82c-cfa0-4f3b-8a46-87a845392f30.marks:
Top band (11-12) Critical, exploratory response. The Rebellion (Ch.2) is Orwell's depiction of a spontaneous popular uprising — it happens 'almost before they knew what was happening,' suggesting revolutions begin with genuine idealism. The Battle of the Cowshed (Ch.4) shows the revolution defending itself. But from Chapter Five onwards, the revolution is hijacked: Napoleon's dogs represent military force, Squealer represents propaganda, and the changing commandments represent the erosion of founding principles. Each event moves the farm further from Old Major's vision. The ending — pigs and humans indistinguishable — shows Orwell's central argument: revolution without democratic safeguards produces new tyrants. The literal meaning of 'revolution' (a full turn) is fulfilled: the farm returns to where it started. Context: Orwell was critiquing not revolution itself but how the Russian Revolution was corrupted by Stalinist totalitarianism.
Upper band (9-10) Thoughtful response.
Top band (7-8): Clear response.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Explained response.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Supported response.
Lower band (1-2): Simple response.

d0f7225a-a197-4e0b-8330-a68fab3092af.text: Identify one key technique relevant to tone and register.
d0f7225a-a197-4e0b-8330-a68fab3092af.marks: 1 mark for correctly identifying a relevant technique with brief reference to the text or concept.

d0f7225a-a197-4e0b-8330-a68fab3092af.text: Select two examples from the extract that relate to tone and register.

d0f7225a-a197-4e0b-8330-a68fab3092af.text: Summarise the key points about tone and register covered in this lesson.
d0f7225a-a197-4e0b-8330-a68fab3092af.marks: 1 mark per valid point up to 5 marks. Points should demonstrate understanding of the core concepts.

d0f7225a-a197-4e0b-8330-a68fab3092af.text: Analyse how a writer applies the skills covered in 'Tone and Register' to create effects. Use evidence.
d0f7225a-a197-4e0b-8330-a68fab3092af.marks:
Top band (8-10): Sophisticated analysis with perceptive comments on effects. Precise evidence, accurate terminology.
Upper-mid band (5-7): Clear analysis with relevant examples.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Some relevant comments.
Lower band (1-2): Simple identification.

d0f7225a-a197-4e0b-8330-a68fab3092af.text: Compare how two writers approach tone and register. Refer to their methods.
d0f7225a-a197-4e0b-8330-a68fab3092af.marks:
Top band (8-10): Perceptive comparison with integrated evidence.
Upper-mid band (5-7): Clear comparison with relevant evidence.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Some comparison.

d0f7225a-a197-4e0b-8330-a68fab3092af.text: Produce a piece of writing that demonstrates the skills covered in 'Tone and Register.'
d0f7225a-a197-4e0b-8330-a68fab3092af.marks:
Content and Organisation (12 marks):
Top band (10–12) Compelling, convincing communication with extensive vocabulary and a secure sense of form, audience and purpose.
Upper-mid band (7–9) Consistent, clear communication with vocabulary chosen for effect and a register suited to the reader.
Lower-mid band (4–6) Mostly successful communication with some awareness of form, audience and purpose.

47dbf20b-984a-49a3-b4a7-9e39a3659f64.text: Starting with Act 2, Scene 3 (Benedick’s gulling scene), explore how Shakespeare presents the theme of deception in Much Ado About Nothing. Write about the extract and the play as a whole.
47dbf20b-984a-49a3-b4a7-9e39a3659f64.marks:
Top band (25–30 + 4 spelling/grammar)Analyses the gulling mechanism (staged conversation, Benedick’s instant belief, comic reversal). Links to the parallel deceptions: Beatrice’s gulling, Don John’s trick, the Friar’s plan, the masked ball. Explores the paradox: deception creates love and destroys it. Embeds context: the “noting/nothing” pun, the unreliability of observation, Elizabethan theatre’s interest in performance and reality. Evaluative: deception is morally neutral — outcomes depend on interpretation.

Upper band (19–24 + 3)Thoughtful.
Upper-mid band (13–18 + 2)Clear.
Mid band (7–12 + 2)Some.
Lower-mid band (3–6 + 1)Limited.
Lower band (1–2 + 1)Simple.

47dbf20b-984a-49a3-b4a7-9e39a3659f64.text: Explore how Shakespeare presents the theme of honour in Much Ado About Nothing. Refer to at least two characters.
47dbf20b-984a-49a3-b4a7-9e39a3659f64.marks:
Top band (25–30 + 4 spelling/grammar)Male honour: Claudio’s public shaming restores his reputation; Benedick’s challenge redefines honour as moral courage. Female honour: Hero’s chastity = family property; Leonato wishes her dead when it’s questioned. Analyses how the honour system enables injustice. Embeds context: Elizabethan honour codes, patriarchal values, the public nature of shame. Explores whether Shakespeare endorses or critiques the system.

Upper band (19–24 + 3)Thoughtful.
Upper-mid band (13–18 + 2)Clear.
Mid band (7–12 + 2)Some.
Lower-mid band (3–6 + 1)Limited.
Lower band (1–2 + 1)Simple.

47dbf20b-984a-49a3-b4a7-9e39a3659f64.text: Analyse how the title Much Ado About Nothing encapsulates the play’s central themes.
47dbf20b-984a-49a3-b4a7-9e39a3659f64.marks:
Upper band (3-4): “Nothing”: the crisis is based on a lie (Hero is innocent), so the “ado” is about nothing real. “Noting”: every plot depends on observing/eavesdropping (gulling, window trick, Dogberry). “Much ado”: small deceptions have disproportionate consequences. The title captures deception, the unreliability of observation, and the gap between appearance and reality in a single phrase.
Lower band (1-2): Basic comment about the title meaning a fuss about nothing.

47dbf20b-984a-49a3-b4a7-9e39a3659f64.text: How does Shakespeare use the contrast between prose and verse to develop character and emotion in Much Ado About Nothing?
47dbf20b-984a-49a3-b4a7-9e39a3659f64.marks:
Top band (7-8): Beatrice and Benedick speak in witty prose during the merry war (informal, equal, comic). Beatrice shifts to verse in her gulling response (“Contempt, farewell!” — emotional depth, sincerity). Claudio speaks in formal verse about Hero (conventional, performative). Hero speaks little in either mode (silenced). Dogberry mangles prose (language unreliable). Shakespeare uses form to signal emotional state: verse = sincerity, prose = wit or social performance.
Top band (5–6) Clear.
Mid band (3–4) Some.
Lower band (1–2) Simple.

47dbf20b-984a-49a3-b4a7-9e39a3659f64.text: Explore how Shakespeare presents different types of love in Much Ado About Nothing. Which is presented as strongest, and why?
47dbf20b-984a-49a3-b4a7-9e39a3659f64.marks:
Top band (7-8): Conventional love (Claudio/Hero): visual, fragile, destroyed by false appearance. Unconventional love (Beatrice/Benedick): verbal, equal, survives “Kill Claudio.” Familial love (Leonato/Hero): destroyed by honour culture. Friendship (Don Pedro/Claudio): enables both deception and pack mentality. B&B’s love is strongest because it is tested morally, not just visually. Shakespeare argues that love based on knowledge and equality outlasts love based on appearance.
Top band (5–6) Clear.
Mid band (3–4) Some.
Lower band (1–2) Simple.

47dbf20b-984a-49a3-b4a7-9e39a3659f64.text: Analyse how Shakespeare uses the Friar’s plan to explore the paradox that truth requires deception in Much Ado About Nothing.
47dbf20b-984a-49a3-b4a7-9e39a3659f64.marks:
Upper band (3-4): The Friar fakes Hero’s death to reveal the truth about her innocence — a lie that serves justice. This mirrors the gulling scenes (lies that create love) and inverts Don John’s trick (a lie that destroys). Shakespeare suggests that in a world where observation fails, managed deception is the only route to truth. The Friar reads Hero’s blush correctly (“a thousand blushing apparitions”) when the men misread it.
Lower band (1-2): Basic comment about the Friar’s plan.

238a6f06-3a7d-4299-9bc0-9a53f27e4b5a.text: Identify the punctuation error in this sentence: 'The park is essential to the community, it should not be closed.'
238a6f06-3a7d-4299-9bc0-9a53f27e4b5a.marks: Comma splice — two independent clauses joined by only a comma. Should be a semicolon, full stop, or conjunction. 1 mark.

238a6f06-3a7d-4299-9bc0-9a53f27e4b5a.text: Select one word from this sentence that could be upgraded and suggest a more precise alternative: 'The council's decision was very bad and has made a lot of people angry.'
238a6f06-3a7d-4299-9bc0-9a53f27e4b5a.marks: 'bad' → 'reckless,' 'detrimental,' or 'catastrophic' (1 mark). Explanation: the upgrade adds precision and emotional weight appropriate to persuasive writing (1 mark). Also accept 'a lot of' → 'thousands of' or 'the vast majority of.'

238a6f06-3a7d-4299-9bc0-9a53f27e4b5a.text: Summarise the key differences between a Level 2 and Level 4 response for AO6 (SPaG).
238a6f06-3a7d-4299-9bc0-9a53f27e4b5a.marks: Lower-mid band: limited punctuation range (1), some errors that occasionally hinder meaning (1). Top band: wide range of punctuation used accurately (1), varied sentence forms for effect (1), ambitious vocabulary choices (1).

238a6f06-3a7d-4299-9bc0-9a53f27e4b5a.text:
Rewrite this paragraph using a semicolon, a colon, and varied sentence lengths:

'School lunches are unhealthy. There are too many processed foods. Students should have healthier options. This would help them concentrate better in the afternoon.'
238a6f06-3a7d-4299-9bc0-9a53f27e4b5a.marks:
Top band (8–10) All three punctuation marks used correctly; clear sentence variety; improved vocabulary.
Upper-mid band (5–7) Two marks used correctly.
Lower-mid band (3–4) One mark attempted.
Lower band (1–2) Simple rewrite.

Example: 'The problem is clear: school lunches are dominated by processed food. Students deserve healthier options; better nutrition would sharpen afternoon concentration and improve academic performance. This is not a luxury. It is a necessity.'

238a6f06-3a7d-4299-9bc0-9a53f27e4b5a.text: 'SPaG is the least important part of Paper 2 because ideas matter more than spelling.' To what extent do you agree?
238a6f06-3a7d-4299-9bc0-9a53f27e4b5a.marks:
Top band (12–15) Perceptive — recognises spelling/grammar and ideas are interdependent.
Upper-mid band (8–11) Clear.
Lower-mid band (4–7) Some.
Lower band (1–3) Simple.

Disagree: 16 marks (40% of writing) is massive; poor spelling/grammar literally hinders meaning; sophisticated punctuation enhances ideas. Agree: AO5 (content/organisation) is 24 marks vs 16 for AO6; a brilliant argument with minor errors will outscore a technically perfect but vacuous response. Nuanced: both are essential — spelling/grammar is the medium through which ideas are communicated.

238a6f06-3a7d-4299-9bc0-9a53f27e4b5a.text: Write a formal letter to a local council (approximately 200 words) arguing against a proposed library closure. Aim for Level 4 technical accuracy: use semicolons, colons, varied sentence structures, and precise vocabulary.
238a6f06-3a7d-4299-9bc0-9a53f27e4b5a.marks:
Content and Organisation (24 marks):
Top band (19–24) Convincingly formal, clear argument, well-organised.
Upper-mid band (13–18) Clear and appropriate.

Technical Accuracy (16 marks):
Top band (13–16) Wide range of punctuation, varied sentences, ambitious vocabulary.
Upper-mid band (9–12) Mostly accurate, some variety.

Look for: semicolons joining related clauses, colons before explanations, dashes for asides, formal vocabulary, no comma splices.

6747d70b-0fb7-4b51-bea7-96f6eff62cf2.text: Explore how Dickens uses the quotation “Mankind was my business” to present Marley’s role in the novella and Dickens’s wider message.
6747d70b-0fb7-4b51-bea7-96f6eff62cf2.marks:
Upper band (3-4): Detailed analysis linking the quotation to Dickens’s message. E.g. ‘Mankind’ is emphatic — Marley now realises that helping others should have been his life’s purpose. ‘Business’ has a double meaning: Marley focused on financial business, but his real business should have been caring for people. The italicised emphasis (in the original text) shows Marley’s anguish. Dickens uses Marley as a mouthpiece for his own social message.
Lower band (1-2): Basic comment with limited analysis. E.g. This shows Marley wishes he had been kinder.

6747d70b-0fb7-4b51-bea7-96f6eff62cf2.text:
Read the following extract from Stave 1:

“Oh! But he was a tight-fisted hand at the grindstone, Scrooge! a squeezing, wrenching, grasping, scraping, clutching, covetous, old sinner! Hard and sharp as flint, from which no steel had ever struck out generous fire, secret, and self-contained, and solitary as an oyster.”

Starting with this extract, explore how Dickens presents Scrooge as an isolated and selfish character.
6747d70b-0fb7-4b51-bea7-96f6eff62cf2.marks:
Top band (7-8): Perceptive analysis of language and structure. Explores the list of aggressive present participles (‘squeezing, wrenching, grasping’) as creating relentless energy of greed. ‘Hard and sharp as flint’ = cold, dangerous, incapable of warmth (‘no steel had ever struck out generous fire’). ‘Solitary as an oyster’ = sealed shut, refusing to open up. Links to Dickens’s purpose: establishing Scrooge at his worst so that his transformation is more dramatic. Contrasts with Stave 5 similes.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Clear analysis with relevant language exploration.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Supported comments with some reference to techniques.
Lower band (1-2): Simple description of Scrooge as mean.

6747d70b-0fb7-4b51-bea7-96f6eff62cf2.text:
Read the following extract from Stave 3 about the Cratchit family Christmas:

“Bob held his withered little hand in his, as if he loved the child, and wished to keep him by his side, and dreaded that he might be taken from him.”

Starting with this extract, explore how Dickens uses the Cratchit family to present the struggles of the poor.
6747d70b-0fb7-4b51-bea7-96f6eff62cf2.marks:
Top band (7-8): Perceptive analysis. Explores ‘withered little hand’ as suggesting premature decay — a child’s hand should not be withered. The tricolon (‘loved’, ‘wished’, ‘dreaded’) shows escalating emotion from love to fear. ‘Taken from him’ implies death, yet Bob cannot prevent it because of poverty. Links to Stave 4 where Tim dies, fulfilling this fear. Discusses Dickens’s message: wealthy people like Scrooge have the power to prevent such suffering.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Clear analysis with relevant language and structural links.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Supported comments with some analysis.
Lower band (1-2): Simple identification of Bob’s love for Tim.

6747d70b-0fb7-4b51-bea7-96f6eff62cf2.text: How does Dickens use the character of Fred to present the true meaning of Christmas and to challenge Scrooge’s attitudes?
6747d70b-0fb7-4b51-bea7-96f6eff62cf2.marks:
Top band (26-30): Convincing analysis. Explores Fred as the embodiment of Christmas spirit: ‘a kind, forgiving, charitable, pleasant time.’ Analyses Fred as a foil to Scrooge — same family, opposite values. Fred’s persistence in inviting Scrooge despite rejection models Dickens’s message about never giving up on people. Links Fred to Fan and the theme of family. Discusses Fred’s role in Stave 5 when Scrooge finally accepts the invitation, completing the reconciliation. References Dickens’s context: Christmas as a time for social unity.
Upper band (21-25): Thoughtful, developed response with well-chosen references and clear analysis of language, form and structure.
Upper-mid band (16-20): Clear analysis with relevant references.
Mid band (11-15): Some explained comments with relevant references and limited analysis of methods.
Lower-mid band (6-10): Supported comments with some analysis.
Lower band (1-5): Simple statements about Fred being kind.

6747d70b-0fb7-4b51-bea7-96f6eff62cf2.text:
Starting with the following extract, explore how Dickens presents the theme of social responsibility through the character of Scrooge in A Christmas Carol.

“‘Are there no prisons?’ asked Scrooge.
‘Plenty of prisons,’ said the gentleman.
‘And the Union workhouses?’ demanded Scrooge. ‘Are they still in operation?’”

Write about:
• how Dickens presents Scrooge’s attitudes in this extract
• how Dickens challenges these attitudes in the novella as a whole.
[30 marks]
6747d70b-0fb7-4b51-bea7-96f6eff62cf2.marks:
Top band (26-30) Convincing, critical response. Analyses Scrooge’s questions as rhetorical — he already knows the answer and is dismissing the charity collector. ‘Demanded’ shows aggression. References to prisons and workhouses echo real Victorian institutions. Links to Malthus (‘surplus population’). Traces how Dickens systematically challenges these attitudes: Marley’s chain (consequences of neglect), Fezziwig (alternative model of wealth), Cratchits (human cost of poverty), Ignorance and Want (Scrooge’s own words thrown back at him), the grave (final reckoning). Argues Dickens wrote the novella as a direct challenge to wealthy Victorians who shared Scrooge’s attitudes.
Upper band (21-25) Thoughtful response with clear analysis and context.
Top band (16-20): Clear understanding with explained comments.
Upper-mid band (11-15): Some explained comments with references.
Lower-mid band (6-10): Supported comments with some textual reference.
Lower band (1-5): Simple comments with limited reference.

6747d70b-0fb7-4b51-bea7-96f6eff62cf2.text: Explore how Dickens uses contrast between Fezziwig and Scrooge to present his message about the responsibilities of employers.
6747d70b-0fb7-4b51-bea7-96f6eff62cf2.marks:
Top band (26-30): Convincing analysis. Contrasts Fezziwig’s joyful, generous personality (‘laughed all over himself’) with Scrooge’s cold, aggressive introduction (‘squeezing, wrenching, grasping’). Explores Scrooge’s own recognition: ‘The happiness he gives, is quite as great as if it cost a fortune’ — showing that kindness costs nothing but means everything. Links to the Victorian context: factory owners who exploited workers. Discusses how Fezziwig makes Scrooge reflect on his treatment of Bob Cratchit.
Upper band (21-25): Thoughtful, developed response with well-chosen references and clear analysis of language, form and structure.
Upper-mid band (16-20): Clear analysis with relevant contrasts.
Mid band (11-15): Some explained comments with relevant references and limited analysis of methods.
Lower-mid band (6-10): Supported comments with some textual reference.
Lower band (1-5): Simple statements about the two employers.

0c152c00-edc6-4682-8b89-7d86e262c367.text: Read the following quotation from Squealer's speech in Chapter 3: 'It is for your sake that we drink that milk and eat those apples.' How does Orwell use this statement to present Squealer as manipulative?
0c152c00-edc6-4682-8b89-7d86e262c367.marks:
Analysis of language.
• The italicised 'your' inverts the truth — the pigs' selfishness is reframed as self-sacrifice (1 mark).
• 'for your sake' uses emotional manipulation, making the animals feel grateful rather than exploited (1 mark).
• The confident declarative sentence presents the lie as fact, leaving no room for question (1 mark).
• Contextually, this mirrors how Soviet propaganda presented the party's privileges as necessary for the welfare of the people (1 mark).

0c152c00-edc6-4682-8b89-7d86e262c367.text:
How does Orwell present the ways that the pigs' clever use of language helps them to control the other animals?

Write about:
• what the pigs say and do
• how Orwell presents the ways the pigs use language to control the other animals.
0c152c00-edc6-4682-8b89-7d86e262c367.marks:
AO1 (up to 4 marks): Response to the question across the text.
AO2 (up to 4 marks): Analysis of methods.
Top band (7-8): May discuss: Squealer's rhetorical questions structured to prevent disagreement; the false appeal to science ('this has been proved by Science'); the fear tactic ('Jones would come back'); the passive voice obscuring who makes decisions; the simplification of commandments to slogans; Napoleon's use of the sheep to drown out debate; Squealer's ability to 'turn black into white'; comparison between Squealer's rhetoric and Pravda.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Clear analysis.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Some analysis.
Lower band (1-2): Simple comments.

0c152c00-edc6-4682-8b89-7d86e262c367.text:
Starting with this moment from Chapter 3, where Boxer responds to the extra work: 'I will work harder', explore how Orwell presents Boxer's dedication and its consequences. Write about:
• how Orwell presents Boxer in this chapter
• how Orwell uses Boxer to explore ideas about the working class across the whole novel.
0c152c00-edc6-4682-8b89-7d86e262c367.marks:
AO1 (up to 4 marks): Response to the quotation and whole text.
AO2 (up to 4 marks): Analysis of methods.
Top band (7-8): May discuss: the motto as characterisation showing both admirable dedication and dangerous naivety; contrast with pigs who 'did not actually work'; Boxer's physical strength versus intellectual vulnerability; his later adoption of 'Napoleon is always right' showing blind obedience; his eventual betrayal (sold to the knacker); Orwell's use of pathos; the parallel with Stakhanovite workers under Stalin; Orwell's sympathy for the proletariat combined with a warning about blind loyalty.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Clear analysis.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Some analysis.
Lower band (1-2): Simple comments.

0c152c00-edc6-4682-8b89-7d86e262c367.text: How does Orwell use the character of Squealer to explore ideas about truth and lies in Animal Farm? Consider the whole text in your response.
0c152c00-edc6-4682-8b89-7d86e262c367.marks:
AO1 (up to 4 marks): Critical, exploratory response.
AO2 (up to 4 marks): Analysis of methods (language of propaganda, rhetorical techniques, passive voice, irony).
AO3 (up to 4 marks): Context (Pravda, Soviet propaganda, totalitarian control of truth).
Top band (10-12): Convincing analysis. May explore: Squealer's introduction as one who could 'turn black into white'; his progressive escalation from justifying milk/apples to rewriting history; his use of fear, false statistics, euphemism and appeal to authority; the animals' inability to challenge him due to poor literacy; how Squealer represents the machinery of propaganda rather than a single person; Orwell's warning about how controlling language means controlling truth.
Upper-mid band (7-9): Clear response.
Lower-mid band (4-6): Supported.
Lower band (1-3): Simple.

0c152c00-edc6-4682-8b89-7d86e262c367.text:
How does Orwell use the character of Squealer to explore ideas about truth and lies in Animal Farm?

Write about:
• what Squealer says and does
• how Orwell uses the character of Squealer to explore ideas about truth and lies.

[34 marks including 4 marks for SPaG]
0c152c00-edc6-4682-8b89-7d86e262c367.marks:
AO1 (up to 12 marks): Critical, exploratory response with judicious references.
AO2 (up to 12 marks): Analysis of language, form, structure.

spelling/grammar (up to 4 marks).

Top band (21-25) Thoughtful response.
Upper-mid band (16-20) Clear analysis.
Mid band (11-15) Some analysis.
Lower-mid band (6-10) Supported.
Lower band (1-5) Simple.
spelling/grammar Mid band (3-4) Consistent accuracy. Lower-mid band (2) Generally accurate. Lower band (1) Some accuracy.

0c152c00-edc6-4682-8b89-7d86e262c367.text:
How does Orwell present the failure of the rebellion in Animal Farm?

Write about:
• the ways the rebellion fails
• how Orwell presents the failure of the rebellion.

[34 marks including 4 marks for SPaG]
0c152c00-edc6-4682-8b89-7d86e262c367.marks:
AO1 (up to 12 marks): Critical, exploratory response.
AO2 (up to 12 marks): Analysis of methods.
AO3 (up to 6 marks): Context.
spelling/grammar (up to 4 marks).

Top band (21-25) Thoughtful response.

Mid band (11-15) Some analysis.

spelling/grammar as above.

a4d85167-83ad-4e47-a1d5-5369415f82b7.text: Read the following extract from Chapter 27, in which Joe visits Pip in London. How does Dickens use language to present the awkwardness and emotional distance between Pip and Joe?
a4d85167-83ad-4e47-a1d5-5369415f82b7.marks:
Top band (17-20) Perceptive analysis of Dickens’ methods. Explores Joe’s discomfort (calling Pip ‘Sir’, the hat falling), Pip’s condescension, the power reversal from forge to London. Analyses physical comedy alongside genuine pathos. Notes how Joe’s dialect contrasts with Pip’s formal register. Discusses Joe’s dignity in withdrawing: ‘You and me is not two figures to be together in London.’
Upper band (13-16) Developed analysis with clear evidence.
Top band (9-12): Clear understanding with some language points.
Upper-mid band (5-8): Basic understanding.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Limited.
Lower band (1-2): Simple.

a4d85167-83ad-4e47-a1d5-5369415f82b7.text: Explore how Dickens presents Pip’s transformation from a content child to a snobbish young gentleman. What is Dickens criticising?
a4d85167-83ad-4e47-a1d5-5369415f82b7.marks:
