0cea6cd9-50f3-4d5c-bb68-a0bbd4dc24dd.text: Describe two ways a writer could use 'show don't tell' to convey a character's fear.
0cea6cd9-50f3-4d5c-bb68-a0bbd4dc24dd.marks:
1 marks for each valid way, up to 2 marks. Possible answers:

• Describe the character's actions, such as backing away, freezing, or gripping something tightly (1 mark)

0cea6cd9-50f3-4d5c-bb68-a0bbd4dc24dd.text: Explain how Peter Fleming uses the verb 'cannonaded' to describe the impact of the suitcase during the train crash in Source A (Paper 2, 2026 sample). You should comment on the effect this has on the reader.
0cea6cd9-50f3-4d5c-bb68-a0bbd4dc24dd.marks:
Award up to 4 marks. Indicative content:
• The verb 'cannonaded' is a metaphor that compares the falling suitcase to a cannon being fired (1 mark)
• This creates the impression of a violent military attack, suggesting the impact was extremely forceful (1 mark)
• It turns an ordinary object (a suitcase) into a weapon, making the writer seem like a victim under bombardment (1 mark)
• The hyperbolic effect exaggerates the incident for humorous or dramatic purposes, fitting the writer's sardonic tone (1 mark)

0cea6cd9-50f3-4d5c-bb68-a0bbd4dc24dd.text: Explain how Yann Martel uses sensory language and powerful verbs to create tension in the Life of Pi extract (Paper 1, 2026 sample). You should refer to specific examples from the text in your answer.
0cea6cd9-50f3-4d5c-bb68-a0bbd4dc24dd.marks:
Award up to 6 marks using a best-fit approach.

Indicative content:
• Onomatopoeic repetition of 'yip yip yip yip yip' appeals to the sense of sound and conveys the relentless, manic energy of the hyena (1–2 marks)
• The sensory detail 'the beating of its legs against the benches made the whole boat shake' uses touch/physical sensation to convey the hyena's power and proximity (1–2 marks)
• 'Its claws were loudly clicking on their surface' uses sound to emphasise the predatory threat (1 mark)
• Dynamic verbs such as 'leapt', 'ran', 'racing' create pace and energy, making the reader feel the hyena's frantic movement (1–2 marks)
• Pi's passive verbs ('could only watch', 'was seized by fear') contrast with the hyena's active verbs, showing his helplessness (1–2 marks)
• 'I pushed myself away on the oar till only the tips of my feet were holding on to the boat' is an example of 'show don't tell' — we understand Pi's terror through his physical actions (1–2 marks)

0cea6cd9-50f3-4d5c-bb68-a0bbd4dc24dd.text:
Evaluate the effectiveness of the following student's creative writing opening. To what extent does it successfully use sensory language, powerful verbs and 'show don't tell'?

'The house was old and creepy. I walked up the path and the door was open. I felt nervous. It was dark inside and I could hear a noise. I went in.'

In your response, you should identify strengths and weaknesses and suggest specific improvements.
0cea6cd9-50f3-4d5c-bb68-a0bbd4dc24dd.marks:
Top band (7-9): Perceptive evaluation that identifies specific weaknesses (generic verbs 'walked', 'went'; directly stating emotion 'I felt nervous'; lack of sensory detail beyond sight; adjectives 'old and creepy' are telling not showing) and offers precise, well-explained improvements demonstrating understanding of all three techniques.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Clear evaluation that identifies several weaknesses and suggests relevant improvements. May not address all three techniques equally.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Some valid comments on the writing. May identify that it is 'too simple' but struggle to explain exactly why or offer specific alternatives.
Lower band (1-2): Simple comments, e.g. 'it could use more description.' Limited understanding of the specific techniques.
Indicative improvements students might suggest:
• Replace 'old and creepy' with sensory showing: describe peeling paint, a sagging roof, the smell of damp wood
• Replace 'walked' with a powerful verb like 'crept', 'edged' or 'stumbled'
• Replace 'I felt nervous' with a physical reaction: sweating palms, dry mouth, tightening stomach
• Add sound detail beyond 'a noise' — specify what the noise sounds like
• Replace 'It was dark inside' with a showing description using imagery

f3ad5f03-ac52-42c2-a3cc-1df3523b44de.text:
Read the following student opening paragraph, then answer the question below.

'Furthermore, I think that public transport is good. Moreover, it is also cheap. Additionally, buses help the environment.'

Explain two problems with how this student has used discourse markers, and suggest how they could improve their paragraph.
f3ad5f03-ac52-42c2-a3cc-1df3523b44de.marks:
Problem 1: The discourse markers are mechanical and repetitive — 'Furthermore,' 'Moreover,' and 'Additionally' all mean the same thing and are placed at the start of every sentence (1 mark). Improvement: Vary connectives and embed them within sentences rather than always at the beginning (1 mark).
Problem 2: The discourse markers suggest development but the ideas are undeveloped — each sentence is a simple, separate statement rather than a connected argument (1 mark). Improvement: Use topic sentences and develop each point with evidence and explanation before moving to the next (1 mark).

f3ad5f03-ac52-42c2-a3cc-1df3523b44de.text: Explain why planning is important for the Paper 2 writing question.
f3ad5f03-ac52-42c2-a3cc-1df3523b44de.marks:
1 marks for each valid point explained, up to 4 marks:
• Planning ensures a clear structure with a logical sequence of ideas — credit goes to 'fluid sequencing of ideas/argument' at Top band (1 mark)• Planning prevents repetition of points, which the mark scheme associates with Lower band ('one or two unlinked ideas')(1 mark)
• Planning allows you to include a counter-argument, showing balanced thinking and a 'convincing argument' (Level 4) (1 mark)
• Planning helps match tone, style and register to the form — e.g. planning a speech allows you to include direct address and rhetorical questions (1 mark)
• Planning saves time overall, leaving time for proofreading (technical accuracy, 16 marks) (1 mark)

0c8d67de-155b-49ca-a4f9-4e20af0da205.text: Read Act 1, Scene 1 from “I wonder that you will still be talking, Signor Benedick” to “A bird of my tongue is better than a beast of yours.” How does Shakespeare use language in this extract to present the relationship between Beatrice and Benedick? Write about the extract and the play as a whole.
0c8d67de-155b-49ca-a4f9-4e20af0da205.marks:
Top band (25–30 + 4 spelling/grammar)Analyses the stichomythia, animal imagery (“bird” vs “beast”), the competitive structure of the exchange, and the underlying attraction. Links to the wider play: the gulling scenes, “Kill Claudio,” the double wedding. Embeds context: patriarchal expectations vs Beatrice’s unconventional independence. Explores how wit functions as both weapon and defence.

0c8d67de-155b-49ca-a4f9-4e20af0da205.text: Analyse Claudio’s description of Hero as a “jewel” (Act 1, Scene 1). What does this metaphor reveal about his attitude towards love?
0c8d67de-155b-49ca-a4f9-4e20af0da205.marks:
Upper band (3-4): “Jewel” reduces Hero to a precious object — beautiful and valuable but passive. It suggests Claudio’s love is based on appearance and possession, not knowledge or personality. A jewel can be stolen (foreshadowing Don John’s trick). The commodity language links to Elizabethan marriage conventions where women were transferred between men.
Lower band (1-2): Basic comment about Claudio thinking Hero is beautiful.

0c8d67de-155b-49ca-a4f9-4e20af0da205.text: How does Shakespeare use the masked ball in Act 2, Scene 1 to introduce the theme of deception?
0c8d67de-155b-49ca-a4f9-4e20af0da205.marks:
Top band (7-8): Everyone wears literal masks. Don Pedro woos as Claudio (proxy wooing = performance). Beatrice insults Benedick while “not recognising” him. Don John lies about Don Pedro. Claudio believes the lie instantly. The ball makes deception physical and visual, foreshadowing how easily characters will be deceived in Acts 3–4. Links to the title’s “noting/nothing” pun.
Top band (5–6) Clear.
Mid band (3–4) Some.
Lower band (1–2) Simple.

0c8d67de-155b-49ca-a4f9-4e20af0da205.text: Explore how Shakespeare establishes the contrast between Claudio/Hero and Beatrice/Benedick as two models of love in Acts 1–2.
0c8d67de-155b-49ca-a4f9-4e20af0da205.marks:
Top band (25–30 + 4 spelling/grammar)Claudio: visual, conventional, performed through proxy, fragile. Beatrice/Benedick: verbal, equal, resistant, built on years of familiarity. Claudio speaks in formal verse about Hero’s beauty; Beatrice and Benedick spar in lively prose about each other’s faults. Links across the play: Claudio’s love breaks at the first test; B&B’s love survives the most demanding test (“Kill Claudio”). Context: conventional vs unconventional courtship.

Upper band (19–24 + 3)Thoughtful.
Upper-mid band (13–18 + 2)Clear.
Mid band (7–12 + 2)Some understanding.
Lower-mid band (3–6 + 1)Limited.
Lower band (1–2 + 1)Simple.

0c8d67de-155b-49ca-a4f9-4e20af0da205.text: Analyse why Claudio instantly believes Don John’s lie at the masked ball. What does this reveal about his character?
0c8d67de-155b-49ca-a4f9-4e20af0da205.marks:
Top band (7-8): Claudio does not verify the claim — he accepts it immediately (“’Tis certain so”). This reveals shallow trust, insecurity, and possessiveness. He treats the situation as a betrayal of friendship rather than investigating the truth. Foreshadows his behaviour in Act 4 (believing Don John’s window trick without evidence). Structural function: Shakespeare shows Claudio’s jealousy is a character flaw, not just a reaction.
Top band (5–6) Clear.
Mid band (3–4) Some.
Lower band (1–2) Simple.

0c8d67de-155b-49ca-a4f9-4e20af0da205.text: Analyse the significance of Beatrice’s nickname “Signor Mountanto” for Benedick. What does it establish about their dynamic?
0c8d67de-155b-49ca-a4f9-4e20af0da205.marks:
Upper band (3-4): “Mountanto” is a fencing thrust, comparing verbal sparring to swordplay. It shows Beatrice views their relationship as combat. The Italian word suggests sophistication and mockery. Crucially, Beatrice asks about Benedick before anyone else — she cannot stop thinking about him. The nickname establishes both hostility and fascination, setting up the merry war.
Lower band (1-2): Basic comment about it being a nickname.

e91b5df7-24df-42b3-bff3-3c33bf30ae73.text: Read Act 5, Scene 4 from “One Hero died defiled, but I do live” to the end of Hero’s speech. How does Shakespeare use language in this extract to present Hero’s return? Write about the extract and the play as a whole.
e91b5df7-24df-42b3-bff3-3c33bf30ae73.marks:
Top band (25–30 + 4 spelling/grammar)Analyses the third-person self-reference (“One Hero died” — linguistic splitting, trauma), the assertion of virginity (“I am a maid” — must still prove her chastity), the brevity of her speech (silenced by the experience). Links to the wider play: the church scene, the Friar’s plan, Hero’s passivity throughout. Context: female honour, the requirement to prove innocence. Modern vs Elizabethan readings.

Upper band (19–24 + 3)Thoughtful.

e91b5df7-24df-42b3-bff3-3c33bf30ae73.text: Explore how Shakespeare uses Dogberry to develop the theme of ‘noting’ and the unreliability of observation in Much Ado About Nothing.
e91b5df7-24df-42b3-bff3-3c33bf30ae73.marks:
Top band (25–30 + 4 spelling/grammar)Dogberry accidentally discovers truth while the intelligent nobles are deceived. His malapropisms show language is unreliable. The watchmen “note” the truth by overhearing, mirroring the gulling scenes and Don John’s plot. Shakespeare suggests truth is found by accident in a world where deliberate observation fails. Links to the title pun, the casket/mask theme. Comedy undercuts the aristocracy’s claim to superior judgement.

Upper band (19–24 + 3)Thoughtful.
Upper-mid band (13–18 + 2)Clear.
Mid band (7–12 + 2)Some.
Lower-mid band (3–6 + 1)Limited.
Lower band (1–2 + 1)Simple.

e91b5df7-24df-42b3-bff3-3c33bf30ae73.text: Analyse whether Claudio’s penance in Act 5 is sufficient for the harm he has caused Hero.
e91b5df7-24df-42b3-bff3-3c33bf30ae73.marks:
Top band (7-8): The penance (tomb visit + marrying “the niece”) lasts one scene. Claudio does not apologise directly to Hero. He agrees to marry sight-unseen again, repeating the superficial pattern of his first courtship. The comic form requires reconciliation, but the emotional logic resists it. An Elizabethan audience may accept it as adequate; a modern audience finds it hollow. Shakespeare leaves the audience to judge.
Top band (5–6) Clear.
Mid band (3–4) Some.
Lower band (1–2) Simple.

e91b5df7-24df-42b3-bff3-3c33bf30ae73.text: Analyse the significance of Benedick’s line “Prince, thou art sad; get thee a wife” (Act 5, Scene 4). What does it suggest about the play’s ending?
e91b5df7-24df-42b3-bff3-3c33bf30ae73.marks:
Upper band (3-4): Don Pedro is isolated at the end — unmarried while the couples celebrate. Benedick’s advice is both comic (a typically blunt Benedick line) and melancholic (it draws attention to Don Pedro’s exclusion). The man who orchestrated love for others finds none for himself. Echoes Antonio’s isolation in The Merchant of Venice. The line prevents a fully joyful ending.
Lower band (1-2): Basic comment about Don Pedro being told to get married.

e91b5df7-24df-42b3-bff3-3c33bf30ae73.text: How does Shakespeare use Hero’s silence after her return to comment on her position within a patriarchal society?
e91b5df7-24df-42b3-bff3-3c33bf30ae73.marks:
Top band (7-8): Hero says almost nothing after being restored. She does not confront Claudio, express anger, or assert herself. Her silence can be read as virtuous forgiveness (Elizabethan) or enforced compliance (modern). She must still prove her chastity (“I am a maid”). The third-person self-reference suggests trauma and identity loss. Shakespeare leaves her silence ambiguous — the comic resolution is imposed on her.
Top band (5–6) Clear.
Mid band (3–4) Some.
Lower band (1–2) Simple.

e91b5df7-24df-42b3-bff3-3c33bf30ae73.text: Analyse why Shakespeare has Dogberry use malapropisms. What is the dramatic and thematic function of his mangled language?
e91b5df7-24df-42b3-bff3-3c33bf30ae73.marks:
Upper band (3-4): Malapropisms create comedy (e.g. “comparisons are odorous”). But they also mirror the play’s theme: if words so easily mean the wrong thing, all language is unstable. Dogberry’s comic misuse of words parallels the aristocrats’ serious misreading of events. The man who cannot speak properly is the one who finds the truth. Shakespeare uses Dogberry to undercut the authority of the educated classes.
Lower band (1-2): Basic comment about Dogberry being funny.

5a64cfd5-a4c5-4902-8c91-074d02099a6f.text: Starting with Act 4, Scene 1 (“O that I were a man!”), explore how Shakespeare presents Beatrice as a powerful character. Write about the extract and the play as a whole.
5a64cfd5-a4c5-4902-8c91-074d02099a6f.marks:
Top band (25–30 + 4 spelling/grammar)Analyses the repetition (“O that I were a man!”), violent imagery (“eat his heart in the market-place”), and the demand (“Kill Claudio”). Tracks her arc: merry war wit → gulling vulnerability → Act 4 fury. Links to patriarchal constraints: she can see injustice but cannot act because she is a woman. Context: proto-feminist readings, Elizabethan gender roles. Explores whether her marriage to Benedick is liberation or compromise.

Upper band (19–24 + 3)Thoughtful.
Upper-mid band (13–18 + 2)Clear.
Mid band (7–12 + 2)Some.
Lower-mid band (3–6 + 1)Limited.
Lower band (1–2 + 1)Simple.

5a64cfd5-a4c5-4902-8c91-074d02099a6f.text: Explore how Shakespeare presents Benedick’s transformation from confirmed bachelor to committed lover across the play.
5a64cfd5-a4c5-4902-8c91-074d02099a6f.marks:
Top band (25–30 + 4 spelling/grammar)Act 1: anti-love declarations, masculine pride, comic overstatement. Act 2: gulled, instant comic reversal (“Love me! Why, it must be requited!”). Act 4: “Kill Claudio” — chooses love over male loyalty, moral growth. Act 5: love poems, marriage. Analyses the shift from prose-comedy to moral seriousness. Context: Elizabethan masculinity, the tension between military bonds and romantic love.

Upper band (19–24 + 3)Thoughtful.
Upper-mid band (13–18 + 2)Clear.
Mid band (7–12 + 2)Some.
Lower-mid band (3–6 + 1)Limited.
Lower band (1–2 + 1)Simple.

5a64cfd5-a4c5-4902-8c91-074d02099a6f.text: Is Claudio a victim of deception or a cruel character? Argue both sides with evidence from the play.
5a64cfd5-a4c5-4902-8c91-074d02099a6f.marks:
Top band (7-8): Victim: deceived by Don John (whom he trusts), following honour culture’s rules, young and inexperienced. Cruel: chooses public humiliation over private confrontation, “rotten orange” reduces Hero to an object, penance is inadequate, second “love” is again sight-unseen. Shakespeare provides evidence for both and refuses to settle the question. Context: honour culture vs modern values.
Top band (5–6) Clear.
Mid band (3–4) Some.
Lower band (1–2) Simple.

5a64cfd5-a4c5-4902-8c91-074d02099a6f.text: Analyse the significance of Hero’s silence throughout the play. What does it reveal about her position in society?
5a64cfd5-a4c5-4902-8c91-074d02099a6f.marks:
Top band (7-8): Hero speaks less than half as much as Beatrice. She does not choose her husband, defend herself effectively, or confront her accusers. Her silence is structural — caused by patriarchal systems that deny women voice. She is not weak but oppressed. Her passivity contrasts with Beatrice’s verbal power, showing two different female responses to the same system. Context: Elizabethan gender roles.
Top band (5–6) Clear.
Mid band (3–4) Some.
Lower band (1–2) Simple.

5a64cfd5-a4c5-4902-8c91-074d02099a6f.text: Analyse the significance of Don John’s line “I am a plain-dealing villain” (Act 1, Scene 3). How does it define his role in the play?
5a64cfd5-a4c5-4902-8c91-074d02099a6f.marks:
Upper band (3-4): The oxymoron (“plain-dealing villain” — honest villainy is a contradiction) signals his function as a catalyst. His self-awareness contrasts with characters who lack self-knowledge. Shakespeare does not develop his psychology because his role is structural: to test Claudio’s trust, Hero’s resilience, and Beatrice’s moral clarity. The real problems are systemic, not individual.
Lower band (1-2): Basic comment about Don John being the villain.

5a64cfd5-a4c5-4902-8c91-074d02099a6f.text: How does Shakespeare use the contrast between Beatrice and Hero to explore different female experiences in a patriarchal society?
5a64cfd5-a4c5-4902-8c91-074d02099a6f.marks:
Upper band (3-4): Beatrice: vocal, independent, witty, resists convention but is powerless to act physically (“O that I were a man”). Hero: obedient, silent, compliant, and destroyed by the very system she follows perfectly. Both suffer under patriarchy, but in opposite ways: Beatrice is marginalised for being too outspoken; Hero is destroyed despite being perfectly obedient. The contrast shows patriarchy harms all women.
Lower band (1-2): Basic comparison.

a7fecd7f-da9d-4268-994b-1cb116ad26e9.text:
'Cars are convenient, comfortable and save time. However, we need to use them less by making public transport such as trains, trams and buses cheaper, more reliable and easier to access.'

Write a speech to be given at a meeting of your local council in which you argue your point of view on this statement.

(24 marks for content and organisation
16 marks for technical accuracy)
a7fecd7f-da9d-4268-994b-1cb116ad26e9.marks:
AO5 Content and Organisation (24 marks):
Top band (19–24) Communication is convincing and compelling. Tone, style and register assuredly matched to purpose and audience. Extensive and ambitious vocabulary with sustained crafting of linguistic devices. Varied and inventive use of structural features. Fluently linked paragraphs with seamlessly integrated discourse markers.
Upper-mid band (13–18) Communication is consistently clear. Tone, style and register consistently matched. Increasingly sophisticated vocabulary chosen for effect with a range of successful linguistic devices. Effective use of structural features. Coherent paragraphs with integrated discourse markers.
Lower-mid band (7–12) Communicates with some success. Some attempt to match tone, style and register. Conscious use of vocabulary with some use of linguistic devices. Some use of structural features and paragraphs.
Lower band (1–6) Communicates simply. Simple awareness of matching tone, style and register. Simple vocabulary and simple linguistic devices.

AO6 Technical Accuracy (16 marks):
Top band (13–16) Consistently secure sentence demarcation. Wide range of punctuation with high accuracy. Full range of sentence forms. Secure control of complex grammar. High-level spelling. Extensive vocabulary.
Upper-mid band (9–12) Mostly secure demarcation. Range of punctuation mostly successful. Variety of sentence forms. Mostly controlled grammar. Generally accurate spelling.
Lower-mid band (5–8) Mostly secure demarcation, sometimes accurate. Some control of punctuation. Attempts variety of sentence forms. Some accurate spelling.
Lower band (1–4) Occasional sentence demarcation. Some evidence of conscious punctuation. Simple sentence forms. Accurate basic spelling.

a7fecd7f-da9d-4268-994b-1cb116ad26e9.text: Write the opening two paragraphs of a speech arguing that public transport should be free for all under-18s. Use at least two rhetorical devices and label them in brackets afterwards.
a7fecd7f-da9d-4268-994b-1cb116ad26e9.marks:
This is a practice exercise rather than a full 40-mark question. Award marks based on:
• Effective use of at least two rhetorical devices (e.g. rhetorical question, rule of three, direct address, anaphora, emotive language, antithesis)
• Devices are used with clear purpose — not just dropped in
• Tone and register are appropriate for a speech
• Writing is engaging and clearly structured
• Correct identification/labelling of the devices used
Level 4 response: devices are layered together, tone is assured, vocabulary is ambitious, and the audience feels directly addressed.

a7fecd7f-da9d-4268-994b-1cb116ad26e9.text:
Read the following paragraph and identify three rhetorical devices used. For each one, explain the effect it has on the reader.

'How can we call ourselves a civilised society when children walk to school in the dark because bus routes have been cut? We have failed our young people. We have failed our elderly. We have failed every single person who depends on public transport to live their life. Investment in buses is not a cost — it is an investment in our future.'
a7fecd7f-da9d-4268-994b-1cb116ad26e9.marks:
Students should identify three of the following:
• Rhetorical question ('How can we call ourselves...') — makes the audience feel guilty and challenges them to act; implies the answer is obvious
• Anaphora ('We have failed...') — repetition builds momentum and emphasises the scale of the failure; the listing of different groups shows how widespread the problem is
• Emotive language ('children walk to school in the dark') — creates a vivid, sympathetic image that provokes concern
• Direct address ('we') — inclusive pronoun makes the audience share responsibility
• Antithesis ('not a cost — it is an investment') — reframes the argument by contrasting two opposing ideas
• Rule of three ('our young people... our elderly... every single person') — builds to a climax with each group becoming broader
Award 1 mark per device correctly identified + 1 mark per clear explanation of effect = up to 6 marks.

a7fecd7f-da9d-4268-994b-1cb116ad26e9.text:
Rewrite the following flat paragraph using at least three rhetorical devices to make it more persuasive:

'Public transport is not very good. Buses are late and expensive. The government should spend more money on making them better because lots of people use them.'
a7fecd7f-da9d-4268-994b-1cb116ad26e9.marks:
A strong response will transform the content using devices such as:
• Rhetorical question: 'Why should hardworking families pay more for a worse service?'
• Emotive language: replace 'not very good' with vivid, emotive alternatives (e.g. 'crumbling', 'neglected', 'failing')
• Rule of three: e.g. 'Buses that are late, overpriced, and overcrowded'
• Anaphora: e.g. 'It is time to invest. It is time to act. It is time to put passengers first.'
• Antithesis: e.g. 'While roads receive billions, bus routes are being slashed.'
• Direct address: shift from 'lots of people' to 'you and your family'
Top band: Three or more devices used naturally, with ambitious vocabulary and a clear, persuasive tone.
Upper-mid band: Three devices present, mostly effective, with clear vocabulary.
Lower-mid band: One or two devices attempted, with some effect.
Lower band: Minimal change from original; devices are absent or incorrect.

a7fecd7f-da9d-4268-994b-1cb116ad26e9.text: Explain why the following sentence would lose marks in a Paper 2 Question 5 response: 'I am now going to use a rhetorical question to make you think. Don't you think buses should be free?'
a7fecd7f-da9d-4268-994b-1cb116ad26e9.marks:
Students should explain:
• The writer labels the device ('I am now going to use a rhetorical question') rather than simply using it — this breaks the illusion of natural, crafted writing
• Examiners reward 'deliberate crafting of linguistic devices' (Level 4) — this means using devices seamlessly, not announcing them
• The labelling makes the tone feel clumsy and self-conscious rather than assured
• A better version would simply ask: 'Don't you think buses should be free?' — the device speaks for itself
• This mistake also undermines tone, style and register, which are key AO5 criteria
Award up to 4 marks: 1 for identifying the problem, 1 for explaining why it loses marks with reference to the mark scheme, 1 for suggesting improvement, 1 for explaining how the improvement meets mark scheme criteria.

a7fecd7f-da9d-4268-994b-1cb116ad26e9.text: Write the concluding paragraph of a speech to your local council arguing that public transport fares should be reduced. Use anaphora and a powerful final sentence to leave a lasting impression on your audience.
a7fecd7f-da9d-4268-994b-1cb116ad26e9.marks:
A strong response will:
• Use anaphora effectively (e.g. 'It is our duty to... It is our duty to... It is our duty to...') to build towards a climactic ending
• End with a powerful, memorable final sentence — possibly a short, declarative sentence for impact or an emotive appeal
• Maintain a formal, respectful tone appropriate for a council speech
• Use 'we' and 'our' to maintain the inclusive, shared-responsibility feel of a speech
• Demonstrate ambitious vocabulary and varied sentence structures
Top band: Anaphora creates genuine momentum; final sentence is striking and memorable; tone is assured and perfectly matched to audience.
Upper-mid band: Anaphora is clear and effective; final sentence has impact; tone is appropriate.
Lower-mid band: Anaphora is attempted but may be clumsy; final sentence present but not particularly powerful.
Lower band: Little evidence of anaphora; conclusion is weak or generic.

f8e7f4b8-2328-48fc-aa47-a322e45c320a.text: Read Darcy’s first proposal from ‘In vain have I struggled’ to Elizabeth’s refusal. How does Austen use language to present the conflict between Darcy’s love and his pride in this extract?
f8e7f4b8-2328-48fc-aa47-a322e45c320a.marks:
Top band (17-20) Perceptive analysis. Discusses: ‘in vain’ and ‘struggled’ framing love as an unwelcome battle; ‘repressed’ implying powerful feelings; the shift from romantic declaration to social objections (Elizabeth’s ‘inferiority,’ her family’s ‘degradation’); the imperious ‘you must allow me’; the contrast between Darcy’s vocabulary of passion and his vocabulary of class consciousness. Analyses how this dual tone provokes Elizabeth’s furious refusal.
Top band (13-16): Clear analysis.
Upper-mid band (9-12): Some analysis.
Lower-mid band (5-8): Limited analysis.
Lower band (1-4): Simple comments.

f8e7f4b8-2328-48fc-aa47-a322e45c320a.text: How does Austen present the theme of appearance versus reality in the novel as a whole?
f8e7f4b8-2328-48fc-aa47-a322e45c320a.marks:
Top band (17-20) Convincing response. Discusses: Wickham’s charm masking dishonesty; Darcy’s poor manners concealing genuine integrity; Elizabeth’s confidence in her own judgement being misplaced; Charlotte’s pragmatic acceptance disguising inner compromise; the contrast between Darcy’s first and second proposals. Uses ‘Till this moment I never knew myself’ as the key moment of recognition. Argues Austen shows that social performance (manners, charm) is an unreliable guide to moral character.
Top band (13-16): Clear analysis.
Upper-mid band (9-12): Some understanding.
Lower-mid band (5-8): Supported comments.
Lower band (1-4): Simple statements.

f8e7f4b8-2328-48fc-aa47-a322e45c320a.text: Analyse the significance of Elizabeth’s line: ‘Till this moment I never knew myself.’
f8e7f4b8-2328-48fc-aa47-a322e45c320a.marks:
Upper band (3-4): This is Elizabeth’s moment of anagnorisis (self-recognition). ‘Till this moment’ implies a sudden, painful revelation. ‘Never knew myself’ admits that her pride in her own judgement was the source of her prejudice. The line marks the novel’s structural midpoint and the beginning of Elizabeth’s moral growth. It also implicates the reader, who has shared her perspective and her mistakes.
Lower band (1-2): Basic comment about Elizabeth realising she was wrong.

f8e7f4b8-2328-48fc-aa47-a322e45c320a.text: Read from Charlotte’s acceptance of Mr Collins to Elizabeth’s reaction. How does Austen use language and structure to present contrasting attitudes to marriage?
f8e7f4b8-2328-48fc-aa47-a322e45c320a.marks:
Top band (17-20) Perceptive analysis. Discusses Charlotte’s language of pragmatism (‘comfortable home,’ ‘not romantic’) versus Elizabeth’s shock; the structural contrast between Charlotte’s acceptance and Elizabeth’s refusal of the same man; Charlotte’s calculated strategy of minimising contact with Collins; Austen’s refusal to condemn Charlotte, suggesting sympathy for women trapped by limited options.
Top band (13-16): Clear analysis.
Upper-mid band (9-12): Some analysis.
Lower-mid band (5-8): Limited analysis.
Lower band (1-4): Simple comments.

f8e7f4b8-2328-48fc-aa47-a322e45c320a.text: How does Austen use the character of Wickham to explore the danger of judging by appearances?
f8e7f4b8-2328-48fc-aa47-a322e45c320a.marks:
Top band (17-20) Convincing response. Traces Wickham’s arc: charming introduction, lies about Darcy, pursuit of Miss King’s fortune, elopement with Lydia. Discusses how Elizabeth’s confirmation bias makes her believe Wickham; how the neighbourhood’s collective trust in charm over evidence mirrors Elizabeth’s error; how Darcy’s letter reveals the truth. Argues Wickham is Austen’s vehicle for demonstrating that appearance versus reality is the novel’s central theme.
Top band (13-16): Clear analysis.
Upper-mid band (9-12): Some understanding.
Lower-mid band (5-8): Supported comments.
Lower band (1-4): Simple statements.

f8e7f4b8-2328-48fc-aa47-a322e45c320a.text: Explain how Mr Collins’s proposal to Elizabeth reveals Austen’s criticism of Regency marriage customs.
f8e7f4b8-2328-48fc-aa47-a322e45c320a.marks:
Upper band (3-4): Collins lists duty, happiness, and Lady Catherine’s advice as reasons — never love. He assumes Elizabeth will accept because of the entailment, treating marriage as a business transaction. His inability to accept her refusal (‘it is usual with young ladies to reject’) denies her genuine agency. Austen uses comedy to expose a system where women were expected to accept any reasonable offer, regardless of their feelings.
Lower band (1-2): Basic comment about Collins being a bad suitor.

Mid band (3-4): States plans with some reason, may lack future tense variety, mostly accurate. Lower band (1-2): Limited response, basic vocabulary, several errors. 0 marks: No relevant content.

c675edcb-a2f3-4614-9732-9e15bf20342f.text: Read from Elizabeth’s first sight of Pemberley to ‘And of this place I might have been mistress!’ How does Austen use language to present Pemberley as a reflection of Darcy’s character?
c675edcb-a2f3-4614-9732-9e15bf20342f.marks:
Top band (17-20) Perceptive analysis. Discusses: the repeated emphasis on ‘natural beauty’ contrasting with artificial social performance; ‘real elegance’ implying authenticity; the grounds not ‘counteracted by an awkward taste’ suggesting Darcy’s restraint is a virtue, not a flaw; Elizabeth’s regretful ‘I might have been mistress’ mixing material envy with genuine reassessment; the estate as a symbol of the Darcy Elizabeth has not yet fully seen.
Top band (13-16): Clear analysis.
Upper-mid band (9-12): Some analysis.
Lower-mid band (5-8): Limited analysis.
Lower band (1-4): Simple comments.

c675edcb-a2f3-4614-9732-9e15bf20342f.text: How does Austen present change in Darcy’s character over the course of the novel?
c675edcb-a2f3-4614-9732-9e15bf20342f.marks:
Top band (17-20) Convincing response tracking Darcy’s arc: pride and condescension at Meryton (‘tolerable’); imperious first proposal (‘in vain have I struggled’); the letter as honest self-defence; transformed behaviour at Pemberley (courtesy to the Gardiners, gentleness with Elizabeth); rescue of Lydia from Wickham without seeking credit. Argues whether Darcy truly changes or whether Elizabeth’s perception of him changes — or both.
Top band (13-16): Clear analysis.
Upper-mid band (9-12): Some understanding.
Lower-mid band (5-8): Supported comments.
Lower band (1-4): Simple statements.

c675edcb-a2f3-4614-9732-9e15bf20342f.text: Analyse the significance of Elizabeth’s reflection: ‘Never had she so honestly felt that she could have loved him, as now, when all love must be vain.’
c675edcb-a2f3-4614-9732-9e15bf20342f.marks:
Upper band (3-4): ‘Honestly’ suggests this is the first time Elizabeth has been truthful with herself about Darcy. ‘All love must be vain’ echoes Darcy’s ‘in vain have I struggled,’ creating a structural parallel — both characters experience frustrated love. Elizabeth recognises her feelings precisely when Lydia’s elopement makes them impossible to act on, heightening the dramatic irony.
Lower band (1-2): Basic comment about Elizabeth being sad.

c675edcb-a2f3-4614-9732-9e15bf20342f.text: Read Mrs Reynolds’s praise of Darcy. How does Austen use the housekeeper’s testimony to challenge Elizabeth’s (and the reader’s) assumptions about Darcy?
c675edcb-a2f3-4614-9732-9e15bf20342f.marks:
Top band (17-20) Perceptive analysis. Mrs Reynolds is a credible witness because she has nothing to gain from flattery. Her language (‘best landlord,’ ‘best master,’ ‘never a cross word’) directly contradicts the neighbourhood’s verdict at the assembly. Austen uses indirect characterisation: Darcy is revealed through others’ experience rather than his own words. Elizabeth’s response (‘what praise is more valuable’) marks her recognition that her own judgement has been flawed.
Top band (13-16): Clear analysis.
Upper-mid band (9-12): Some analysis.
Lower-mid band (5-8): Limited analysis.
Lower band (1-4): Simple comments.

c675edcb-a2f3-4614-9732-9e15bf20342f.text: How does Austen use the character of Lydia to explore the consequences of poor judgement and parental failure?
c675edcb-a2f3-4614-9732-9e15bf20342f.marks:
Top band (17-20) Convincing response. Discusses: Lydia’s vanity and lack of moral education; Mr Bennet’s failure to discipline her; Mrs Bennet’s encouragement of flirtation; the Brighton trip as preventable disaster; the elopement threatening all five sisters’ prospects. Contrasts Lydia with Georgiana (both targeted by Wickham, but Georgiana had Darcy’s protection). Argues Lydia is both culprit and victim of a system that failed to educate or protect her.
Top band (13-16): Clear analysis.
Upper-mid band (9-12): Some understanding.
Lower-mid band (5-8): Supported comments.
Lower band (1-4): Simple statements.

c675edcb-a2f3-4614-9732-9e15bf20342f.text: Explain how Darcy’s line ‘I was in the middle before I knew that I had begun’ reveals Austen’s presentation of love in the novel.
c675edcb-a2f3-4614-9732-9e15bf20342f.marks:
Upper band (3-4): The line suggests love is not a conscious choice but a gradual, irresistible process. ‘In the middle before I knew’ implies that Darcy’s feelings grew beneath his awareness, undermining his earlier attempts to resist them (‘in vain have I struggled’). Austen presents genuine love as something that overwhelms social barriers and rational objections — a stark contrast to the calculated marriages of Collins and Charlotte.
Lower band (1-2): Basic comment about Darcy not realising he was in love.

d171c631-27fb-43d2-96c0-c3efe1a975a2.text: Read Act 4, Scene 1 from “The quality of mercy is not strained” to “When mercy seasons justice.” How does Shakespeare use language in this extract to present ideas about mercy? Write about the extract and the play as a whole.
d171c631-27fb-43d2-96c0-c3efe1a975a2.marks:
Top band (25–30 + 4 spelling/grammar)Analyses the rain metaphor, “twice blest,” “mightiest in the mightiest,” and the comparison to God. Then explores the irony: Portia preaches mercy but shows none. Links to the wider play: Shylock’s forced conversion, Antonio’s “merciful” conditions. Embeds context: Christian mercy vs Christian hypocrisy, Elizabethan vs modern readings. Precise quotations with word-level analysis.

Upper band (19–24 + 3)Thoughtful with evidence.
Upper-mid band (13–18 + 2)Clear.
Mid band (7–12 + 2)Some understanding.
Lower-mid band (3–6 + 1)Limited.
Lower band (1–2 + 1)Simple.

d171c631-27fb-43d2-96c0-c3efe1a975a2.text: Analyse the significance of Shylock’s line “I am content” (Act 4, Scene 1). Consider at least two possible interpretations.
d171c631-27fb-43d2-96c0-c3efe1a975a2.marks:
Upper band (3-4): The line is devastatingly ambiguous. “Content” could mean resigned acceptance, broken defeat, or bitter sarcasm. Shylock has lost his wealth, his faith, and his daughter’s inheritance. The brevity contrasts with his earlier eloquence (“Hath not a Jew eyes?”), suggesting he has been silenced. Elizabethan audience: his soul is saved. Modern audience: his identity is destroyed.
Lower band (1-2): Basic comment that Shylock agrees.

d171c631-27fb-43d2-96c0-c3efe1a975a2.text: How does Shakespeare use Portia’s disguise as Balthazar to explore the theme of appearance versus reality?
d171c631-27fb-43d2-96c0-c3efe1a975a2.marks:
Top band (7-8): Portia can only wield power by disguising herself as a man, reflecting patriarchal constraints. Creates dramatic irony (audience knows, characters do not). The wisest person in the room appears to be a young male lawyer but is actually a woman. Links to the caskets (surface vs substance), Shylock’s stereotype vs reality, and the ring subplot.
Top band (5–6) Clear analysis.
Mid band (3–4) Some points.
Lower band (1–2) Simple.

d171c631-27fb-43d2-96c0-c3efe1a975a2.text: Explore how Shakespeare presents the conflict between mercy and justice in the trial scene (Act 4, Scene 1).
d171c631-27fb-43d2-96c0-c3efe1a975a2.marks:
Top band (25–30 + 4 spelling/grammar)Analyses Portia’s mercy speech vs Shylock’s insistence on the bond. Both have legitimate arguments: mercy is divine, but the law must apply equally. Explores the hypocrisy: Christians demand mercy from Shylock but show none themselves. Forced conversion as the ultimate denial of mercy. Embeds context: Christian doctrine of mercy, Jewish legal protections in Venice, Elizabethan vs modern interpretations.

Upper band (19–24 + 3)Thoughtful.
Upper-mid band (13–18 + 2)Clear.
Mid band (7–12 + 2)Some understanding.
Lower-mid band (3–6 + 1)Limited.
Lower band (1–2 + 1)Simple.

d171c631-27fb-43d2-96c0-c3efe1a975a2.text: Analyse why Shylock insists on the bond rather than accepting three times the money. What does his refusal reveal about his character and his position in Venice?
d171c631-27fb-43d2-96c0-c3efe1a975a2.marks:
Top band (7-8): Shylock refuses money because the bond is about principle, not profit. The law is the only thing protecting him in a hostile society. If Venice breaks its own contract to save a Christian, no Jewish person’s rights are safe. His repetition of “my bond” shows determination. Links to his accumulated suffering: the abuse, Jessica, Leah’s ring.
Top band (5–6) Clear analysis.
Mid band (3–4) Some points.
Lower band (1–2) Simple.

d171c631-27fb-43d2-96c0-c3efe1a975a2.text: Analyse the metaphor “It droppeth as the gentle rain from heaven” in Portia’s mercy speech. How does it develop her argument?
d171c631-27fb-43d2-96c0-c3efe1a975a2.marks:
Upper band (3-4): Rain falls freely and naturally on everyone — mercy should be equally universal and unsolicited. “Gentle” suggests mercy is soft, nourishing, and life-giving. “From heaven” connects mercy to God, reinforcing the Christian argument. The metaphor positions mercy as divine law above human law. Ironic given what follows.
Lower band (1-2): Basic comment about mercy being like rain.

15e159ba-c6f0-4291-b6e8-75590d43b227.text: Your Spanish friend asks: '¿Qué vas a hacer después del instituto?' Write a response in Spanish of approximately 40 words. Include: your plans after school, a reason for your choice, and what job you would like in the future.
15e159ba-c6f0-4291-b6e8-75590d43b227.marks: Top band (5-6): States plans using future tense, gives a reason with 'porque', mentions a career aspiration, accurate Spanish with tense variety. Mid band (3-4): States plans with some reason, may lack future tense variety, mostly accurate. Lower band (1-2): Limited response, basic vocabulary, several errors. 0 marks: No relevant content.

87b60b35-30cb-44df-bb2a-28bce2001596.text: Read the following extract from the final chapter, beginning ‘Reader, I married him.’ Explore how Brontë uses language to present marriage as a partnership of equals.
87b60b35-30cb-44df-bb2a-28bce2001596.marks:
Top band (17-20) Judicious analysis. Examines: the active voice (‘I married him’ — Jane is the subject), the direct address to the reader, the description of mutual dependence (‘I am my husband’s life as fully as he is mine’), the absence of material wealth or beauty from the description of their happiness. Analyses how Brontë’s language choices reflect the novel’s central argument about equality in love.
Upper band (13-16) Thoughtful analysis with well-chosen references.
Top band (9-12): Clear understanding with some analysis.
Upper-mid band (5-8): Some relevant comments.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Limited response.
Lower band (1-2): Simple, brief response.

87b60b35-30cb-44df-bb2a-28bce2001596.text: In the novel as a whole, explore how Brontë presents the concept of equality between men and women.
87b60b35-30cb-44df-bb2a-28bce2001596.marks:
Top band (17-20) Convincing exploration across the text. Discusses: Jane’s childhood inequality at Gateshead, the master-servant dynamic at Thornfield, the proposal speech (‘my spirit addresses your spirit’), the reversal of power after the fire, the final marriage of equals. Links to Victorian gender norms and Brontë’s proto-feminist argument. Traces how equality must be earned through moral growth on both sides.
Upper band (13-16) Thoughtful response with relevant evidence.
Top band (9-12): Clear understanding with some analysis.
Upper-mid band (5-8): Some understanding.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Limited response.
Lower band (1-2): Simple comments.

87b60b35-30cb-44df-bb2a-28bce2001596.text: Read the following extract in which Jane discovers that Thornfield has been destroyed by fire. Explore how Brontë uses language to present the significance of the building’s destruction.
87b60b35-30cb-44df-bb2a-28bce2001596.marks:
Top band (17-20) Sophisticated analysis. Examines: the physical description of the ruins (blackened walls, empty windows), the symbolic destruction of secrets and deception, the Gothic imagery of fire and ruin, the emotional impact on Jane. Analyses how Brontë uses the destroyed building as a metaphor for the removal of everything false from the relationship.
Upper band (13-16) Thoughtful analysis with clear language focus.
Top band (9-12): Clear response with relevant evidence.
Upper-mid band (5-8): Some relevant comments.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Limited response.
Lower band (1-2): Simple, brief response.

87b60b35-30cb-44df-bb2a-28bce2001596.text: In the novel as a whole, explore how Brontë uses the theme of suffering and its consequences.
87b60b35-30cb-44df-bb2a-28bce2001596.marks:
Top band (17-20) Convincing exploration. Discusses: Jane’s childhood suffering (Gateshead, Lowood), Helen Burns’s suffering and death, Rochester’s suffering as penance (blindness, mutilation), Bertha’s imprisonment and death, St John’s self-imposed suffering. Analyses how Brontë presents suffering as both unjust (when imposed by others) and redemptive (when it leads to moral growth).
Upper band (13-16) Thoughtful response with relevant evidence.
Top band (9-12): Clear understanding with some references.
Upper-mid band (5-8): Some understanding.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Limited response.
Lower band (1-2): Simple comments.

87b60b35-30cb-44df-bb2a-28bce2001596.text: Read the following extract in which Jane finds Rochester at Ferndean. Explore how Brontë uses language to present the reversal of power between them.
87b60b35-30cb-44df-bb2a-28bce2001596.marks:
Top band (17-20) Perceptive analysis of the power reversal. Examines: Rochester’s physical dependence (blindness, reduced mobility), Jane’s confident, assertive language, the contrast with their earlier dynamic at Thornfield, the sensory details of Rochester’s diminished state. Analyses how Brontë uses this reversal to establish the conditions for an equal marriage.
Upper band (13-16) Thoughtful analysis with clear language focus.
Top band (9-12): Clear understanding with relevant evidence.
Upper-mid band (5-8): Some relevant points.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Limited response.
Lower band (1-2): Simple, brief response.

87b60b35-30cb-44df-bb2a-28bce2001596.text: In the novel as a whole, explore how Brontë structures the novel to create a satisfying resolution.
87b60b35-30cb-44df-bb2a-28bce2001596.marks:
Top band (17-20) Convincing analysis of structural choices. Discusses: the five locations as stages of Jane’s development (Gateshead, Lowood, Thornfield, Moor House, Ferndean), the parallel proposals (Rochester and St John), the symmetry of departure and return, the final paragraph about St John as a deliberate contrast. Analyses how Brontë uses structure to reinforce the theme of moral growth and earned happiness.
Upper band (13-16) Thoughtful response with relevant evidence.
Top band (9-12): Clear understanding with some analysis.
Upper-mid band (5-8): Some understanding.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Limited response.
Lower band (1-2): Simple comments.

def5e288-9add-4645-a0b6-e7f75bb25678.text: Write an article for a national newspaper arguing that the voting age should be lowered to 16. You should write between 300 and 400 words.
def5e288-9add-4645-a0b6-e7f75bb25678.marks:
Content and Organisation (24 marks):
Top band (19–24) Compelling, convincing communication. Extensive, ambitious vocabulary with sustained crafting of linguistic devices. Varied, effective structural features. Fluently linked complex ideas across the whole text.
Upper-mid band (13–18) Clearly communicated with a range of successful linguistic devices and structural features.
Lower-mid band (7–12) Some successful communication with some linguistic devices and structural features.
Lower band (1–6) Simple communication with simple vocabulary and structural features.

Technical Accuracy (16 marks):
Top band (13–16) Consistently secure sentence demarcation. Wide range of punctuation used accurately. Extensive, ambitious vocabulary. Spelling of ambitious words mostly accurate. Varied sentence structures.
Upper-mid band (9–12) Mostly secure demarcation. Range of punctuation mostly accurate. Increasingly sophisticated vocabulary.
Lower-mid band (5–8) Mostly accurate demarcation. Some controlled punctuation. Varied vocabulary.
Lower band (1–4) Occasionally accurate demarcation. Simple vocabulary.

def5e288-9add-4645-a0b6-e7f75bb25678.text: Write a letter to the head of your school council explaining why the school should invest in better mental health support for students.
def5e288-9add-4645-a0b6-e7f75bb25678.marks: As per standard Component 01 Section B mark scheme: Content and Organisation (24 marks) + Technical Accuracy (16 marks).

def5e288-9add-4645-a0b6-e7f75bb25678.text: Identify the Purpose, Audience, and Form (PAF) for the following task: 'Write an article for your local newspaper arguing that more cycle lanes should be built in your town.'
def5e288-9add-4645-a0b6-e7f75bb25678.marks: 1 mark for correctly identifying two of the three elements, 2 marks for all three. Purpose: to argue. Audience: local newspaper readers (adults). Form: article.

def5e288-9add-4645-a0b6-e7f75bb25678.text: Explain how a student could use the reading texts in Section A to improve their writing in Section B.
def5e288-9add-4645-a0b6-e7f75bb25678.marks:
Upper band (3-4): Clear explanation that Section B tasks link thematically to Section A texts, so students can borrow techniques (vocabulary, rhetorical devices, structural approaches) and adapt them. Thematic connection provides ideas.
Lower band (1-2): Some comment with limited detail.

def5e288-9add-4645-a0b6-e7f75bb25678.text: Analyse what makes the difference between a Level 3 and a Level 4 response in Section B. Consider both Content and Organisation and Technical Accuracy.
def5e288-9add-4645-a0b6-e7f75bb25678.marks:
Top band (7-8): Perceptive analysis showing Level 4 requires 'sustained' crafting (consistent throughout), 'compelling' communication (not just clear), 'varied' structures (not just some), and 'extensive' vocabulary. Links to specific mark scheme descriptors.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Clear analysis.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Some relevant comments.
Lower band (1-2): Simple identification.

def5e288-9add-4645-a0b6-e7f75bb25678.text: Evaluate the effectiveness of spending 5 minutes planning before writing in a timed exam. Consider the potential benefits and the argument that it 'wastes time'.
def5e288-9add-4645-a0b6-e7f75bb25678.marks:
Top band (10-12): Perceptive evaluation showing that planning improves structure, prevents repetition, ensures form conventions are adopted, and allows a deliberate ending. Addresses the counter-argument that 5 minutes reduces writing time but argues the trade-off is worthwhile because organised writing scores higher.
Upper-mid band (7-9): Clear evaluation.
Lower-mid band (4-6): Some evaluation.
Lower band (1-3): Simple statements.

96b4ea68-2891-4c65-9ef7-d2c4a13c6b9c.text: Identify two things you learn about the narrator from the opening paragraph of the extract.
96b4ea68-2891-4c65-9ef7-d2c4a13c6b9c.marks: 1 mark for each valid piece of explicit information correctly identified from the text. E.g. The narrator is alone / The narrator is in a particular location / The narrator feels a specific emotion. Must be directly supported by the text. Accept any two clear, distinct points.

96b4ea68-2891-4c65-9ef7-d2c4a13c6b9c.text: Select two quotations from lines 5 to 15 that show the mood of the setting.
96b4ea68-2891-4c65-9ef7-d2c4a13c6b9c.marks: 1 mark per correctly selected quotation that relates to mood/atmosphere. Quotations must come from the specified lines. E.g. selecting a phrase containing pathetic fallacy, sensory detail, or emotive vocabulary that establishes a particular mood. Both quotations must be distinct (not overlapping phrases).

96b4ea68-2891-4c65-9ef7-d2c4a13c6b9c.text: Summarise the main events described in the extract. You should identify at least three key points.
96b4ea68-2891-4c65-9ef7-d2c4a13c6b9c.marks: 1 mark per valid summary point up to 5 marks. Points must cover the main events/ideas, not minor details. Answers should be concise and in the student's own words where possible. Look for: clear identification of what happens, who is involved, and how the situation develops across the extract.

96b4ea68-2891-4c65-9ef7-d2c4a13c6b9c.text: Analyse how the writer uses vocabulary to create a sense of unease in the extract. You should comment on specific words and phrases.
96b4ea68-2891-4c65-9ef7-d2c4a13c6b9c.marks:
Top band (8-10): Sophisticated analysis of vocabulary with perceptive comments on effects. Multiple well-chosen examples with detailed exploration of connotations and impact on the reader.
Upper-mid band (5-7): Clear analysis with relevant examples and explained effects. Uses some subject terminology.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Some relevant comments on vocabulary with limited analysis of effects.
Lower band (1-2): Simple identification of words with no explanation of effect.

96b4ea68-2891-4c65-9ef7-d2c4a13c6b9c.text: Compare how two writers present their attitudes towards danger. You should compare their ideas and the methods they use.
96b4ea68-2891-4c65-9ef7-d2c4a13c6b9c.marks:
Top band (8-10): Perceptive comparison of both writers' ideas and methods. Clear understanding of different perspectives with well-integrated evidence from both texts. Analyses how methods shape meaning.
Upper-mid band (5-7): Clear comparison with relevant evidence from both texts. Some analysis of methods.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Some comparison attempted but may be unbalanced or lack method analysis.
Lower band (1-2): Simple reference to one or both texts with no real comparison.

96b4ea68-2891-4c65-9ef7-d2c4a13c6b9c.text: Write a narrative about a journey that changes the main character. Choose your own title. You should aim to write about 450–600 words.
96b4ea68-2891-4c65-9ef7-d2c4a13c6b9c.marks:
Content and Organisation (24 marks):
Top band (19–24) Compelling, convincing communication with extensive, ambitious vocabulary. Writing is compelling with varied, effective structural features.
Upper-mid band (13–18) Consistent, clear communication with increasingly sophisticated vocabulary. Effective structure.
Mid band (7–12) Mostly successful communication with varied vocabulary. Some structural features used.
Lower-mid band (4–6) Some success in communication. Simple vocabulary. Limited structure.
Lower band (1–3) Limited communication.

Technical Accuracy (16 marks):
Top band (13–16) Extensive accuracy in spelling, punctuation and grammar. Wide range of sentence structures.
Upper-mid band (10–12) Consistent accuracy with some variety of sentence structures.
Mid band (7–9) Mostly accurate with some variety.
Lower-mid band (4–6) Some accuracy. Simple sentence structures.
Lower band (1–3) Limited accuracy.

6c73d5c3-cc14-4075-8b09-e46843e64dd0.text: Identify two relevant features from the specified lines.
6c73d5c3-cc14-4075-8b09-e46843e64dd0.marks: 1 mark per valid feature identified with brief evidence, up to 2 marks.

6c73d5c3-cc14-4075-8b09-e46843e64dd0.text: Explain how the writer uses language to create a specific effect. Use evidence from the text.
6c73d5c3-cc14-4075-8b09-e46843e64dd0.marks:
Upper band (3-4): Clear explanation with relevant evidence and analysis of effect.
Lower band (1-2): Some identification with limited comment.

6c73d5c3-cc14-4075-8b09-e46843e64dd0.text: Analyse how the writer uses language and/or structure to achieve their purpose. Use subject terminology.
6c73d5c3-cc14-4075-8b09-e46843e64dd0.marks:
Top band (7-8): Perceptive analysis with precise terminology.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Clear analysis.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Some relevant comments.
Lower band (1-2): Simple identification.

6c73d5c3-cc14-4075-8b09-e46843e64dd0.text: Compare how the two writers convey their perspectives. Consider ideas and methods.
6c73d5c3-cc14-4075-8b09-e46843e64dd0.marks:
Top band (10-12): Perceptive comparison with well-integrated evidence.
Upper-mid band (7-9): Clear comparison.
Lower-mid band (4-6): Some comparison.
Lower band (1-3): Simple statements.

6c73d5c3-cc14-4075-8b09-e46843e64dd0.text: Write a piece of non-fiction for a specified audience and purpose.
6c73d5c3-cc14-4075-8b09-e46843e64dd0.marks:
Content and Organisation (24 marks):
Top band (19–24) Compelling communication.
Upper-mid band (13–18) Clearly communicated.
Lower-mid band (7–12) Some success.
Lower band (1–6) Simple.

Technical Accuracy (16 marks):
Top band (13–16) Highly accurate.
Upper-mid band (9–12) Mostly accurate.
Lower-mid band (5–8) Some accuracy.
Lower band (1–4) Limited accuracy.

6c73d5c3-cc14-4075-8b09-e46843e64dd0.text: Explain how a specific word or phrase affects the reader's understanding.
6c73d5c3-cc14-4075-8b09-e46843e64dd0.marks:
Upper band (3-4): Analyses connotations and effect with evidence.
Lower band (1-2): Basic comment.

6e9ff192-4d7b-4f81-89a6-1ea433ce62bb.text: Identify the technique used in this sentence: 'The city was a beast, growling and restless.'
6e9ff192-4d7b-4f81-89a6-1ea433ce62bb.marks: Metaphor (1 mark) — the city is directly compared to a beast without using 'like' or 'as.' Also accept personification ('growling and restless' gives the city animal qualities).

6e9ff192-4d7b-4f81-89a6-1ea433ce62bb.text: Select one term from this list — simile, personification, semantic field — and explain how a 19th-century writer might use it to create a Gothic atmosphere.
6e9ff192-4d7b-4f81-89a6-1ea433ce62bb.marks: 1 mark for selecting a term. 1 mark for a clear explanation (e.g. 'A semantic field of darkness — words like shadow, gloom, and twilight — would build a consistently threatening atmosphere associated with Gothic fiction').

6e9ff192-4d7b-4f81-89a6-1ea433ce62bb.text: Summarise the difference between effective and ineffective use of subject terminology in an exam answer.
6e9ff192-4d7b-4f81-89a6-1ea433ce62bb.marks: Effective use: terminology is integrated into analysis (1 mark), followed by quotation and explanation of effect (1 mark), accurate identification (1 mark). Ineffective use: technique named without analysis — 'feature-spotting' (1 mark). Students should prioritise depth over breadth — fewer terms analysed well beats many terms listed superficially (1 mark).

6e9ff192-4d7b-4f81-89a6-1ea433ce62bb.text:
Read the following extract:

'The snow fell softly, silently, smothering the fields in white. Beneath the surface, the earth was frozen solid — dead, hard, unforgiving.'

Analyse how the writer uses language techniques in this extract. Use subject terminology accurately in your response.
6e9ff192-4d7b-4f81-89a6-1ea433ce62bb.marks:
Top band (8–10) Perceptive analysis with accurate terminology.
Upper-mid band (5–7) Clear analysis with mostly accurate terminology.
Lower-mid band (3–4) Some relevant comments.
Lower band (1–2) Simple identification.

Expected points: Sibilance in 'softly, silently, smothering' creates a hushed, gentle quality but 'smothering' shifts to menace (suffocation); tricolon 'softly, silently, smothering' builds accumulation; personification in 'smothering' gives the snow agency; dash creates a structural pause before the contrasting description of earth; tricolon 'dead, hard, unforgiving' — adjectives escalate, semantic field of death; contrast/juxtaposition between the soft surface and the harsh earth beneath.

6e9ff192-4d7b-4f81-89a6-1ea433ce62bb.text:
Evaluate the following student response:

'The writer uses sibilance. There is also alliteration. The snow is described as soft. This makes the reader feel calm.'

How could this answer be improved?
6e9ff192-4d7b-4f81-89a6-1ea433ce62bb.marks:
Top band (12–15) Perceptive evaluation with specific improvements.
Upper-mid band (8–11) Clear evaluation.
Lower-mid band (4–7) Some evaluation.
Lower band (1–3) Simple response.

Weaknesses: lists techniques without analysis; doesn't quote specific evidence; 'makes the reader feel calm' is too vague; doesn't explore connotations or effects. Improvements: quote the specific words ('softly, silently, smothering'); explore connotations of 'smothering' — it shifts from calm to sinister; integrate terminology into analysis sentences; explain how sibilance creates a hushed quality that contrasts with the violence of 'smothering.'

6e9ff192-4d7b-4f81-89a6-1ea433ce62bb.text: Write a paragraph of descriptive writing (approximately 150 words) about a thunderstorm. Deliberately include at least three different language techniques and aim for vivid, atmospheric writing.
6e9ff192-4d7b-4f81-89a6-1ea433ce62bb.marks:
Content and Organisation (24 marks):
Top band (19–24) Compelling writing with sophisticated technique use.
Upper-mid band (13–18) Engaging writing with clear technique use.
Lower-mid band (7–12) Some successful writing.
Lower band (1–6) Simple writing.

Technical Accuracy (16 marks):
Top band (13–16) Accurate with varied sentences.
Upper-mid band (9–12) Mostly accurate.
Lower-mid band (5–8) Some accuracy.
Lower band (1–4) Limited accuracy.

Techniques might include: personification of the storm, onomatopoeia, simile/metaphor, sensory language, pathetic fallacy, varied sentence structures.

c90dfe31-8efe-4f15-816d-286530356959.text: Read Act 5, Scene 1 from “In such a night as this” to “In such a night / Did Jessica steal from the wealthy Jew.” How does Shakespeare use language and structure in this extract to create a sense of both romance and unease? Write about the extract and the play as a whole.
c90dfe31-8efe-4f15-816d-286530356959.marks:
Top band (25–30 + 4 spelling/grammar)Analyses the lyrical language (moonlight, music, "sweet wind"), the stichomythia (alternating lines), and the classical allusions (all stories of tragic love). The word “steal” applied to Jessica echoes “thief” and connects love to loss. Links to the wider play: appearance vs reality, the play’s resistance to comic resolution. Embeds context: Elizabethan expectations of comedy, modern critical readings.

Upper band (19–24 + 3)Thoughtful.
Upper-mid band (13–18 + 2)Clear.
Mid band (7–12 + 2)Some understanding.
Lower-mid band (3–6 + 1)Limited.
Lower band (1–2 + 1)Simple.

c90dfe31-8efe-4f15-816d-286530356959.text: Analyse the significance of Jessica’s line “I am never merry when I hear sweet music” (Act 5, Scene 1).
c90dfe31-8efe-4f15-816d-286530356959.marks:
Upper band (3-4): In a scene celebrating harmony, Jessica feels no joy. “Never merry” suggests permanent sadness, not temporary mood. Music represents Christian civilisation in Lorenzo’s speech, so Jessica’s inability to enjoy it implies she remains an outsider despite her conversion. Possible interpretations: guilt over abandoning Shylock, homesickness for her Jewish community, awareness that she does not fully belong.
Lower band (1-2): Basic comment about Jessica being sad.

c90dfe31-8efe-4f15-816d-286530356959.text: Explore how Shakespeare uses the ring trick in Act 5 to develop the theme of fidelity and trust.
c90dfe31-8efe-4f15-816d-286530356959.marks:
Top band (7-8): The ring symbolises Bassanio’s oath; giving it away breaks his promise within hours. Portia’s threat to sleep with the lawyer (herself) exposes the fragility of male honour. The trick gives Portia power: she controls the revelation and the resolution. Parallels the bond plot — both involve promises with consequences for breaking them. Gratiano’s crude final line undermines romantic idealism.
Top band (5–6) Clear analysis.
Mid band (3–4) Some points.
Lower band (1–2) Simple.

c90dfe31-8efe-4f15-816d-286530356959.text: How does Shakespeare present Antonio at the end of the play? Is his story resolved?
c90dfe31-8efe-4f15-816d-286530356959.marks:
Top band (7-8): Antonio’s ships return, restoring his wealth, but he remains unmarried and alone. He opened the play with “I know not why I am so sad” and ends in a similar position. The couples are paired; Antonio is the odd one out. Some critics read this as unresolved grief over losing Bassanio. His generosity (funding Bassanio, interceding for Shylock) may mask emptiness. The comic resolution fails to include him.
Top band (5–6) Clear analysis.
Mid band (3–4) Some points.
Lower band (1–2) Simple.

c90dfe31-8efe-4f15-816d-286530356959.text: Starting with Act 5, Scene 1, explore how Shakespeare uses music and harmony to present the ending of The Merchant of Venice. Write about the extract and the play as a whole.
c90dfe31-8efe-4f15-816d-286530356959.marks:
Top band (25–30 + 4 spelling/grammar)Analyses Lorenzo’s music speech (“the man that hath no music”), its implicit condemnation of Shylock, and its celebration of civilisation. Then explores the contradictions: Jessica’s unease, the tragic allusions, the exclusionary nature of Belmont’s harmony. Links to the wider play: Shylock’s forced silence, the caskets’ lesson about surfaces. Embeds context: Elizabethan ideas about music and cosmic harmony, the play as a problem comedy.

Upper band (19–24 + 3)Thoughtful.
Upper-mid band (13–18 + 2)Clear.
Mid band (7–12 + 2)Some understanding.
Lower-mid band (3–6 + 1)Limited.
Lower band (1–2 + 1)Simple.

c90dfe31-8efe-4f15-816d-286530356959.text: Analyse why Shakespeare names tragic classical lovers (Troilus, Pyramus, Dido) in Act 5, Scene 1. What effect does this create?
c90dfe31-8efe-4f15-816d-286530356959.marks:
Upper band (3-4): The allusions create irony: the scene’s romantic surface is undercut by references to betrayal, miscommunication, and abandonment. The audience recognises these as unhappy endings, which foreshadows the ring trick conflict and suggests the play’s “happy ending” may be superficial. Shakespeare uses dramatic irony — the characters cite these lovers playfully, unaware of the ominous parallels.
Lower band (1-2): Basic comment about the classical references.

0bc380fd-7b3f-463c-9d70-f9cfdcf4bb3b.text: Read the following extract from Chapter 12, in which Jane reflects on women’s need for intellectual stimulation: ‘Women are supposed to be very calm generally: but women feel just as men feel.’ Explore how Brontë uses language to present her views on gender.
0bc380fd-7b3f-463c-9d70-f9cfdcf4bb3b.marks:
Top band (17-20) Judicious analysis. Examines: the direct, assertive tone, the use of ‘supposed to be’ highlighting societal expectation versus reality, the parallel structure (‘women feel just as men feel’), the address to an implied audience who holds these assumptions. Analyses how Brontë breaks the fourth wall to make a direct feminist argument through Jane’s narration.
Upper band (13-16) Thoughtful analysis with well-chosen references.
Top band (9-12): Clear understanding with relevant evidence.
Upper-mid band (5-8): Some relevant comments.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Limited response.
Lower band (1-2): Simple, brief response.

0bc380fd-7b3f-463c-9d70-f9cfdcf4bb3b.text: In the novel as a whole, explore how Brontë presents the theme of independence.
0bc380fd-7b3f-463c-9d70-f9cfdcf4bb3b.marks:
Top band (17-20) Convincing exploration tracing independence across the novel. Discusses: Jane’s powerlessness at Gateshead, her education and early self-assertion at Lowood, her employment at Thornfield, her refusal to be Rochester’s mistress (‘I care for myself’), her financial independence through the inheritance, and her free choice to return to Rochester. Shows how Brontë structures each stage of the novel as a step towards autonomy.
Upper band (13-16) Thoughtful response with relevant evidence.
Top band (9-12): Clear understanding with some analysis.
Upper-mid band (5-8): Some understanding.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Limited response.
Lower band (1-2): Simple comments.

0bc380fd-7b3f-463c-9d70-f9cfdcf4bb3b.text: Read the following extract from Chapter 27, in which Jane resists Rochester’s plea to stay. Explore how Brontë uses language to present the conflict between passion and principle.
0bc380fd-7b3f-463c-9d70-f9cfdcf4bb3b.marks:
Top band (17-20) Sophisticated analysis of the internal conflict. Examines: Jane’s resolute, declarative sentences, the imagery of self-respect and survival, the tension between emotional language (love, longing) and moral language (duty, conscience), how Brontë uses dialogue to dramatise an ethical crisis. Precise word-level analysis.

10ed47ce-c22e-4247-b475-8ee9f117aeda.text: Read Act 1, Scene 3 from “Three thousand ducats; well” to “I will be assured I may.” How does Shakespeare present the relationship between Shylock and Bassanio in this extract? Write about the extract and the play as a whole.
10ed47ce-c22e-4247-b475-8ee9f117aeda.marks:

Links to the wider play: the bond, the trial, Shylock’s revenge. Embeds context: usury, Venice’s dependence on Jewish finance. Explores ambiguity: is Shylock cautious or predatory?

Upper band (19–24 + 3)Thoughtful response with evidence and context.
Upper-mid band (13–18 + 2)Clear response with some analysis.
Mid band (7–12 + 2)Some understanding.
Lower-mid band (3–6 + 1)Limited.

10ed47ce-c22e-4247-b475-8ee9f117aeda.text: Analyse the significance of Antonio’s line “I am as like to call thee so again, / To spit on thee again” (Act 1, Scene 3). What does this reveal about his character?
10ed47ce-c22e-4247-b475-8ee9f117aeda.marks:
Upper band (3-4): Antonio refuses to show remorse or change his behaviour, even while asking Shylock for money. The repetition of “again” shows defiance. His honesty is striking but morally troubling — he sees no contradiction in borrowing from someone he openly despises. This reflects the wider Christian hypocrisy in the play.
Lower band (1-2): Basic identification that Antonio is rude to Shylock.

10ed47ce-c22e-4247-b475-8ee9f117aeda.text: Read the casket inscriptions in Act 2. How does Shakespeare use the three caskets to explore the theme of appearance versus reality?
10ed47ce-c22e-4247-b475-8ee9f117aeda.marks:
Top band (7-8): Gold appeals to greed ("what many men desire"), silver to arrogance ("as much as he deserves"), lead to selflessness ("give and hazard all he hath"). The correct casket is the least attractive externally, reinforcing that true value is hidden beneath the surface. Morocco and Arragon fail because they judge by appearances. Links to the play’s wider themes: Shylock judged by his religion, Portia disguised as Balthazar.
Top band (5–6) Clear analysis with several points.
Mid band (3–4) Some relevant comments.
Lower band (1–2) Simple.

10ed47ce-c22e-4247-b475-8ee9f117aeda.text: Explore how Shakespeare presents Jessica’s elopement in Act 2. Is it an act of love, betrayal, or both?

Links to the theme of appearance vs reality and the wider marginalisation of Shylock.
Top band (5–6) Clear analysis.
Mid band (3–4) Some points.
Lower band (1–2) Simple.

Mid band (7–12 + 2)Some understanding.
Lower-mid band (3–6 + 1)Limited.

10ed47ce-c22e-4247-b475-8ee9f117aeda.text: Analyse how Portia’s line “Let all of his complexion choose me so” (Act 2, Scene 7) complicates the audience’s view of her character.

8d45eaa7-05bc-43de-abc9-a75cb0a0942a.marks: An independent clause is a group of words that contains a subject and a verb and can stand alone as a complete sentence (1 mark).

8d45eaa7-05bc-43de-abc9-a75cb0a0942a.text: Describe two effects a semicolon can create in creative writing.
8d45eaa7-05bc-43de-abc9-a75cb0a0942a.marks:
1 marks for each effect, up to 2 marks. Possible answers:
• It can create contrast/juxtaposition by placing two opposing ideas side by side (1)
• It can extend a description by adding a second layer of detail (1)
• It can build tension or suspense by linking stillness with action (1)
• It can control pace by creating a pause shorter than a full stop (1)

8d45eaa7-05bc-43de-abc9-a75cb0a0942a.text: Explain why the following sentence uses the semicolon incorrectly: 'He ran through the forest; gasping for air.' Write a corrected version.
8d45eaa7-05bc-43de-abc9-a75cb0a0942a.marks:
Award up to 4 marks:
• Identifies that 'gasping for air' is not a complete/independent clause (1)
• Explains that both sides of a semicolon must be able to stand alone as sentences (1)
• Explains that 'gasping for air' is a fragment/phrase without a subject and main verb (1)
• Provides a correct version, e.g. 'He ran through the forest; his lungs burned with every breath' (1)

8d45eaa7-05bc-43de-abc9-a75cb0a0942a.text: Explain how a writer could use semicolons alongside other sentence structures (such as short sentences) to create a varied and effective piece of descriptive writing. Use examples in your answer.
8d45eaa7-05bc-43de-abc9-a75cb0a0942a.marks:

• Explains that short sentences create sharp, punchy effects such as tension or shock (1)
• Explains that semicolons create longer, flowing sentences that can develop or contrast ideas (1)
• Explains that varying between short and semicolon-linked sentences shows control of pace (1)
• Provides an effective example of a short sentence used for impact (1)
• Provides an effective example of a semicolon sentence used for contrast, description, or suspense (1)
• Links this variation to the AO6 requirement for a range of sentence structures and punctuation (1)

8d45eaa7-05bc-43de-abc9-a75cb0a0942a.text:
Read the following extract from a student's creative writing:

'The house stood at the end of the lane. It was old. The windows were dark. The garden was overgrown. Nobody had lived there for years.'

Evaluate this extract and rewrite it to include at least one semicolon, explaining how your changes improve the writing.
8d45eaa7-05bc-43de-abc9-a75cb0a0942a.marks:
Award marks across two areas:

Evaluation of the original (up to 4 marks):
• Identifies that the original uses only simple/short sentences with full stops (1)
• Comments that this creates a repetitive, monotonous rhythm (1)
• Notes the lack of punctuation range limits the technical accuracy mark (1)
• Recognises that while short sentences can create tension, using only short sentences loses impact (1)

Rewrite and explanation (up to 5 marks):
• Rewrites with at least one correctly used semicolon (both halves are independent clauses) (1)
• Explains the effect of the semicolon (e.g. contrast, extension, tension) (1)
• Shows variation in sentence structure beyond just the semicolon (1)
• Explains how the rewrite demonstrates a wider range of punctuation for AO6 (1)
• Quality and sophistication of the rewritten passage (1)

1ccb1a24-4de7-44df-9d77-48ce1d099c4a.text: Read the following quotation describing Snowball during the Battle of the Cowshed: 'Without halting for an instant, Snowball flung his fifteen stone against Jones's legs.' How does Orwell use this moment to present Snowball's leadership?
1ccb1a24-4de7-44df-9d77-48ce1d099c4a.marks:
Analysis of language.
• The verb 'flung' conveys physical courage and decisive action (1 mark).
• 'Without halting for an instant' suggests fearlessness — Snowball attacks the enemy leader personally, even after being shot (1 mark).
• The contrast with Napoleon's absence highlights two opposing models of leadership — action versus manipulation (1 mark).
• Contextually, this parallels Trotsky's role as commander of the Red Army, leading from the front (1 mark).

1ccb1a24-4de7-44df-9d77-48ce1d099c4a.text:
How far does Orwell present Snowball as the hero of Animal Farm?

Write about:
• what Snowball says and does
• how far Orwell presents Snowball as the hero of Animal Farm.
1ccb1a24-4de7-44df-9d77-48ce1d099c4a.marks:
AO1 (up to 4 marks): Response to the question across the text.
AO2 (up to 4 marks): Analysis of methods.
Top band (7-8): May discuss: Snowball's bravery at the Battle of the Cowshed; his wound as a badge of honour; his eloquence in debates; his windmill plans showing genuine desire to improve the animals' lives; his care for education; BUT also his participation in the pigs' early privileges; his use of simplified slogans; his willingness to accept the milk/apples arrangement; the nuance of Orwell's characterisation — Snowball is better than Napoleon but still a pig; parallel with Trotsky — intellectual, idealistic but ultimately outmanoeuvred.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Clear analysis.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Some analysis.
Lower band (1-2): Simple comments.

1ccb1a24-4de7-44df-9d77-48ce1d099c4a.text:
Starting with the medal the animals create after the battle in Chapter 4, 'Animal Hero, First Class', explore how Orwell uses rituals and ceremonies to develop ideas about power. Write about:
• how Orwell presents the rituals created after the battle
• how Orwell uses rituals across the whole novel to explore ideas about power.
1ccb1a24-4de7-44df-9d77-48ce1d099c4a.marks:
AO1 (up to 4 marks): Response to the quotation and whole text.
AO2 (up to 4 marks): Analysis of methods.
Top band (7-8): May discuss: 'Animal Hero, First Class' creating a hierarchy that contradicts equality; the gun-firing ritual generating emotional loyalty; how Napoleon later uses rituals to strengthen his cult of personality (Minimus's poem, spontaneous demonstrations); the banning of 'Beasts of England' as the ultimate ritual removal; how rituals replace genuine democracy — ceremony instead of debate; parallel with Soviet military parades and Stalin's cult of personality.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Clear analysis.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Some analysis.
Lower band (1-2): Simple comments.

1ccb1a24-4de7-44df-9d77-48ce1d099c4a.text: How does Orwell use the character of Snowball to explore ideas about leadership in Animal Farm? Consider the whole text in your response.
1ccb1a24-4de7-44df-9d77-48ce1d099c4a.marks:
AO1 (up to 4 marks): Critical, exploratory response.
AO2 (up to 4 marks): Analysis of methods.
AO3 (up to 4 marks): Context.
Top band (10-12): Convincing analysis. May explore: Snowball as intellectual leader who uses debate; his bravery at the Cowshed; his windmill as symbol of progress; the contrast with Napoleon's behind-the-scenes manipulation; Snowball's expulsion showing that principled leadership is no match for ruthless force; the rewriting of his heroism into treachery — Orwell's warning about how regimes control historical memory; parallel with Trotsky — exiled, demonised, eventually murdered; Orwell's suggestion that good leadership requires more than intelligence — it requires awareness of power politics.
Upper-mid band (7-9): Clear response.
Lower-mid band (4-6): Supported.
Lower band (1-3): Simple.

Lower band (1-5) Simple.
