a743ffec-de42-4021-8d08-73623c6de2fa.text: Identify two pieces of explicit information from this sentence: 'The old man sat alone in the darkened parlour, a half-empty glass of port beside him.'
a743ffec-de42-4021-8d08-73623c6de2fa.marks: Any two from: the man is old / he is alone / the parlour is dark / there is a glass of port / the glass is half-empty. 1 mark for two correct identifications.

a743ffec-de42-4021-8d08-73623c6de2fa.text: Select one word from the following sentence and explain what it implicitly suggests: 'She crept down the corridor, pressing herself against the cold wall.'
a743ffec-de42-4021-8d08-73623c6de2fa.marks: 'Crept' (1 mark) — implies she is trying to avoid being seen or heard, suggesting fear, secrecy, or caution (1 mark). OR 'pressing' — implies urgency or a desire to make herself small, suggesting she feels threatened. OR 'cold' — implies an unwelcoming, possibly hostile environment.

a743ffec-de42-4021-8d08-73623c6de2fa.text: Summarise the difference between explicit and implicit information, using an example of each from 19th-century fiction.
a743ffec-de42-4021-8d08-73623c6de2fa.marks: Explicit information is directly stated in the text (1 mark). Example: 'It was December' — the time of year is clearly stated (1 mark). Implicit information is suggested rather than stated, requiring the reader to infer meaning from clues (1 mark). Example: 'The bare branches scratched at the window like bony fingers' — implies a threatening, Gothic atmosphere without stating it directly (1 mark). The key difference: explicit can be pointed to; implicit must be interpreted (1 mark).

a743ffec-de42-4021-8d08-73623c6de2fa.text:
Read the following extract:

'The house stood at the end of a narrow lane, half-hidden by overgrown hedgerows. No smoke rose from the chimney. The gate hung open on a single rusted hinge.'

Analyse how the writer uses language to create a sense of neglect and abandonment.
a743ffec-de42-4021-8d08-73623c6de2fa.marks:
Top band (8–10) Perceptive analysis with well-chosen evidence and detailed understanding of effects.
Upper-mid band (5–7) Clear analysis with appropriate evidence.
Lower-mid band (3–4) Some relevant comments with limited evidence.
Lower band (1–2) Simple identification.

Expected points: 'half-hidden' suggests the house is forgotten or deliberately concealed; 'overgrown hedgerows' implies no one has maintained the property; 'No smoke rose from the chimney' — the absence of smoke implies no warmth, no life, no inhabitants; 'hung open' suggests the gate has been left — no one closed it, implying sudden departure or long absence; 'single rusted hinge' — 'rusted' connotes decay and the passage of time; 'single' emphasises fragility. Overall effect: the accumulation of neglect details creates unease.

a743ffec-de42-4021-8d08-73623c6de2fa.text: A student said: 'Implicit information is more important than explicit information in the Edexcel English Language exam.' To what extent do you agree?
a743ffec-de42-4021-8d08-73623c6de2fa.marks:
Top band (12–15) Perceptive evaluation with convincing reasoning.
Upper-mid band (8–11) Clear evaluation with relevant reasoning.
Lower-mid band (4–7) Some evaluation with basic reasoning.
Lower band (1–3) Simple response.

Students may argue: agree — higher-mark questions (analyse language, evaluate) all require inference; implicit reading is what separates grade boundaries; AO1 includes 'interpret' which demands implicit understanding. Partial agreement — both are needed; explicit info provides the evidence base for implicit analysis; you cannot infer without first identifying. Disagree — the exam starts with explicit identification questions; getting these right builds confidence and secures foundation marks.

a743ffec-de42-4021-8d08-73623c6de2fa.text: Write a short paragraph (approximately 100 words) describing a character arriving at a house for the first time. Include at least two pieces of explicit information and two implicit suggestions about the character's mood.
a743ffec-de42-4021-8d08-73623c6de2fa.marks:
Content and Organisation (24 marks):
Top band (19–24) Compelling writing with sophisticated vocabulary and structural control.
Upper-mid band (13–18) Engaging writing with clear ideas.
Lower-mid band (7–12) Some successful writing.
Lower band (1–6) Simple writing.

Technical Accuracy (16 marks):
Top band (13–16) Wide range of accurate sentence structures and spelling.
Upper-mid band (9–12) Mostly accurate.
Lower-mid band (5–8) Some accuracy.
Lower band (1–4) Limited accuracy.

Explicit details might include: time of day, weather, physical description of the house. Implicit mood details might include: word choices suggesting anxiety, excitement, or reluctance; sentence structure reflecting emotional state.

1ce5dc92-964f-4195-9acd-dce652dae27b.text: Identify one example of figurative language from this sentence: 'The fog crept through the streets like a grey cat.'
1ce5dc92-964f-4195-9acd-dce652dae27b.marks: Simile — 'like a grey cat' compares the fog's movement to that of a cat. 1 mark.

1ce5dc92-964f-4195-9acd-dce652dae27b.text: Select the word 'crept' from the sentence above and explain what it suggests about the fog.
1ce5dc92-964f-4195-9acd-dce652dae27b.marks: 'Crept' (1 mark) suggests the fog moves slowly and stealthily, like something alive trying to go unnoticed (1 mark). It personifies the fog, giving it a quiet, slightly sinister quality.

1ce5dc92-964f-4195-9acd-dce652dae27b.text: Summarise the difference between connotation and denotation, giving an example of each for the word 'cold.'
1ce5dc92-964f-4195-9acd-dce652dae27b.marks: Denotation is the literal dictionary meaning of a word (1 mark). The denotation of 'cold' is a low temperature (1 mark). Connotation is the associations or feelings a word evokes beyond its literal meaning (1 mark). The connotations of 'cold' include hostility, emotional distance, death, or loneliness (1 mark). Writers choose words for their connotations to shape how readers feel about characters and settings (1 mark).

1ce5dc92-964f-4195-9acd-dce652dae27b.text:
Read the following extract:

'The river was a black ribbon winding through the valley. Its banks were choked with dead reeds, and the water moved sluggishly, as if reluctant to continue its journey.'

Analyse how the writer uses language to present the river.
1ce5dc92-964f-4195-9acd-dce652dae27b.marks:
Top band (8–10) Perceptive analysis with detailed understanding of effects.
Upper-mid band (5–7) Clear analysis with appropriate evidence.
Lower-mid band (3–4) Some relevant comments.
Lower band (1–2) Simple identification.

Expected points: 'black ribbon' — metaphor comparing river to a ribbon suggests something decorative yet 'black' connotes death, mourning, or foreboding; 'choked' — personification suggesting suffocation, the riverbanks are overwhelmed; 'dead reeds' — semantic field of death and decay; 'sluggishly' — implies heaviness, reluctance, lack of energy; 'as if reluctant to continue its journey' — personification gives the river human emotion, suggests weariness or hopelessness; overall creates an atmosphere of stagnation and despair.

1ce5dc92-964f-4195-9acd-dce652dae27b.text: A student wrote: 'The writer uses a metaphor to describe the river.' Evaluate this response. How could it be improved to achieve a higher mark?
1ce5dc92-964f-4195-9acd-dce652dae27b.marks:
Top band (12–15) Perceptive evaluation.
Upper-mid band (8–11) Clear evaluation.
Lower-mid band (4–7) Some evaluation.
Lower band (1–3) Simple response.

The student's response is feature-spotting without analysis. To improve: (1) quote the specific metaphor — 'a black ribbon'; (2) explore connotations — 'ribbon' suggests something decorative and perhaps fragile, while 'black' connotes death; (3) explain the effect — the combination suggests the river is both beautiful and sinister; (4) link to the question — this creates an unsettling atmosphere. The improved version demonstrates AO2 by analysing how language achieves effects, rather than just naming a technique.

Upper-mid band (9–12) Mostly accurate.
Lower-mid band (5–8) Some accuracy.
Lower band (1–4) Limited accuracy.

Look for: consistent semantic field of sadness/decay, effective figurative language, sensory detail, vocabulary with appropriate connotations.

7030faca-056d-47de-9eb1-7bafbc89579e.text: Write an article for a national newspaper arguing that social media should be banned for under-16s.

7030faca-056d-47de-9eb1-7bafbc89579e.text: Identify two features of effective argumentative writing.
7030faca-056d-47de-9eb1-7bafbc89579e.marks: 1 mark per valid feature, up to 2 marks. Accept: clear thesis/position, counter-arguments, evidence/examples, logical structure, rhetorical devices, formal register, discourse markers, etc.

7030faca-056d-47de-9eb1-7bafbc89579e.text: Explain why acknowledging counter-arguments can strengthen a piece of argumentative writing.

Lower band (1-2): Some comment on counter-arguments with limited explanation.

7030faca-056d-47de-9eb1-7bafbc89579e.text: Analyse how a writer could use rhetorical techniques to make an argument about reducing plastic waste more compelling. Consider at least three techniques.

Upper-mid band (5-6): Clear analysis with relevant examples.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Some relevant comments.

7030faca-056d-47de-9eb1-7bafbc89579e.text: Evaluate the statement: 'The best argumentative writing is always completely objective and never uses emotional language.'

Upper-mid band (7-9): Clear evaluation with some nuance.
Lower-mid band (4-6): Some evaluation with basic points.

6c6d2adb-b6b9-4931-bb62-45e23414cb5b.text: Read Act 4, Scene 1 from “Do not live, Hero; do not ope thine eyes” to “Would the two princes lie?” How does Shakespeare use language in this extract to present Leonato’s response to Hero’s shaming? Write about the extract and the play as a whole.
6c6d2adb-b6b9-4931-bb62-45e23414cb5b.marks:
Top band (25–30 + 4 spelling/grammar)Analyses Leonato’s imperatives (“Do not live”), his prioritising of reputation over his daughter’s life, and his willingness to believe the accusation without evidence. Links to the wider play: the Friar’s plan, Hero’s restoration, Leonato’s later rage at Claudio. Embeds context: patriarchal honour culture, female chastity as family property. Explores whether Shakespeare endorses or critiques Leonato’s response.

Upper band (19–24 + 3)Thoughtful.
Upper-mid band (13–18 + 2)Clear.
Mid band (7–12 + 2)Some understanding.
Lower-mid band (3–6 + 1)Limited.
Lower band (1–2 + 1)Simple.

6c6d2adb-b6b9-4931-bb62-45e23414cb5b.text: Explore how Shakespeare presents different attitudes towards love and marriage through Claudio/Hero and Beatrice/Benedick.
6c6d2adb-b6b9-4931-bb62-45e23414cb5b.marks:
Top band (25–30 + 4 spelling/grammar)Claudio follows courtship conventions (proxy wooing, paternal consent, public betrothal) — his love is performative and fragile (easily destroyed by Don John). Beatrice/Benedick resist convention: their “merry war” values wit and equality. Discusses how the two couples represent different models of love. Embeds context: Elizabethan marriage practices, female autonomy. Analyses key quotations.

Upper band (19–24 + 3)Thoughtful.
Upper-mid band (13–18 + 2)Clear.
Mid band (7–12 + 2)Some understanding.
Lower-mid band (3–6 + 1)Limited.
Lower band (1–2 + 1)Simple.

6c6d2adb-b6b9-4931-bb62-45e23414cb5b.text: Analyse the significance of the title Much Ado About Nothing. How does the “nothing/noting” pun relate to the play’s themes?
6c6d2adb-b6b9-4931-bb62-45e23414cb5b.marks:
Upper band (3-4): “Nothing” = the crisis is based on a lie (Hero is innocent). “Noting” = the plot is driven by observation and eavesdropping (gulling scenes, window trick, Dogberry’s overhearing). The pun connects to the theme of deception: what characters see and hear is unreliable. Links to appearance vs reality across the play.
Lower band (1-2): Basic comment about the title meaning a fuss about nothing.

6c6d2adb-b6b9-4931-bb62-45e23414cb5b.text: How does Shakespeare present the theme of honour in Much Ado About Nothing? Refer to at least two characters.
6c6d2adb-b6b9-4931-bb62-45e23414cb5b.marks:
Top band (7-8): Male honour: Claudio’s public rejection restores his reputation at Hero’s expense; Benedick challenges Claudio to defend Beatrice’s honour. Female honour: Hero’s chastity = family honour; Leonato wishes her dead. Honour is performative and public. Shakespeare shows honour culture as destructive, valuing reputation over truth. Embeds context: Elizabethan honour codes.
Top band (5–6) Clear analysis.
Mid band (3–4) Some points.
Lower band (1–2) Simple.

6c6d2adb-b6b9-4931-bb62-45e23414cb5b.text: Explore how Shakespeare uses the military context of Act 1, Scene 1 to establish ideas about masculinity.
6c6d2adb-b6b9-4931-bb62-45e23414cb5b.marks:
Top band (7-8): Soldiers returning from war defines masculinity as combat and camaraderie. Claudio’s shift from soldier to lover is mocked (“he was wont to speak plain and to the purpose” becomes love-sick prose). Benedick’s resistance to love is framed as maintaining masculine independence. Shakespeare establishes a tension between military masculinity and romantic vulnerability that drives both relationships.
Top band (5–6) Clear.

6c6d2adb-b6b9-4931-bb62-45e23414cb5b.text: Analyse how Beatrice’s line “I had rather hear my dog bark at a crow than a man swear he loves me” (Act 1, Scene 1) establishes her character.
6c6d2adb-b6b9-4931-bb62-45e23414cb5b.marks:
Upper band (3-4): Beatrice rejects romantic language (“swear he loves me”) and compares it unfavourably to an ugly, discordant sound (dog barking at a crow). The hyperbole establishes her as witty, independent, and resistant to conventional courtship. It also creates dramatic irony: the audience suspects she will fall in love. Her wit masks vulnerability, which the gulling scene later exposes.
Lower band (1-2): Basic comment about Beatrice not wanting love.

194aaf40-4e38-4f8f-934e-790f63bccaa6.text: How does Shakespeare use Caliban’s claim “This island’s mine, by Sycorax my mother” to explore ideas about ownership and colonialism?
194aaf40-4e38-4f8f-934e-790f63bccaa6.marks:
Upper band (3-4): Detailed analysis of the legal/birthright language (“mine, by Sycorax my mother”), the parallel with indigenous land claims, and the colonial subtext. Discusses how Prospero’s response reveals the coloniser’s assumption that civilisation overrides native rights. Links to Jacobean colonial ventures.
Lower band (1-2): Basic identification that Caliban thinks the island belongs to him.

194aaf40-4e38-4f8f-934e-790f63bccaa6.text: Read the epilogue from “Now my charms are all o’erthrown” to “Let your indulgence set me free.” How does Shakespeare use language and form in this speech to present the theme of freedom?
194aaf40-4e38-4f8f-934e-790f63bccaa6.marks:
Top band (7-8): Sophisticated analysis of the power reversal (magician becomes supplicant), the triple function (character/actor/playwright), the religious echo of “indulgence” and its link to the Lord’s Prayer, and the structural significance of ending outside the play’s fiction. Discusses how the epilogue enacts the play’s themes of power, freedom, and mercy.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Clear analysis with relevant features.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Some relevant points.
Lower band (1-2): Simple comments.

194aaf40-4e38-4f8f-934e-790f63bccaa6.text: Read Act 5, Scene 1 from “I have bedimmed / The noontide sun” to “I’ll drown my book.” How does Shakespeare use this speech to present magic as an allegory for art and creative power?
194aaf40-4e38-4f8f-934e-790f63bccaa6.marks:
Top band (7-8): Sophisticated analysis of the metatheatrical reading: Prospero listing his magical achievements mirrors Shakespeare listing his dramatic achievements. Discusses the staff as pen, the book as script, and the act of renunciation as retirement. Analyses the imagery of power (controlling nature) and its deliberate abandonment. Links to Shakespeare’s biography.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Clear analysis with some metatheatrical understanding.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Some relevant points.
Lower band (1-2): Simple identification.

194aaf40-4e38-4f8f-934e-790f63bccaa6.text: Starting with Act 1, Scene 2 (“This island’s mine, by Sycorax my mother”), explore how Shakespeare presents ideas about colonialism and power in The Tempest. Write about: how Shakespeare presents colonialism in this extract, and how Shakespeare presents colonialism in the play as a whole.
194aaf40-4e38-4f8f-934e-790f63bccaa6.marks:

References post-colonial critics and Jacobean colonial context. Considers whether Shakespeare endorses or critiques colonialism. Sustained argument with word-level analysis.

Lower-mid band (3–6 marks + 1 spelling/grammar)Limited response.

194aaf40-4e38-4f8f-934e-790f63bccaa6.text: How does Shakespeare use Prospero’s line “A devil, a born devil, on whose nature / Nurture can never stick” to explore the theme of nature versus nurture?
194aaf40-4e38-4f8f-934e-790f63bccaa6.marks:
Upper band (3-4): Detailed analysis of Prospero’s belief in innate evil (“born devil”), the educational failure implied by “nurture can never stick,” and how the play complicates this through Caliban’s poetry and Antonio’s equal treachery. Notes that Prospero’s position reflects the coloniser’s justification for subjugation.
Lower band (1-2): Basic identification that Prospero thinks Caliban cannot be educated.

6d7fa1a3-281a-46bf-8af5-d75f970b6216.text: How does Shakespeare use Gonzalo’s commonwealth speech in Act 2, Scene 1 to explore ideas about colonialism and civilisation?
6d7fa1a3-281a-46bf-8af5-d75f970b6216.marks:
Upper band (3-4): Detailed analysis linking Gonzalo’s utopian vision to Montaigne’s “Of Cannibals” and the colonial context. Notes how Antonio and Sebastian undercut his idealism. Explores whether Shakespeare endorses or mocks the “noble savage” idea.
Lower band (1-2): Basic identification that Gonzalo describes a perfect society with limited analysis.

6d7fa1a3-281a-46bf-8af5-d75f970b6216.text: Read Act 4, Scene 1 from “Our revels now are ended” to “We are such stuff as dreams are made on.” How does Shakespeare use language in this extract to present ideas about illusion and reality?
6d7fa1a3-281a-46bf-8af5-d75f970b6216.marks:
Top band (7-8): Sophisticated analysis of the metaphor of life as theatre/dream. Discusses “the great globe itself” as a metatheatrical reference, the extended metaphor comparing human life to a dissolving masque, the context of Jacobean court masques, and the possible reading as Shakespeare’s farewell to theatre. Analysis of “insubstantial pageant faded” and its implications.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Clear analysis with several features and some contextual links.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Some relevant points with limited analysis.
Lower band (1-2): Simple identification with no analysis of effect.

6d7fa1a3-281a-46bf-8af5-d75f970b6216.text: Explore how Shakespeare uses the classical unities of time, place, and action in The Tempest. What effect does this tight structure have on the audience’s experience?
6d7fa1a3-281a-46bf-8af5-d75f970b6216.marks:
Top band (7-8): Sophisticated discussion of how the unities create intensity and mirror Prospero’s controlled orchestration. Links real-time action to the sense that Prospero is directing events like a playwright. Discusses how the single island setting makes the play feel like a contained experiment. Connects to Shakespeare’s deliberate structural choice as a late-career work.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Clear analysis with relevant structural observations.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Some awareness of structure with limited analysis.
Lower band (1-2): Simple comments about the play’s setting.

6d7fa1a3-281a-46bf-8af5-d75f970b6216.text: Explain how The Tempest reflects Jacobean England’s attitudes towards colonialism and the New World. Refer to specific characters and moments in the play.
6d7fa1a3-281a-46bf-8af5-d75f970b6216.marks:
Top band (11-12) Convincing analysis linking Prospero’s takeover of the island to European colonisation, Caliban’s dispossession to indigenous displacement, and Gonzalo’s commonwealth to Montaigne. Discusses the Sea Venture shipwreck as inspiration. Considers whether Shakespeare critiques or endorses colonialism. Uses precise quotations.
Upper band (9-10) Thoughtful analysis with clear evidence and contextual links.
Top band (7-8): Clear understanding with relevant examples.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Some understanding with basic contextual points.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Limited response with surface-level observations.
Lower band (1-2): Simple statements with no analysis.

6d7fa1a3-281a-46bf-8af5-d75f970b6216.text: Starting with Act 2, Scene 1 (Gonzalo’s commonwealth speech), explore how Shakespeare presents different ideas about power and society in The Tempest. Write about: how Shakespeare presents ideas about society in this extract, and how Shakespeare presents ideas about power and society in the play as a whole.
6d7fa1a3-281a-46bf-8af5-d75f970b6216.marks:
Top band (25–30 marks + 4 spelling/grammar)Critical, exploratory response. Analyses Gonzalo’s utopian speech and its source in Montaigne, Antonio and Sebastian’s mockery as revealing their own corruption, Prospero’s authoritarian rule, Caliban’s claim to the island, and the parallel conspiracies. Embeds colonial and Jacobean context throughout. Considers whether the play endorses any single model of society. Well-structured argument with precise quotation analysis.

Upper band (19–24 marks + 3 spelling/grammar)Thoughtful, developed response with relevant evidence and contextual understanding.

Upper-mid band (13–18 marks + 2 spelling/grammar)Clear response with some analysis and context.

Mid band (7–12 marks + 2 spelling/grammar)Some understanding with basic points.

Lower-mid band (3–6 marks + 1 spelling/grammar)Limited response.

Lower band (1–2 marks + 1 spelling/grammar)Simple, brief response.

6d7fa1a3-281a-46bf-8af5-d75f970b6216.text: Analyse how the wedding masque in Act 4, Scene 1 reflects Jacobean court entertainment and explores the theme of illusion.
6d7fa1a3-281a-46bf-8af5-d75f970b6216.marks:
Upper band (3-4): Detailed analysis linking the masque to Jacobean court tradition, noting Iris, Ceres, and Juno as classical figures of fertility and royalty. Discusses the masque’s abrupt ending as Prospero remembers the conspiracy, and the metatheatrical implication of a performance within a performance. Links to “Our revels now are ended.”
Lower band (1-2): Basic identification that the masque is a celebration with limited analysis.

6e887670-bef4-4880-9e5e-68caf2c84678.text: Read the opening paragraph of Pride and Prejudice. How does Austen use language to establish the novel’s ironic narrative voice?
6e887670-bef4-4880-9e5e-68caf2c84678.marks:
Top band (17-20) Perceptive analysis. ‘Truth universally acknowledged’ adopts the register of philosophical certainty for a social observation about money. ‘Must be in want of’ implies inevitability, but the irony is that society ‘wants’ the man’s fortune, not the man himself. ‘Single man in possession of a good fortune’ reduces a person to an economic unit. Discusses how the narrator performs the same social politeness she satirises — stating the unpleasant truth in elegant language.
Top band (13-16): Clear analysis.
Upper-mid band (9-12): Some analysis.
Lower-mid band (5-8): Limited analysis.
Lower band (1-4): Simple comments.

6e887670-bef4-4880-9e5e-68caf2c84678.text: How does Austen use narrative techniques to shape the reader’s understanding of characters in the novel as a whole?
6e887670-bef4-4880-9e5e-68caf2c84678.marks:
Top band (17-20) Convincing response discussing: free indirect discourse sharing Elizabeth’s perspective (and prejudice); the omniscient narrator’s ironic commentary; letters as direct character voice (Darcy’s letter, Collins’s letter); Mrs Reynolds’s indirect characterisation of Darcy; dialogue as self-revelation (Collins’s proposal). Argues that Austen controls the reader’s sympathies through technique, making us complicit in Elizabeth’s mistakes.
Top band (13-16): Clear analysis.
Upper-mid band (9-12): Some understanding.
Lower-mid band (5-8): Supported comments.
Lower band (1-4): Simple statements.

6e887670-bef4-4880-9e5e-68caf2c84678.text: Analyse how Austen’s description of Mrs Bennet as ‘a woman of mean understanding, little information, and uncertain temper’ demonstrates her satirical technique.
6e887670-bef4-4880-9e5e-68caf2c84678.marks:
Upper band (3-4): The tricolon (‘mean understanding, little information, uncertain temper’) delivers a comprehensive demolition in polite, balanced syntax. ‘Mean’ (limited) and ‘little’ are measured rather than vicious, but the cumulative effect is devastating. The narrator performs the same social propriety she satirises — delivering harsh truths in elegant language. This is Austen’s characteristic ironic mode: the form (politeness) contradicts the content (criticism).
Lower band (1-2): Basic comment about Mrs Bennet being described negatively.

6e887670-bef4-4880-9e5e-68caf2c84678.text: Read Darcy’s letter to Elizabeth (Chapter 35). How does Austen use the letter form to present Darcy’s perspective and challenge Elizabeth’s assumptions?
6e887670-bef4-4880-9e5e-68caf2c84678.marks:
Top band (17-20) Perceptive analysis. The letter allows Darcy extended self-defence without interruption — something his reserved manner prevents in conversation. Its logical structure (addressing each accusation in turn) reveals a rational, principled mind. The factual tone contrasts with the emotional turmoil of the proposal scene. Discusses how the letter form gives the reader direct access to Darcy’s voice without the narrator’s ironic filter, forcing reassessment.
Top band (13-16): Clear analysis.
Upper-mid band (9-12): Some analysis.
Lower-mid band (5-8): Limited analysis.
Lower band (1-4): Simple comments.

6e887670-bef4-4880-9e5e-68caf2c84678.text: How does Austen use satire in the novel as a whole to criticise Regency society? Refer to at least two characters.
6e887670-bef4-4880-9e5e-68caf2c84678.marks:
Top band (17-20) Convincing response. Discusses: Collins as satire of obsequiousness and the social hierarchy; Lady Catherine as satire of unchecked class arrogance; Mrs Bennet as satire of the marriage market (but also a product of the system); the narrator’s ironic tone throughout. Argues Austen satirises through understatement and comedy, inviting the reader to feel superior while exposing the systemic absurdities that produce the characters’ behaviour.
Top band (13-16): Clear analysis.
Upper-mid band (9-12): Some understanding.
Lower-mid band (5-8): Supported comments.
Lower band (1-4): Simple statements.

6e887670-bef4-4880-9e5e-68caf2c84678.text: Explain how Austen uses parallel structure (the two proposals) to develop the novel’s central themes.
6e887670-bef4-4880-9e5e-68caf2c84678.marks:
Upper band (3-4): First proposal: proud, lists objections, assumes acceptance (‘in vain have I struggled’). Second: humble, defers to Elizabeth, fears rejection (‘one word from you will silence me’). The parallel forces the reader to compare and measure Darcy’s growth. Structurally, the two proposals bracket the novel’s transformation: the first triggers the crisis; the second resolves it. Austen uses symmetry to show that pride must become humility and prejudice must become understanding.
Lower band (1-2): Basic observation that the second proposal is different.

7051cbce-8af8-4c0f-9098-efce2130b3db.text: Read Act 4, Scene 1 from “Sweet Prince, you learn me noble thankfulness” to “Give not this rotten orange to your friend.” How does Shakespeare use language in this extract to present Claudio’s rejection of Hero? Write about the extract and the play as a whole.
7051cbce-8af8-4c0f-9098-efce2130b3db.marks:
Top band (25–30 + 4 spelling/grammar)Analyses the “rotten orange” metaphor (reduces Hero to commodity, beautiful outside/corrupt inside), the public setting (honour culture demands public shaming), Claudio’s self-righteousness. Links to the wider play: the masked ball jealousy, Don John’s manipulation, Claudio’s eventual penance. Context: patriarchy, female chastity as property, honour codes. Explores whether Claudio is cruel or culturally conditioned.

Upper band (19–24 + 3)Thoughtful.
Upper-mid band (13–18 + 2)Clear.
Mid band (7–12 + 2)Some understanding.
Lower-mid band (3–6 + 1)Limited.
Lower band (1–2 + 1)Simple.

7051cbce-8af8-4c0f-9098-efce2130b3db.text: Starting with Act 4, Scene 1, explore how Shakespeare presents Beatrice’s response to Hero’s shaming. Write about the extract and the play as a whole.
7051cbce-8af8-4c0f-9098-efce2130b3db.marks:
Top band (25–30 + 4 spelling/grammar)Analyses “Kill Claudio” (brevity, power, demand), “O that I were a man!” (rage at patriarchy), “eat his heart in the market-place” (violent imagery showing depth of fury). Links to Beatrice across the play: the merry war’s wit now becomes lethal seriousness. Contrast with Hero’s silence. Context: women’s powerlessness to act, Beatrice as proto-feminist figure. Word-level analysis.

Upper band (19–24 + 3)Thoughtful.
Upper-mid band (13–18 + 2)Clear.
Mid band (7–12 + 2)Some.
Lower-mid band (3–6 + 1)Limited.
Lower band (1–2 + 1)Simple.

7051cbce-8af8-4c0f-9098-efce2130b3db.text: Analyse the significance of Leonato’s line “Do not live, Hero; do not ope thine eyes” (Act 4, Scene 1). What does it reveal about patriarchal values?
7051cbce-8af8-4c0f-9098-efce2130b3db.marks:
Upper band (3-4): Leonato wishes his own daughter dead rather than dishonoured. The imperative “Do not live” shows he prioritises family reputation over his child’s life. “Ope thine eyes” — he cannot bear to see her alive and shamed. Reflects Elizabethan honour culture where female unchastity destroys the father’s social standing. Shakespeare reveals patriarchy’s cruelty through its most intimate relationship.
Lower band (1-2): Basic comment about Leonato being upset.

7051cbce-8af8-4c0f-9098-efce2130b3db.text: How does Shakespeare use the Friar’s plan to explore the theme of deception in Much Ado About Nothing?
7051cbce-8af8-4c0f-9098-efce2130b3db.marks:
Top band (7-8): The Friar uses deception (faking Hero’s death) to undo the damage of deception (Don John’s plot). This mirrors the benevolent gulling scenes — the solution to lies is more lies. Shakespeare suggests that in a world where observation is unreliable, truth can only be reached through managed performance. The Friar reads Hero’s blush correctly when everyone else misreads it. Links to the “noting/nothing” theme.
Top band (5–6) Clear.
Mid band (3–4) Some.
Lower band (1–2) Simple.

7051cbce-8af8-4c0f-9098-efce2130b3db.text: Explore how Shakespeare presents “Kill Claudio” as a turning point in Beatrice and Benedick’s relationship.
7051cbce-8af8-4c0f-9098-efce2130b3db.marks:
Top band (7-8): The merry war has been comic; “Kill Claudio” is deadly serious. Beatrice tests whether Benedick’s love is real by demanding he choose her over male loyalty. His agreement (“I am engaged”) proves it is. The moment transforms their relationship from witty sparring into genuine commitment. Links to the play’s wider treatment of honour: Benedick defies the male code for a woman’s sake.
Top band (5–6) Clear.
Mid band (3–4) Some.
Lower band (1–2) Simple.

7051cbce-8af8-4c0f-9098-efce2130b3db.text: Analyse the significance of Don Pedro’s use of the word “stale” (prostitute) to describe Hero in Act 4, Scene 1.
7051cbce-8af8-4c0f-9098-efce2130b3db.marks:
Upper band (3-4): “Stale” (prostitute) is the most degrading word available. A prince using it publicly against a noblewoman shows the complete destruction of Hero’s social standing. Don Pedro’s involvement turns the accusation from one man’s jealousy into an institutional condemnation. His authority makes the accusation seem unchallengeable. Context: male solidarity in honour culture.
Lower band (1-2): Basic comment about Don Pedro calling Hero a bad name.

f39e1018-1d96-4b4f-8521-a1c92743e425.text: How does Shakespeare use Caliban’s “Be not afeard; the isle is full of noises” speech (Act 3, Scene 2) to complicate the audience’s view of Caliban?
f39e1018-1d96-4b4f-8521-a1c92743e425.marks:
Upper band (3-4): Detailed analysis of the lyrical language (“sweet airs, that give delight and hurt not”), the contrast with Caliban’s angry language elsewhere, his deep emotional connection to the island, and how this challenges the “monster” label applied by Stephano and Trinculo. Notes that neither Stephano nor Trinculo can match Caliban’s sensitivity.
Lower band (1-2): Basic identification that Caliban describes the island beautifully.

f39e1018-1d96-4b4f-8521-a1c92743e425.text: Read Act 2, Scene 1 from “My strong imagination sees a crown” to “Draw together; and when I rear my hand, do you the like.” How does Shakespeare present Antonio as a tempter in this extract?
f39e1018-1d96-4b4f-8521-a1c92743e425.marks:
Top band (7-8): Sophisticated analysis of Antonio’s manipulative rhetoric, the echo of his past usurpation, the pragmatic tone (“What’s past is prologue”), the lack of guilt or moral hesitation, and Sebastian’s willing complicity. Links to Jacobean anxieties about usurpation and the structural parallel with Caliban’s later conspiracy.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Clear analysis with several features and structural awareness.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Some relevant points with limited analysis.
Lower band (1-2): Simple identification with no analysis.

f39e1018-1d96-4b4f-8521-a1c92743e425.text: Read Act 3, Scene 3 from “You are three men of sin” to “Lingering perdition.” How does Shakespeare use Ariel’s speech as a harpy to present ideas about justice and punishment?
f39e1018-1d96-4b4f-8521-a1c92743e425.marks:
Top band (7-8): Sophisticated analysis of the harpy as a figure of divine vengeance, the vanishing banquet as a symbol of treachery’s empty rewards, Ariel as Prospero’s instrument of justice, and the question of whether Prospero’s actions constitute justice or revenge. Discusses the masque-like spectacle and the powerlessness of the “men of sin.”
Upper-mid band (5-6): Clear analysis with relevant mythological and thematic understanding.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Some relevant points.
Lower band (1-2): Simple comments.

f39e1018-1d96-4b4f-8521-a1c92743e425.text: Explore how Shakespeare uses the subplot of Caliban, Stephano, and Trinculo to mirror and comment on the main plot’s themes of power and conspiracy.
f39e1018-1d96-4b4f-8521-a1c92743e425.marks:
Top band (11-12) Convincing analysis of how the comic subplot mirrors the Antonio/Sebastian conspiracy at a lower social level. Discusses Caliban’s repetition of the colonisation cycle (offering island knowledge to a new master), Stephano as a parody of a ruler, and the structural parallel with Antonio’s usurpation. Precise quotations with word-level analysis.
Upper band (9-10) Thoughtful analysis with clear structural understanding.
Top band (7-8): Clear understanding with relevant comparisons.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Some understanding with basic points.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Limited response.
Lower band (1-2): Simple statements.

f39e1018-1d96-4b4f-8521-a1c92743e425.text: Starting with Act 3, Scene 1 (Ferdinand carrying logs), explore how Shakespeare presents different kinds of service and slavery in The Tempest. Write about: how Shakespeare presents service in this extract, and how Shakespeare presents service and slavery in the play as a whole.
f39e1018-1d96-4b4f-8521-a1c92743e425.marks:
Top band (25–30 marks + 4 spelling/grammar)Critical response comparing Ferdinand’s willing service (love), Ariel’s bound service (obligation), and Caliban’s forced labour (enslavement). Analyses how Shakespeare uses these contrasts to explore the spectrum from freedom to slavery. Embeds colonial context, discusses Caliban’s “isle is full of noises” as evidence of inner dignity, and explores the question of whether any character is truly free. Well-structured argument.

Upper band (19–24 marks + 3 spelling/grammar)Thoughtful response with relevant evidence and context.

Upper-mid band (13–18 marks + 2 spelling/grammar)Clear response with some analysis.

Mid band (7–12 marks + 2 spelling/grammar)Some understanding.

Lower-mid band (3–6 marks + 1 spelling/grammar)Limited response.

Lower band (1–2 marks + 1 spelling/grammar)Simple, brief response.

f39e1018-1d96-4b4f-8521-a1c92743e425.text: Analyse how Shakespeare uses Antonio’s line “What’s past is prologue” (Act 2, Scene 1) to reveal his character and attitudes towards power.
f39e1018-1d96-4b4f-8521-a1c92743e425.marks:
Upper band (3-4): Detailed analysis of the metaphor (life as a story where the past is merely an introduction), Antonio’s refusal to feel guilt, his pragmatic view of power as something to be seized, and the link to his earlier usurpation. Notes the irony that Antonio’s “past” of treachery is about to be repeated.
Lower band (1-2): Basic identification that Antonio is talking about moving on from the past.

c6dadf8b-930e-4c7d-af2e-3bc7df64b76f.text: How does Shakespeare use the contrast between Caliban’s language in his exchanges with Prospero and his “isle is full of noises” speech to complicate the audience’s view of him?
c6dadf8b-930e-4c7d-af2e-3bc7df64b76f.marks:
Upper band (3-4): Detailed analysis contrasting the angry, resentful register (“I know how to curse”) with the lyrical, sensitive register (“sounds and sweet airs”). Discusses how Shakespeare uses this gap to challenge the “monster” label used by Stephano and Trinculo and reveal Caliban’s rich inner life. Links to the nature vs nurture debate.
Lower band (1-2): Basic identification that Caliban speaks differently in different scenes.

c6dadf8b-930e-4c7d-af2e-3bc7df64b76f.text: Read Act 5, Scene 1 from “For you, most wicked sir” to “Thy rankest fault.” How does Shakespeare present the limits of Prospero’s forgiveness in this extract?
c6dadf8b-930e-4c7d-af2e-3bc7df64b76f.marks:
Top band (7-8): Sophisticated analysis of the hostile language within the act of forgiveness (“wicked,” “infect my mouth,” “rankest fault”), Antonio’s silence as ambiguous, and the question of whether this constitutes genuine mercy or merely strategic clemency. Links to the play’s wider exploration of whether forgiveness can be complete when the offender shows no remorse.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Clear analysis with relevant language features.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Some relevant points.
Lower band (1-2): Simple comments.

c6dadf8b-930e-4c7d-af2e-3bc7df64b76f.text: Read Act 5, Scene 1 from “Your charm so strongly works ’em” to “were I human.” How does Shakespeare use Ariel’s words to present the relationship between compassion and humanity?
c6dadf8b-930e-4c7d-af2e-3bc7df64b76f.marks:
Top band (7-8): Sophisticated analysis of the irony that a spirit feels more compassion than humans, Ariel’s function as Prospero’s conscience, the phrase “were I human” as a challenge to Prospero’s own humanity, and how this moment catalyses Prospero’s choice of mercy. Discusses what Shakespeare implies about the nature of compassion.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Clear analysis with relevant evidence.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Some points about Ariel’s feelings.
Lower band (1-2): Simple identification.

c6dadf8b-930e-4c7d-af2e-3bc7df64b76f.text: Explore how Shakespeare uses the character of Miranda to present ideas about innocence, wonder, and agency in The Tempest.
c6dadf8b-930e-4c7d-af2e-3bc7df64b76f.marks:
Top band (11-12) Convincing analysis covering Miranda’s empathy (“I have suffered with those that I saw suffer”), her ironic wonder (“O brave new world”), her defiance of Prospero (telling her name, proposing marriage), and the tension between her innocence and her father’s controlling behaviour. Considers whether she is a passive object or an agent in her own right. Precise quotations.
Upper band (9-10) Thoughtful analysis with clear evidence.
Top band (7-8): Clear understanding with relevant examples.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Some understanding.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Limited response.
Lower band (1-2): Simple statements.

c6dadf8b-930e-4c7d-af2e-3bc7df64b76f.text: Starting with Act 1, Scene 2 (Prospero’s first exchange with Caliban), explore how Shakespeare presents the relationship between Prospero and Caliban. Write about: how Shakespeare presents the relationship in this extract, and how Shakespeare presents this relationship in the play as a whole.
c6dadf8b-930e-4c7d-af2e-3bc7df64b76f.marks:
Top band (25–30 marks + 4 spelling/grammar)Critical response tracking the relationship from initial cooperation to enslavement. Analyses Prospero’s labels (“thing of darkness,” “a born devil”), Caliban’s counter-narrative (“This island’s mine”), the language debate (“I know how to curse”), Caliban’s poetry (“isle is full of noises”), and the ambiguous ending (“This thing of darkness I acknowledge mine”). Embeds colonial context and post-colonial readings. Considers nature vs nurture. Well-structured with word-level analysis.

Upper band (19–24 marks + 3 spelling/grammar)Thoughtful response with clear evidence and context.

Upper-mid band (13–18 marks + 2 spelling/grammar)Clear response with some analysis.

Mid band (7–12 marks + 2 spelling/grammar)Some understanding.

Lower-mid band (3–6 marks + 1 spelling/grammar)Limited response.

Lower band (1–2 marks + 1 spelling/grammar)Simple, brief response.

c6dadf8b-930e-4c7d-af2e-3bc7df64b76f.text: How does Shakespeare present Gonzalo as a moral compass in The Tempest? Refer to at least two moments in the play.
c6dadf8b-930e-4c7d-af2e-3bc7df64b76f.marks:
Upper band (3-4): Detailed analysis of Gonzalo’s role: saving Prospero with books and supplies (backstory), his utopian commonwealth speech (Act 2), and Prospero’s warm acknowledgement “Holy Gonzalo, honourable man” (Act 5). Discusses how Gonzalo’s consistent goodness contrasts with Antonio’s corruption and provides a moral benchmark.
Lower band (1-2): Basic identification that Gonzalo is a good character.

cad3ec2d-485d-48db-84d6-0e1e4c9f0f97.text: How does Shakespeare use the contrast between Ferdinand’s willing service and Caliban’s enslavement to explore the theme of freedom?
cad3ec2d-485d-48db-84d6-0e1e4c9f0f97.marks:
Upper band (3-4): Detailed analysis contrasting Ferdinand’s language of willing devotion (“The mistress which I serve quickens what’s dead”) with Caliban’s forced obedience under threat of cramps. Discusses how Shakespeare uses this structural contrast to define a spectrum from loving service to slavery. Links to the colonial theme.
Lower band (1-2): Basic identification that Ferdinand serves willingly while Caliban does not.

cad3ec2d-485d-48db-84d6-0e1e4c9f0f97.text: Read Act 5, Scene 1 from “For you, most wicked sir” to “I do forgive / Thy rankest fault.” How does Shakespeare present the complexity of forgiveness in this extract?
cad3ec2d-485d-48db-84d6-0e1e4c9f0f97.marks:
Top band (7-8): Sophisticated analysis of the tension between the words of forgiveness and the hostile language (“wicked,” “infect my mouth,” “rankest”). Discusses Antonio’s silence as deeply ambiguous. Analyses how Shakespeare shows forgiveness as a difficult, imperfect act rather than a simple resolution. Links to the romance genre’s emphasis on reconciliation.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Clear analysis with relevant language features.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Some relevant points.
Lower band (1-2): Simple identification.

cad3ec2d-485d-48db-84d6-0e1e4c9f0f97.text: Read Act 4, Scene 1 from “Our revels now are ended” to “rounded with a sleep.” How does Shakespeare use extended metaphor in this extract to explore the relationship between art and life?
cad3ec2d-485d-48db-84d6-0e1e4c9f0f97.marks:
Top band (7-8): Sophisticated analysis of the three-layer metaphor (masque/life/theatre), “the great globe” as Globe Theatre reference, “insubstantial pageant” as theatrical language applied to existence, and “rounded with a sleep” as death enclosing life. Discusses the metatheatrical implications and how Shakespeare equates his art with Prospero’s magic.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Clear analysis with relevant features.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Some relevant points.
Lower band (1-2): Simple identification.

cad3ec2d-485d-48db-84d6-0e1e4c9f0f97.text: Explore how Shakespeare uses the theme of nature versus nurture in The Tempest to question assumptions about civilisation and savagery.
cad3ec2d-485d-48db-84d6-0e1e4c9f0f97.marks:
Top band (11-12) Convincing analysis covering Prospero’s “born devil” judgement, Caliban’s poetic sensitivity as counter-evidence, Antonio’s treachery despite European civilisation, Miranda’s goodness despite isolation, and the play’s refusal to definitively answer the question. Links to colonial assumptions about “savage” peoples. Precise quotations.
Upper band (9-10) Thoughtful analysis with clear evidence.
Top band (7-8): Clear understanding with relevant examples.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Some understanding.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Limited response.
Lower band (1-2): Simple statements.

cad3ec2d-485d-48db-84d6-0e1e4c9f0f97.text: Starting with the epilogue (“Now my charms are all o’erthrown”), explore how Shakespeare presents the theme of power in The Tempest. Write about: how Shakespeare presents power in this extract, and how Shakespeare presents power in the play as a whole.
cad3ec2d-485d-48db-84d6-0e1e4c9f0f97.marks:
Top band (25–30 marks + 4 spelling/grammar)Critical response tracking power from Prospero’s absolute magical control to his vulnerability in the epilogue. Analyses the opening storm (nature vs authority), Prospero’s control of Ariel and Caliban (colonial power), Antonio’s political power-grabbing, the masque as staged power, and the epilogue’s reversal where the audience holds power. Embeds context throughout. Considers whether the play endorses any form of power as legitimate. Well-structured sustained argument.

Upper band (19–24 marks + 3 spelling/grammar)Thoughtful response with relevant evidence.

Upper-mid band (13–18 marks + 2 spelling/grammar)Clear response with some analysis.

Mid band (7–12 marks + 2 spelling/grammar)Some understanding.

Lower-mid band (3–6 marks + 1 spelling/grammar)Limited response.

Lower band (1–2 marks + 1 spelling/grammar)Simple response.

cad3ec2d-485d-48db-84d6-0e1e4c9f0f97.text: Analyse how Shakespeare uses the quotation “We are such stuff / As dreams are made on” to present the theme of illusion and reality in The Tempest.
cad3ec2d-485d-48db-84d6-0e1e4c9f0f97.marks:
Upper band (3-4): Detailed analysis of “stuff” as something insubstantial, “dreams” as illusions, “rounded with a sleep” as death/oblivion, and the metatheatrical layer where “dreams” also means the plays Shakespeare has created. Links to the dissolving masque and the play’s wider argument that all human constructs — power, revenge, art — are temporary.
Lower band (1-2): Basic identification that Prospero says life is like a dream.

00325d8d-9d58-4091-9adc-d37c3682aa4b.text: Read the following extract from Chapter 28, in which Jane wanders the moors after leaving Thornfield. Explore how Brontë uses language to present Jane’s suffering and her determination to survive.
00325d8d-9d58-4091-9adc-d37c3682aa4b.marks:
Top band (17-20) Judicious analysis. Examines: the sensory description of physical suffering (hunger, cold, exposure), the pathetic fallacy of the moors as both beautiful and dangerous, Jane’s resolute internal voice, the contrast between her physical weakness and her moral strength. Analyses specific word choices and how Brontë uses the landscape to externalise Jane’s emotional state.
Upper band (13-16) Thoughtful analysis with clear language focus.
Top band (9-12): Clear understanding with relevant evidence.
Upper-mid band (5-8): Some relevant comments.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Limited response.
Lower band (1-2): Simple, brief response.

00325d8d-9d58-4091-9adc-d37c3682aa4b.text: In the novel as a whole, explore how Brontë presents different types of love.
00325d8d-9d58-4091-9adc-d37c3682aa4b.marks:
Top band (17-20) Convincing exploration. Discusses: Rochester’s passionate, possessive love; St John’s cold, dutiful version of love; Helen Burns’s spiritual love; Jane’s model of love as mutual respect between equals. Traces how Jane’s understanding of love develops through the novel and how she ultimately achieves a love that combines passion with principle.
Upper band (13-16) Thoughtful response with relevant evidence.
Top band (9-12): Clear understanding with some analysis.
Upper-mid band (5-8): Some understanding.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Limited response.
Lower band (1-2): Simple comments.

00325d8d-9d58-4091-9adc-d37c3682aa4b.text: Read the following extract in which St John Rivers proposes to Jane. Explore how Brontë uses language to present the contrast between duty and emotion.
00325d8d-9d58-4091-9adc-d37c3682aa4b.marks:
Top band (17-20) Sophisticated analysis. Examines: St John’s formal, impersonal language (he speaks of ‘suitability’ rather than love), the absence of emotional warmth, Jane’s internal conflict between respect for his dedication and horror at his coldness. Analyses how Brontë uses dialogue to dramatise two opposing philosophies of life. Links to the wider theme of religion and morality.
Upper band (13-16) Thoughtful analysis with clear focus.
Top band (9-12): Clear response with relevant evidence.
Upper-mid band (5-8): Some relevant comments.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Limited response.
Lower band (1-2): Simple, brief response.

00325d8d-9d58-4091-9adc-d37c3682aa4b.text: In the novel as a whole, explore how Brontë presents the importance of independence for women.
00325d8d-9d58-4091-9adc-d37c3682aa4b.marks:
Top band (17-20) Convincing, critical exploration. Discusses: Jane’s dependence at Gateshead, her gradual building of self-sufficiency at Lowood, her economic vulnerability as a governess, her refusal to become Rochester’s mistress, her inheritance and financial independence, her return to Rochester as an equal. Links to Victorian women’s limited options and Brontë’s proto-feminist message.
Upper band (13-16) Thoughtful response with well-chosen evidence.
Top band (9-12): Clear understanding with relevant references.
Upper-mid band (5-8): Some understanding.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Limited response.
Lower band (1-2): Simple comments.

00325d8d-9d58-4091-9adc-d37c3682aa4b.text: Read the following extract in which Jane divides her inheritance among her cousins. Explore how Brontë uses language to present Jane’s values and her attitude to wealth.
00325d8d-9d58-4091-9adc-d37c3682aa4b.marks:
Top band (17-20) Perceptive analysis. Examines: Jane’s excited, generous language, her joy at discovering family (she values kinship over money), the contrast between her attitude and Victorian materialism. Analyses how Brontë uses this moment to show that independence for Jane is about self-determination, not accumulation of wealth.
Upper band (13-16) Thoughtful analysis with clear language focus.
Top band (9-12): Clear understanding with some evidence.
Upper-mid band (5-8): Some relevant points.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Limited response.
Lower band (1-2): Simple, brief response.

00325d8d-9d58-4091-9adc-d37c3682aa4b.text: In the novel as a whole, explore how Brontë uses the moors as a setting to reflect Jane’s inner world.
00325d8d-9d58-4091-9adc-d37c3682aa4b.marks:
Top band (17-20) Convincing exploration. Discusses: the moors as a space of freedom and danger, the emptiness and exposure of the moor after Jane leaves Thornfield, the contrast between the moors’ wildness and Thornfield’s enclosure, the moors as the setting where Jane hears Rochester’s supernatural voice. Analyses how Brontë uses landscape to externalise psychological and emotional states throughout the novel.
Upper band (13-16) Thoughtful response with relevant evidence.
Top band (9-12): Clear understanding with some references.
Upper-mid band (5-8): Some understanding.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Limited response.
Lower band (1-2): Simple comments.

d4b2e695-9b50-401b-b506-bcaf4d28e705.text: Read from ‘Mr Bingley was good-looking and gentlemanlike’ to ‘She is tolerable, but not handsome enough to tempt me.’ How does Austen use language to contrast Bingley and Darcy in this extract?
d4b2e695-9b50-401b-b506-bcaf4d28e705.marks:
Top band (17-20) Perceptive analysis. Discusses: the accumulation of positive adjectives for Bingley (‘good-looking,’ ‘gentlemanlike,’ ‘pleasant countenance’); the shift in public opinion on Darcy from admiration (‘ten thousand a year’) to ‘disgust’; the word ‘tempt’ implying Elizabeth is an object to be appraised; Darcy’s dismissive tone reducing Elizabeth to her appearance; the structural juxtaposition of the two men’s responses to the same social situation.
Top band (13-16): Clear analysis with relevant evidence.
Upper-mid band (9-12): Some analysis.
Lower-mid band (5-8): Limited analysis.
Lower band (1-4): Simple comments.

d4b2e695-9b50-401b-b506-bcaf4d28e705.text: How does Austen present the theme of first impressions in the novel as a whole?
d4b2e695-9b50-401b-b506-bcaf4d28e705.marks:
Top band (17-20) Convincing response. Discusses: Darcy’s misjudgement of Elizabeth at the assembly; Elizabeth’s misjudgement of Darcy and trust in Wickham; the original title First Impressions; Darcy’s letter as the turning point where first impressions are corrected; Elizabeth’s self-reflection (‘Till this moment I never knew myself’). Argues that Austen shows first impressions as products of pride and prejudice that must be overcome through self-knowledge.
Top band (13-16): Clear analysis.
Upper-mid band (9-12): Some understanding.
Lower-mid band (5-8): Supported comments.
Lower band (1-4): Simple statements.

d4b2e695-9b50-401b-b506-bcaf4d28e705.text: Analyse the significance of Darcy’s remark: ‘She is tolerable, but not handsome enough to tempt me.’
d4b2e695-9b50-401b-b506-bcaf4d28e705.marks:
Upper band (3-4): ‘Tolerable’ is deliberately faint praise, implying Elizabeth is adequate but unremarkable. ‘Tempt’ positions Darcy as a passive object of attraction and Elizabeth as failing to meet his standard — revealing his arrogance. ‘Not handsome enough’ reduces her to physical appearance. The remark plants Elizabeth’s prejudice and drives the novel’s central conflict. Ironically, Darcy later admits he was ‘in the middle before I knew that I had begun.’
Lower band (1-2): Basic identification of the insult.

d4b2e695-9b50-401b-b506-bcaf4d28e705.text: Read from ‘Oh! She is the most beautiful creature’ to ‘everybody said how well she looked.’ How does Austen present Jane and Bingley’s growing attraction in this extract?
d4b2e695-9b50-401b-b506-bcaf4d28e705.marks:
Top band (17-20) Perceptive analysis. Bingley’s superlatives (‘most beautiful creature’) show immediate infatuation; the neighbourhood’s agreement validates the match socially; Jane’s reserved response contrasts with Bingley’s openness, foreshadowing Charlotte’s warning about concealing affection; the repetition of dancing language situates romance within social ritual.
Top band (13-16): Clear analysis.
Upper-mid band (9-12): Some analysis.
Lower-mid band (5-8): Limited analysis.
Lower band (1-4): Simple comments.

d4b2e695-9b50-401b-b506-bcaf4d28e705.text: How does Austen use Elizabeth’s reaction to Darcy’s insult to establish her character?
d4b2e695-9b50-401b-b506-bcaf4d28e705.marks:
Upper band (3-4): Elizabeth tells the story with ‘great spirit’ rather than showing hurt, establishing her as witty, resilient, and proud. Her ability to turn an insult into entertainment shows social intelligence and self-possession. However, this defiant response also plants her prejudice against Darcy: she has decided he is arrogant, and this colours her judgement for the first half of the novel.
Lower band (1-2): Basic comment about Elizabeth being offended.

d4b2e695-9b50-401b-b506-bcaf4d28e705.text: How does Austen present public opinion as unreliable in the novel as a whole? Refer to at least two examples.
d4b2e695-9b50-401b-b506-bcaf4d28e705.marks:
Top band (17-20) Convincing response. Discusses: the assembly’s rapid reversal on Darcy (admiration to ‘disgust’); the neighbourhood’s trust in Wickham based on charm alone; Lady Catherine’s assumed authority based on rank, not character; the Gardiners being judged for living in Cheapside despite being the novel’s most sensible characters. Argues Austen shows that Regency society judged by wealth and manners rather than moral worth.
Top band (13-16): Clear analysis.
Upper-mid band (9-12): Some analysis.
Lower-mid band (5-8): Supported comments.
Lower band (1-4): Simple statements.

45c9498d-aae6-45ed-9584-49d9bf2ea5f1.text: Read from Elizabeth’s response to Darcy’s letter (‘How despicably have I acted!’) to ‘Till this moment I never knew myself.’ How does Austen use language to present Elizabeth’s moment of self-recognition?
45c9498d-aae6-45ed-9584-49d9bf2ea5f1.marks:
Top band (17-20) Perceptive analysis. ‘Despicably’ is self-condemnation, not mild regret. ‘Prided myself on my discernment’ reveals the irony: pride caused prejudice. ‘Till this moment’ implies sudden revelation. ‘Never knew myself’ is a philosophical admission of self-ignorance. Discusses how Austen uses free indirect discourse to blur narrator and character, making the reader share Elizabeth’s shock.
Top band (13-16): Clear analysis.
Upper-mid band (9-12): Some analysis.
Lower-mid band (5-8): Limited analysis.
Lower band (1-4): Simple comments.

45c9498d-aae6-45ed-9584-49d9bf2ea5f1.text: How does Austen present the relationship between pride and prejudice in the characters of Elizabeth and Darcy?
45c9498d-aae6-45ed-9584-49d9bf2ea5f1.marks:
Top band (17-20) Convincing response arguing both characters have BOTH pride and prejudice. Darcy’s social pride leads to prejudice against the Bennets’ connections; Elizabeth’s intellectual pride leads to prejudice against Darcy’s character. Traces both arcs: Darcy’s transformation through the letter and Pemberley; Elizabeth’s through the letter and self-reflection. Argues the title applies to both characters, not just one each.
Top band (13-16): Clear analysis.
Upper-mid band (9-12): Some understanding.
Lower-mid band (5-8): Supported comments.
Lower band (1-4): Simple statements.

45c9498d-aae6-45ed-9584-49d9bf2ea5f1.text: Analyse the significance of Darcy’s statement: ‘My good opinion once lost, is lost forever.’
45c9498d-aae6-45ed-9584-49d9bf2ea5f1.marks:
Upper band (3-4): Darcy presents inflexibility as a virtue, believing permanent judgements are principled. Elizabeth challenges this as ‘a shade in a character.’ The line is significant because the novel proves Darcy wrong — he DOES change his opinion. Austen argues that moral growth requires the willingness to reassess, not rigid adherence to first judgements. The line also applies to Elizabeth, whose opinion of Darcy is equally fixed until the letter.
Lower band (1-2): Basic comment about Darcy being stubborn.

45c9498d-aae6-45ed-9584-49d9bf2ea5f1.text: Read Mr Collins’s proposal to Elizabeth. How does Austen use language and structure to satirise the Regency marriage system?
45c9498d-aae6-45ed-9584-49d9bf2ea5f1.marks:
Top band (17-20) Perceptive analysis. Collins’s reasons are listed in order: duty, happiness, Lady Catherine — love is never mentioned. The structural list exposes marriage as transaction. His assumption that Elizabeth ‘secretly means to accept’ denies her agency. His pompous register (‘my attentions have been too marked to be mistaken’) contrasts with Elizabeth’s plain refusal. Discusses Austen’s comic technique: satire through exaggeration of real attitudes.
Top band (13-16): Clear analysis.
Upper-mid band (9-12): Some analysis.
Lower-mid band (5-8): Limited analysis.
Lower band (1-4): Simple comments.

45c9498d-aae6-45ed-9584-49d9bf2ea5f1.text: How does Austen use Mrs Bennet to explore the consequences of women’s economic dependence in Regency society?
45c9498d-aae6-45ed-9584-49d9bf2ea5f1.marks:
Top band (17-20) Convincing response. Moves beyond comedy to analyse Mrs Bennet’s genuine fear of poverty (entailment, five daughters, no savings). Discusses her ‘nerves’ as a symptom of anxiety, not just a comic device; her public embarrassments as desperate social performance; her joy at marriages as relief, not just vanity. Argues Austen uses Mrs Bennet to show how the system produces the behaviour society then mocks.
Top band (13-16): Clear analysis.
Upper-mid band (9-12): Some understanding.
Lower-mid band (5-8): Supported comments.
Lower band (1-4): Simple statements.

45c9498d-aae6-45ed-9584-49d9bf2ea5f1.text: Explain how Austen uses the contrast between Wickham and Darcy to develop the theme of appearance versus reality.
45c9498d-aae6-45ed-9584-49d9bf2ea5f1.marks:
Upper band (3-4): Wickham has charm, good looks, and easy manners but is dishonest and predatory. Darcy has poor social skills but genuine integrity, generosity, and constancy. The contrast shows that in a society obsessed with surface behaviour, charm can disguise villainy while awkwardness conceals virtue. Elizabeth’s mistake — trusting Wickham over Darcy — is the novel’s central illustration of this theme.
Lower band (1-2): Basic observation that one is good and one is bad.

5d51487d-faeb-440c-8025-0cb85245b30f.text: Read Darcy’s second proposal from ‘If your feelings are still what they were last April’ to the end of the scene. How does Austen use language to present Darcy as changed from his first proposal?
5d51487d-faeb-440c-8025-0cb85245b30f.marks:
Top band (17-20) Perceptive analysis. Contrasts first proposal (‘in vain have I struggled’ — imperious, listing objections) with second (‘one word from you will silence me’ — humble, deferential). Analyses: ‘too generous to trifle’ shows respect for Elizabeth’s character; ‘unchanged’ confirms constancy; ‘silence me on this subject for ever’ gives Elizabeth complete power. Discusses how the reversal of gender dynamics (man deferring to woman) challenges Regency social norms.
Top band (13-16): Clear analysis.
Upper-mid band (9-12): Some analysis.
Lower-mid band (5-8): Limited analysis.
Lower band (1-4): Simple comments.

5d51487d-faeb-440c-8025-0cb85245b30f.text: How does Austen use the four marriages in the novel to explore different attitudes to love and marriage?
5d51487d-faeb-440c-8025-0cb85245b30f.marks:
Top band (17-20) Convincing response covering: Elizabeth/Darcy (love + respect + growth); Jane/Bingley (warmth + goodness); Charlotte/Collins (pragmatism without love); Lydia/Wickham (passion without substance). May include Mr/Mrs Bennet as a fifth model (youthful attraction without intellectual equality). Argues Austen presents marriage as successful only when it combines genuine affection with mutual respect and self-knowledge.
Top band (13-16): Clear analysis across at least three marriages.
Upper-mid band (9-12): Some analysis.
Lower-mid band (5-8): Supported comments.
Lower band (1-4): Simple statements.

5d51487d-faeb-440c-8025-0cb85245b30f.text: Analyse the significance of Lady Catherine’s question: ‘Are the shades of Pemberley to be thus polluted?’
5d51487d-faeb-440c-8025-0cb85245b30f.marks:
Upper band (3-4): ‘Polluted’ implies Elizabeth is a contaminant who would corrupt the Darcy name through inferior birth. ‘Shades’ evokes Pemberley’s ancestral dignity. Lady Catherine treats class as a matter of purity versus contamination — the language of biological contamination applied to social hierarchy. Ironically, her visit gives Darcy hope to propose again, so her attempt to preserve class boundaries actually breaks them.
Lower band (1-2): Basic comment about Lady Catherine being rude.

5d51487d-faeb-440c-8025-0cb85245b30f.text: Read from Lady Catherine’s arrival at Longbourn to Elizabeth’s refusal to promise. How does Austen use language to present the confrontation between class hierarchy and individual agency?
5d51487d-faeb-440c-8025-0cb85245b30f.marks:
Top band (17-20) Perceptive analysis. Lady Catherine’s imperious language (‘polluted,’ ‘obstinate, headstrong girl’) versus Elizabeth’s measured, rational refusal (‘resolved to act in that manner which will constitute my happiness’). Discusses: Lady Catherine assuming her rank gives her authority over Elizabeth’s choices; Elizabeth’s claim to self-determination; the ironic outcome where Lady Catherine’s interference enables the marriage. Analyses Austen’s structural irony.
Top band (13-16): Clear analysis.
Upper-mid band (9-12): Some analysis.
Lower-mid band (5-8): Limited analysis.
Lower band (1-4): Simple comments.

5d51487d-faeb-440c-8025-0cb85245b30f.text: How does Austen present Darcy’s rescue of Lydia as the completion of his character arc?
5d51487d-faeb-440c-8025-0cb85245b30f.marks:
Top band (17-20) Convincing response. Traces Darcy’s arc from public arrogance (Meryton), through honest self-defence (the letter), to courteous behaviour (Pemberley), to secret generosity (rescuing Lydia). Argues the secrecy is crucial: Darcy acts without expectation of reward, proving his transformation is genuine. Links to Elizabeth’s earlier accusation of ‘selfish disdain of the feelings of others.’ Discusses how Darcy’s pride has been redirected, not eliminated.
Top band (13-16): Clear analysis.
Upper-mid band (9-12): Some understanding.
Lower-mid band (5-8): Supported comments.
Lower band (1-4): Simple statements.

5d51487d-faeb-440c-8025-0cb85245b30f.text: Explain how the contrast between Darcy’s two proposals demonstrates the novel’s central theme.
5d51487d-faeb-440c-8025-0cb85245b30f.marks:
Upper band (3-4): First proposal: ‘in vain have I struggled’ — proud, lists objections, assumes acceptance. Second: ‘one word from you will silence me’ — humble, vulnerable, defers to Elizabeth. The contrast shows that pride must be tempered by self-knowledge, and prejudice corrected by evidence. Both characters have grown: Darcy is humbler, Elizabeth recognises his worth. The resolution of the title’s twin flaws is achieved through mutual transformation.
Lower band (1-2): Basic identification that the second proposal is nicer.

fc324391-25d6-4e4a-9984-2c32ca7ea858.text: Compare how Hood and Wordsworth present the relationship between childhood and belonging. You should consider the poets' use of language, form and structure, as well as the contexts in which the poems were written. [20 marks]
fc324391-25d6-4e4a-9984-2c32ca7ea858.marks:
Top band (17-20) Perceptive, comparative analysis of both poems. Explores how Hood's elegiac tone and past-tense structure contrast with Wordsworth's urgent, present-tense imperatives. Analyses specific language choices (e.g. Hood's 'childish ignorance,' Wordsworth's 'blessing in the air'). Integrates AO3 context: Romantic idealisation of childhood, Hood's Victorian sense of loss vs Wordsworth's belief in nature's restorative power.
Top band (13-16): Sustained, developed comparison with clear analysis of methods and some context.
Upper-mid band (9-12): Clear comparison with some analysis of language/structure.
Lower-mid band (5-8): Supported response with some comparison.
Lower band (1-4): Simple comments on one or both poems.

fc324391-25d6-4e4a-9984-2c32ca7ea858.text: How does Clare use language and structure to present a sense of communal belonging in 'The Sunday Dip'? [10 marks]
fc324391-25d6-4e4a-9984-2c32ca7ea858.marks:
Top band (9-10) Perceptive analysis. Explores sensory detail, rhyming couplets as reflecting ritual, the boys presented as one group, nature as shared space. Clare's rural working-class background.
Top band (7-8): Sustained analysis with clear understanding of methods.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Clear explanation with some relevant analysis.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Supported response with some understanding.
Lower band (1-2): Simple comment on content.

fc324391-25d6-4e4a-9984-2c32ca7ea858.text: Explore how the theme of loss is presented in 'I Remember, I Remember.' You should refer to language, form and structure in your response. [10 marks]
fc324391-25d6-4e4a-9984-2c32ca7ea858.marks:
Top band (9-10) Perceptive analysis of Hood's techniques for conveying loss. Explores anaphora ('I remember, I remember'), the structural contrast between past joy and present grief in each stanza, the final stanza's spiritual dimension ('farther off from Heav'n'). Context: Victorian nostalgia, Romantic influence.
Top band (7-8): Sustained analysis with clear understanding of methods.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Clear explanation with relevant textual references.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Some supported points about loss.
Lower band (1-2): Simple identification of sad tone.

fc324391-25d6-4e4a-9984-2c32ca7ea858.text: Compare how belonging to nature is presented in 'To My Sister' and one other poem from the Belonging collection. [20 marks]
fc324391-25d6-4e4a-9984-2c32ca7ea858.marks:
Top band (17-20) Perceptive, sustained comparison. Analyses Wordsworth's imperative voice and spiritual imagery alongside chosen poem's techniques. Integrates AO3 (Romantic movement, biographical context). Explores similarities and differences in how nature enables belonging.
Top band (13-16): Developed comparison with clear analysis and some context.
Upper-mid band (9-12): Clear comparison with some analysis.
Lower-mid band (5-8): Some comparison with limited analysis.
Lower band (1-4): Simple comments.

fc324391-25d6-4e4a-9984-2c32ca7ea858.text: How does Hood use the image of the fir trees in the final stanza to convey his feelings about childhood and adulthood?
fc324391-25d6-4e4a-9984-2c32ca7ea858.marks:
Award up to 4 marks:
- Identifies that the fir trees seemed to 'touch the sky' in childhood, suggesting wonder and elevation (1 mark)
- Explains that the adult speaker recognises this as 'childish ignorance,' showing loss of wonder (1 mark)
- Analyses the metaphor of being 'farther off from Heav'n' as suggesting spiritual decline, not just physical growth (1 mark)
- Links to the wider theme: childhood offered a sense of belonging to something transcendent that adulthood has destroyed (1 mark)

fc324391-25d6-4e4a-9984-2c32ca7ea858.text: Explain how Wordsworth's use of imperatives in 'To My Sister' contributes to the poem's message about belonging.
fc324391-25d6-4e4a-9984-2c32ca7ea858.marks:
Award up to 4 marks:
- Identifies imperative verbs such as 'come forth' and 'put on' (1 mark)
- Explains that these create a sense of urgency and invitation, suggesting belonging requires action (1 mark)
- Analyses how the direct address to Dorothy creates intimacy, making belonging personal and relational (1 mark)
- Links to Romantic context: Wordsworth believed nature offered spiritual renewal, so the invitation is both physical and philosophical (1 mark)

aeb75a49-5d80-463a-b65b-03907ddda2ba.text: Read the following extract from Chapter 2, in which Jane is imprisoned in the Red Room. Explore how Brontë uses language to present Jane’s fear and isolation.
aeb75a49-5d80-463a-b65b-03907ddda2ba.marks:
Top band (17-20) Judicious analysis of language. Examines: colour symbolism (red = anger, blood, danger), sensory details (cold, dark, silence), the mirror image (‘strange little figure’ suggesting alienation from self), Gothic atmosphere (the dead uncle’s ghost). Analyses how Brontë uses the first-person perspective to immerse the reader in a child’s terror. Precise word-level analysis.

aeb75a49-5d80-463a-b65b-03907ddda2ba.text: In the novel as a whole, explore how Brontë presents Jane’s response to injustice.

Discusses: Jane’s confrontation with Mrs Reed, the Red Room rebellion, her public humiliation by Brocklehurst, her refusal to become Rochester’s mistress, her rejection of St John’s proposal. Shows how Jane’s response matures from childhood rage to principled adult resistance. Well-chosen quotations with perceptive analysis.

aeb75a49-5d80-463a-b65b-03907ddda2ba.text: Read the following extract from Chapter 7, in which Mr Brocklehurst publicly humiliates Jane at Lowood. Explore how Brontë uses language to present Brocklehurst’s hypocrisy and cruelty.
aeb75a49-5d80-463a-b65b-03907ddda2ba.marks:

7435ab96-b8a6-446c-a1ea-02c69effdeab.text: Read from Elizabeth’s defiance of Lady Catherine (‘I am only resolved to act in that manner’) to the end of the confrontation. How does Austen use language to present the conflict between individual agency and social hierarchy?

Discusses: Elizabeth claiming the right to self-determination; Lady Catherine assuming rank equals authority; the irony that this confrontation enables the marriage; Austen presenting Elizabeth’s calm rationality as morally superior to Lady Catherine’s inherited privilege.

7435ab96-b8a6-446c-a1ea-02c69effdeab.text: How does Austen present the theme of appearance versus reality in the novel as a whole?
7435ab96-b8a6-446c-a1ea-02c69effdeab.marks:
Top band (17-20) Convincing response. Discusses: Wickham’s charm masking dishonesty; Darcy’s reserve concealing integrity; the neighbourhood’s unreliable collective judgement; Elizabeth’s trust in her own perception being misplaced; Pemberley revealing the real Darcy. Argues Austen shows that Regency society’s emphasis on manners and social performance rewarded appearance over reality, and that genuine understanding requires evidence, not first impressions.
Top band (13-16): Clear analysis.
Upper-mid band (9-12): Some understanding.
Lower-mid band (5-8): Supported comments.
Lower band (1-4): Simple statements.

7435ab96-b8a6-446c-a1ea-02c69effdeab.text: Analyse how Elizabeth’s joke about falling in love with Darcy ‘on first seeing his beautiful grounds at Pemberley’ reflects Austen’s treatment of marriage and money.
7435ab96-b8a6-446c-a1ea-02c69effdeab.marks:
Upper band (3-4): The joke acknowledges what the novel has shown: economic reality shapes romantic choices. Elizabeth is self-aware enough to laugh at the connection between love and money, but the humour contains truth — Pemberley did trigger her reassessment of Darcy. Austen’s point is not that money is irrelevant, but that it should be combined with love, respect, and self-knowledge. The joke is characteristic of Elizabeth’s wit and honesty.
Lower band (1-2): Basic comment about Elizabeth liking Pemberley.

7435ab96-b8a6-446c-a1ea-02c69effdeab.text: Read the description of Mrs Bennet from Chapter 1. How does Austen use language to introduce her as both a comic and a sympathetic character?
7435ab96-b8a6-446c-a1ea-02c69effdeab.marks:
Top band (17-20) Perceptive analysis. The narrator’s tricolon (‘mean understanding, little information, uncertain temper’) delivers polite demolition. ‘The business of her life was to get her daughters married’ — ‘business’ transforms marriage into work, suggesting genuine economic pressure beneath the comedy. Her ‘nerves’ are both a comic device and a symptom of real anxiety. Discusses how the narrator’s ironic tone creates comedy while the underlying situation (five daughters, entailed estate, no financial safety net) creates sympathy.
Top band (13-16): Clear analysis.
Upper-mid band (9-12): Some analysis.
Lower-mid band (5-8): Limited analysis.
Lower band (1-4): Simple comments.

7435ab96-b8a6-446c-a1ea-02c69effdeab.text: How does Austen use the theme of gender to explore women’s limited options in the novel as a whole?
7435ab96-b8a6-446c-a1ea-02c69effdeab.marks:
Top band (17-20) Convincing response. Discusses: entailment trapping the Bennet women; Charlotte’s pragmatic marriage (‘a comfortable home’); Elizabeth’s refusal of Collins as defiance of the system; Lydia’s vulnerability to Wickham; Elizabeth’s independence ultimately enabled by Darcy’s wealth. Argues Austen celebrates Elizabeth’s agency while acknowledging that the system constrains all women — even the heroine’s happy ending depends on marrying a rich man.
Top band (13-16): Clear analysis.
Upper-mid band (9-12): Some understanding.
Lower-mid band (5-8): Supported comments.
Lower band (1-4): Simple statements.

7435ab96-b8a6-446c-a1ea-02c69effdeab.text: Explain why both Elizabeth and Darcy possess both pride and prejudice, and how this complicates the novel’s title.
7435ab96-b8a6-446c-a1ea-02c69effdeab.marks:
Upper band (3-4): Elizabeth’s intellectual pride (‘prided myself on my discernment’) causes prejudice against Darcy. Darcy’s social pride (‘tolerable’) causes prejudice against Elizabeth’s family. The title does not assign one flaw to each character — both share both. The novel argues that self-knowledge, not the removal of pride, is the cure. Darcy and Elizabeth learn to direct their pride better, not to abandon it.
Lower band (1-2): Basic statement that Darcy is proud and Elizabeth is prejudiced.
