918be679-94df-4394-acaf-f0f7fdc4dbea.text: Summarise the key themes you would expect to find in a 19th-century extract about a factory in an industrial city.
918be679-94df-4394-acaf-f0f7fdc4dbea.marks: Industrialisation and progress (1 mark). Social class and inequality — workers vs factory owners (1 mark). Dehumanisation — people treated like machines (1 mark). Suffering and hardship — dangerous conditions (1 mark). Power and control — those with money dominate those without (1 mark).

918be679-94df-4394-acaf-f0f7fdc4dbea.text:
Read the following extract:

'The children worked in silence, their small fingers darting between the machinery. The overseer paced behind them, his shadow falling across their bent backs like a dark wing. Not one of them raised their eyes.'

Analyse how the writer uses language to present the theme of power and control.
918be679-94df-4394-acaf-f0f7fdc4dbea.marks:
Top band (8–10) Perceptive analysis with well-integrated evidence.
Upper-mid band (5–7) Clear analysis with appropriate evidence.
Lower-mid band (3–4) Some relevant comments.
Lower band (1–2) Simple identification.

Expected points: 'worked in silence' implies fear and suppression; 'small fingers' emphasises the children's youth and vulnerability; 'darting' suggests rapid, anxious movement; 'overseer paced' connotes surveillance and authority; 'shadow falling across their bent backs like a dark wing' — simile compares his presence to a bird of prey, suggesting he is predatory and threatening; 'bent backs' implies submission and physical oppression; 'Not one of them raised their eyes' — absolute obedience, total control.

918be679-94df-4394-acaf-f0f7fdc4dbea.text: A student said: 'You need to know the context of 19th-century literature to identify themes in an unseen extract.' To what extent do you agree?
918be679-94df-4394-acaf-f0f7fdc4dbea.marks:
Top band (12–15) Perceptive evaluation with convincing reasoning.
Upper-mid band (8–11) Clear evaluation with relevant reasoning.
Lower-mid band (4–7) Some evaluation.
Lower band (1–3) Simple response.

Students may argue: agree — knowledge of Victorian society, Gothic tradition, or industrialisation helps identify themes faster and interpret them more deeply. Partial agreement — contextual knowledge enriches interpretation but the extract should provide enough clues for a careful reader to identify themes without it. Disagree — the exam tests reading skills, not historical knowledge; themes like power, isolation, and fear are universal and recognisable without context.

918be679-94df-4394-acaf-f0f7fdc4dbea.text: Write the opening of a story (approximately 200 words) that explores the theme of isolation. Use at least two methods to present your theme, such as setting, symbolism, or characterisation.
918be679-94df-4394-acaf-f0f7fdc4dbea.marks:
Content and Organisation (24 marks):
Top band (19–24) Compelling writing with sophisticated structural and language choices that clearly present the theme.
Upper-mid band (13–18) Engaging writing with clear thematic presentation.
Lower-mid band (7–12) Some successful writing with some thematic awareness.
Lower band (1–6) Simple writing with limited thematic connection.

Technical Accuracy (16 marks):
Top band (13–16) Accurate with varied sentence structures.
Upper-mid band (9–12) Mostly accurate.
Lower-mid band (5–8) Some accuracy.
Lower band (1–4) Limited accuracy.

Methods might include: isolated setting (remote house, empty landscape), character alone, symbolism (locked door, single candle), pathetic fallacy.

88ffc58e-aab3-496e-aca9-b18e7eeca153.text: Identify one example of a simple sentence used for dramatic effect in a 19th-century extract.
88ffc58e-aab3-496e-aca9-b18e7eeca153.marks: 1 mark for identifying any short, single-clause sentence that creates emphasis, surprise, or a change in pace (e.g. 'Then it stopped.' / 'He was dead.' / 'She screamed.').

88ffc58e-aab3-496e-aca9-b18e7eeca153.text: Select one punctuation feature from this sentence and explain its effect: 'The man — if he could be called a man — emerged from the shadows.'
88ffc58e-aab3-496e-aca9-b18e7eeca153.marks: Dashes / parenthetical clause (1 mark). The dashes interrupt the sentence to insert a moment of doubt, suggesting the figure may not be fully human, creating horror or unease (1 mark).

88ffc58e-aab3-496e-aca9-b18e7eeca153.text: Summarise the effects of three different sentence types (simple, compound, complex) that a 19th-century writer might use.
88ffc58e-aab3-496e-aca9-b18e7eeca153.marks: Simple sentence: short, direct, creates sudden emphasis or a dramatic pause (1 mark). Compound sentence: joins two ideas, creating balance, continuation, or contrast (1 mark). Complex sentence: adds detail through subordinate clauses, can build suspense by delaying the main point (1 mark). Writers vary between these types to control pace (1 mark). Shifts between sentence types are always deliberate and create specific effects (1 mark).

88ffc58e-aab3-496e-aca9-b18e7eeca153.text:
Read the following extract:

'The forest was silent. No bird sang; no insect hummed; no breeze stirred the heavy canopy of leaves above her. She stood perfectly still, listening. Nothing.'

Analyse how the writer uses sentence structure to create tension.
88ffc58e-aab3-496e-aca9-b18e7eeca153.marks:
Top band (8–10) Perceptive analysis of structural choices and their effects.
Upper-mid band (5–7) Clear analysis with appropriate evidence.
Lower-mid band (3–4) Some relevant comments.
Lower band (1–2) Simple identification.

Expected points: Opening simple sentence 'The forest was silent' establishes the mood directly; triple negative construction 'No bird sang; no insect hummed; no breeze stirred' — listing of absences creates a sense of unnatural stillness; semicolons create balanced, rhythmic pauses; 'She stood perfectly still, listening' — simple sentence mirrors her stillness; single-word sentence 'Nothing' — the shortest possible sentence creates maximum impact, suggests both emptiness and anticipation; progressive shortening of sentences builds tension by accelerating the pace.

88ffc58e-aab3-496e-aca9-b18e7eeca153.text: A student said: 'Analysing sentence structure is less important than analysing vocabulary in the exam.' To what extent do you agree?
88ffc58e-aab3-496e-aca9-b18e7eeca153.marks:
Top band (12–15) Perceptive evaluation.
Upper-mid band (8–11) Clear evaluation.
Lower-mid band (4–7) Some evaluation.
Lower band (1–3) Simple response.

Arguments: agree — vocabulary offers more tangible evidence (specific words to quote and analyse); many students find it easier; connotation analysis is the bread and butter of language responses. Partial agreement — both are required by AO2; the best answers integrate both; examiners notice when students ignore structure entirely. Disagree — sentence structure analysis can distinguish top-grade answers; it shows the examiner a wider range of analytical skills; some extracts rely more on structural effects than vocabulary.

88ffc58e-aab3-496e-aca9-b18e7eeca153.text: Write a tense scene (approximately 200 words) where a character hears an unexpected noise at night. Deliberately vary your sentence lengths to control the pace and build suspense.
88ffc58e-aab3-496e-aca9-b18e7eeca153.marks:
Content and Organisation (24 marks):
Top band (19–24) Compelling writing with sophisticated structural control.
Upper-mid band (13–18) Engaging writing with clear pace control.
Lower-mid band (7–12) Some successful writing.
Lower band (1–6) Simple writing.

Technical Accuracy (16 marks):
Top band (13–16) Accurate with varied sentence structures.
Upper-mid band (9–12) Mostly accurate.
Lower-mid band (5–8) Some accuracy.
Lower band (1–4) Limited accuracy.

Look for: deliberate variation between long and short sentences, effective use of single-word or very short sentences for impact, punctuation choices that control pace.

dad53d1c-3b06-413f-8611-2451f605240f.text: Identify one structural feature a writer might use at the opening of a 19th-century fiction extract.
dad53d1c-3b06-413f-8611-2451f605240f.marks: Any one from: in medias res (opening in the middle of action) / descriptive establishing shot / dialogue opening / wide-angle setting description / first-person reflection. 1 mark.

dad53d1c-3b06-413f-8611-2451f605240f.text: Select one type of structural shift and explain what effect it creates for the reader.
dad53d1c-3b06-413f-8611-2451f605240f.marks: 1 mark for naming a shift (e.g. calm to tension, external to internal, wide focus to close-up). 1 mark for explaining the effect (e.g. 'A shift from calm description to sudden action creates surprise and heightens the reader's sense of danger').

dad53d1c-3b06-413f-8611-2451f605240f.text: Summarise the difference between analysing language and analysing structure in a fiction extract.
dad53d1c-3b06-413f-8611-2451f605240f.marks: Language analysis focuses on individual word choices and their connotations (1 mark). Structure analysis focuses on how the whole text is organised (1 mark). Language operates at the micro level (words, phrases) while structure operates at the macro level (openings, shifts, endings) (1 mark). Both are required by AO2 (1 mark). The best answers integrate both — e.g. explaining how a structural shift is reinforced by a change in vocabulary (1 mark).

dad53d1c-3b06-413f-8611-2451f605240f.text:
Read the following extract:

'The ball was in full swing. Chandeliers blazed overhead, and the orchestra played a waltz that seemed to lift the dancers from the floor. [Paragraph break] In the corridor beyond the ballroom, a single candle guttered in its sconce. A figure stood in the half-darkness, watching the door.'

Analyse how the writer uses structure to create contrast in this extract.
dad53d1c-3b06-413f-8611-2451f605240f.marks:
Top band (8–10) Perceptive analysis of structural choices.
Upper-mid band (5–7) Clear analysis with evidence.
Lower-mid band (3–4) Some relevant comments.
Lower band (1–2) Simple identification.

Expected points: The paragraph break creates a dramatic structural shift from the bright, energetic ballroom to the dark, still corridor. The first paragraph uses expansive description (chandeliers, orchestra, dancers) creating warmth and movement. The second narrows the focus to a single candle and a solitary figure, creating menace through contrast. The 'zoom in' from many to one intensifies the sense of threat. The vocabulary shifts too — from 'blazed' to 'guttered,' from 'dancers' to 'a figure' — reinforcing the structural contrast.

dad53d1c-3b06-413f-8611-2451f605240f.text: A student said: 'The opening of an extract is always the most important structural feature to analyse.' To what extent do you agree?
dad53d1c-3b06-413f-8611-2451f605240f.marks:
Top band (12–15) Perceptive evaluation.
Upper-mid band (8–11) Clear evaluation.
Lower-mid band (4–7) Some evaluation.
Lower band (1–3) Simple response.

Arguments: agree — the opening sets the tone, establishes the reader's expectations, and determines how the rest of the extract is experienced. Partial agreement — the opening matters but structural shifts within the extract are often more revealing because they show deliberate change; the ending is also crucial as it determines the reader's lasting impression. Disagree — the most important feature depends on the extract; in some texts, a mid-point twist or a dramatic ending is the most significant structural choice.

dad53d1c-3b06-413f-8611-2451f605240f.text: Write the opening two paragraphs (approximately 200 words) of a story that uses a clear structural shift between the first and second paragraph. Your first paragraph should establish a calm setting; your second should introduce tension.
dad53d1c-3b06-413f-8611-2451f605240f.marks:
Content and Organisation (24 marks):
Top band (19–24) Compelling writing with clear structural shift and effective contrast.
Upper-mid band (13–18) Engaging writing with discernible shift.
Lower-mid band (7–12) Some structural awareness.
Lower band (1–6) Simple writing.

Technical Accuracy (16 marks):
Top band (13–16) Accurate with varied sentences.
Upper-mid band (9–12) Mostly accurate.
Lower-mid band (5–8) Some accuracy.
Lower band (1–4) Limited accuracy.

Look for: clear contrast between paragraphs, effective use of description vs action, vocabulary that reinforces the structural shift.

e2038a53-3989-4a9d-b9c2-3f7c3e4e6520.text: Read Act 3, Scene 1 from “Hath not a Jew eyes?” to “I will better the instruction.” How does Shakespeare use language in this extract to present Shylock’s response to persecution? Write about the extract and the play as a whole.
e2038a53-3989-4a9d-b9c2-3f7c3e4e6520.marks:
Top band (25–30 + 4 spelling/grammar)Analyses rhetorical questions, the shift from shared humanity to revenge, the argument that Christians taught him cruelty. Links to the wider play: the bond, the trial, forced conversion. Embeds context: anti-Semitism, the Elizabethan audience’s likely reaction. Explores the ambiguity: sympathy vs villainy. Word-level analysis of “prick,” “bleed,” “revenge.”

Upper band (19–24 + 3)Thoughtful with evidence and context.
Upper-mid band (13–18 + 2)Clear with some analysis.
Mid band (7–12 + 2)Some understanding.
Lower-mid band (3–6 + 1)Limited.
Lower band (1–2 + 1)Simple.

e2038a53-3989-4a9d-b9c2-3f7c3e4e6520.text: Analyse the significance of Shylock’s line “I would not have given it for a wilderness of monkeys” (Act 3, Scene 1). What does it reveal about his character?
e2038a53-3989-4a9d-b9c2-3f7c3e4e6520.marks:
Upper band (3-4): The turquoise ring was from his dead wife Leah. “Wilderness of monkeys” uses hyperbole to show the ring’s emotional value is infinite. Jessica traded it for a single monkey, showing her carelessness towards her mother’s memory. The line humanises Shylock — he is not just grieving money but personal, irreplaceable loss. Contrasts with the comedic “my ducats! my daughter!” report.
Lower band (1-2): Basic comment about Shylock being upset.

e2038a53-3989-4a9d-b9c2-3f7c3e4e6520.text: Explore how Shakespeare uses the song during Bassanio’s casket choice to develop the theme of appearance versus reality.
e2038a53-3989-4a9d-b9c2-3f7c3e4e6520.marks:
Top band (7-8): The song contains words rhyming with “lead” (bred, head, fed, nourished), possibly hinting at the answer. The song’s theme (“Tell me where is fancy bred”) warns against superficial attraction. This either shows Portia guiding Bassanio (subverting her father’s will) or Shakespeare guiding the audience. Either way, it complicates the idea of a fair test.
Top band (5–6) Clear analysis.
Mid band (3–4) Some points.
Lower band (1–2) Simple.

e2038a53-3989-4a9d-b9c2-3f7c3e4e6520.text: How does Shakespeare present Shylock’s reaction to Jessica’s elopement? Refer to Act 2, Scene 8 and Act 3, Scene 1 in your answer.
e2038a53-3989-4a9d-b9c2-3f7c3e4e6520.marks:
Top band (7-8): Analyses Solanio’s “my daughter! my ducats!” report from Act 2, Scene 8, the turquoise ring detail, and the line about wishing Jessica dead. Explores ambiguity: comedic miser or grief-stricken father. Notes that we see Shylock’s pain only through hostile witnesses. Links to his motivation for pursuing the bond.
Top band (5–6) Clear analysis.
Mid band (3–4) Some points.
Lower band (1–2) Simple.

e2038a53-3989-4a9d-b9c2-3f7c3e4e6520.text: Starting with Act 3, Scene 1, explore how Shakespeare presents Shylock as both a victim and a threat. Write about the extract and the play as a whole.
e2038a53-3989-4a9d-b9c2-3f7c3e4e6520.marks:
Top band (25–30 + 4 spelling/grammar)Explores the duality: victim of abuse (gaberdine, Jessica, isolation) and threat (the bond, “I will better the instruction”). Analyses how Shakespeare structures the speech to move between sympathy and menace. Links across the play: the trial, forced conversion. Embeds context: Elizabethan expectations of a Jewish villain, modern rereadings. Explores whether the play endorses or challenges anti-Semitism.

Upper band (19–24 + 3)Thoughtful with evidence.
Upper-mid band (13–18 + 2)Clear.
Mid band (7–12 + 2)Some understanding.
Lower-mid band (3–6 + 1)Limited.
Lower band (1–2 + 1)Simple.

e2038a53-3989-4a9d-b9c2-3f7c3e4e6520.text: Analyse how Shakespeare uses Portia’s ring as a symbol. What does it represent when she gives it to Bassanio in Act 3, Scene 2?
e2038a53-3989-4a9d-b9c2-3f7c3e4e6520.marks:
Upper band (3-4): The ring symbolises fidelity, trust, and Portia’s transfer of power (“This house, these servants, and this same myself / Are yours”). The condition attached (“presage the ruin of your love”) foreshadows conflict. It parallels the bond: both are promises with penalties for breaking them. Links to appearance vs reality — Bassanio’s oath will be tested.
Lower band (1-2): Basic comment about the ring meaning love.

0187309a-cb9d-40f6-a667-8b848f69dc22.text: Identify the audience, purpose, and form in this task: 'Write an article for a local newspaper persuading readers to support a new youth centre in your area.'
0187309a-cb9d-40f6-a667-8b848f69dc22.marks: Audience: local newspaper readers / general public. Purpose: persuade. Form: article. 1 mark for all three correctly identified.

0187309a-cb9d-40f6-a667-8b848f69dc22.text: Select one element from the AO5 Level 4 descriptor and explain why it matters for achieving top marks.
0187309a-cb9d-40f6-a667-8b848f69dc22.marks: Any valid element: 'compelling communication' (1 mark) — means the writing is engaging and holds the reader's attention throughout, not just technically correct (1 mark). Also accept: 'convincingly matched register,' 'extensive and ambitious vocabulary,' 'fluently linked paragraphs,' 'sustained crafting of linguistic devices.'

0187309a-cb9d-40f6-a667-8b848f69dc22.text: Summarise the four steps of the Section B exam strategy and the time allocated to each.
0187309a-cb9d-40f6-a667-8b848f69dc22.marks: 1. Choose task — 3 minutes (1). 2. Plan — 5 minutes (1). 3. Write — 32 minutes (1). 4. Edit (three-pass) — 5 minutes (1). Total: 45 minutes (1).

0187309a-cb9d-40f6-a667-8b848f69dc22.text:
Read this student's opening paragraph for a speech:

'Today I am going to talk about school lunches. I think they should be healthier. There are many reasons for this. I will explain them now.'

Rewrite this opening to achieve Level 4, using at least two rhetorical devices and an appropriate register.
0187309a-cb9d-40f6-a667-8b848f69dc22.marks:
Top band (8–10) Compelling opening with 2+ devices, strong voice, appropriate speech conventions.
Upper-mid band (5–7) Improved with 1-2 devices.
Lower-mid band (3–4) Some improvement.
Lower band (1–2) Minimal change.

Example: 'How many of you have looked at your school lunch and thought: is this really the best we can do? Processed, tasteless, and nutritionally empty — this is what we are expected to fuel our afternoons with. Today, I want to argue that we deserve better.' (Rhetorical question, tricolon, direct address.)

0187309a-cb9d-40f6-a667-8b848f69dc22.text: 'Planning wastes valuable writing time in the exam.' To what extent do you agree?
0187309a-cb9d-40f6-a667-8b848f69dc22.marks:
Top band (12–15) Perceptive — recognises planning saves time and improves quality.
Upper-mid band (8–11) Clear.
Lower-mid band (4–7) Some.
Lower band (1–3) Simple.

Disagree: 5 minutes planning prevents structural drift, writer's block, and weak endings; planned responses are consistently higher-scoring; planning ensures rhetorical devices are placed deliberately. Agree: some students plan naturally in their heads; over-planning can eat into writing time. Nuanced: brief planning (topic sentences, devices, conclusion) is optimal — extensive planning is unnecessary.

0187309a-cb9d-40f6-a667-8b848f69dc22.text: Complete this full exam-style task in 45 minutes: 'Write a letter to the editor of a national newspaper arguing that social media companies should be held responsible for the mental health impact of their platforms on young people.'
0187309a-cb9d-40f6-a667-8b848f69dc22.marks:
Content and Organisation (24 marks):
Top band (19–24) Compelling argument, convincingly formal register, fluent paragraphing, sustained devices.
Upper-mid band (13–18) Clear argument, appropriate register.

Technical Accuracy (16 marks):
Top band (13–16) Wide range of punctuation, varied sentences, ambitious vocabulary.

Full 40-mark assessment against standard descriptors. Must be completed under timed conditions.

f1dad116-49d3-44b3-abdd-70461a16e332.text: Identify two pieces of information that the 19th-century writer gives about working conditions in the factory.
f1dad116-49d3-44b3-abdd-70461a16e332.marks: 1 mark for each valid piece of information identified from the text, up to 2 marks. Accept direct quotation or paraphrase.

f1dad116-49d3-44b3-abdd-70461a16e332.text: Explain how the 19th-century writer uses vocabulary to convey the harshness of industrial life. Use evidence from lines 8 to 18.
f1dad116-49d3-44b3-abdd-70461a16e332.marks:
Upper band (3-4): Clear explanation selecting relevant vocabulary with analysis of its effect. Uses terminology such as emotive language, connotation, or imagery.
Lower band (1-2): Identifies some vocabulary with limited comment on effect.

f1dad116-49d3-44b3-abdd-70461a16e332.text: Analyse how the writer of the 19th-century text uses language to create sympathy for the poor. Refer to specific examples in your answer.
f1dad116-49d3-44b3-abdd-70461a16e332.marks:
Top band (7-8): Perceptive analysis of language choices with detailed exploration of effects on the reader. Uses well-chosen evidence and precise terminology.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Clear analysis with relevant evidence and appropriate terminology.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Some relevant comments with limited analysis.
Lower band (1-2): Simple identification with no analysis.

f1dad116-49d3-44b3-abdd-70461a16e332.text: Compare how the 19th-century writer and the modern writer present their attitudes towards poverty. Support your answer with evidence from both texts.
f1dad116-49d3-44b3-abdd-70461a16e332.marks:
Top band (10-12): Perceptive comparison exploring how methods convey different attitudes. Well-integrated evidence from both texts with precise analysis.
Upper-mid band (7-9): Clear comparison with relevant evidence from both texts.
Lower-mid band (4-6): Some comparison with some evidence. May focus more on one text.
Lower band (1-3): Simple statements about both texts with limited evidence.

f1dad116-49d3-44b3-abdd-70461a16e332.text: Write a letter to your local council in which you argue that more should be done to support homeless people in your area.
f1dad116-49d3-44b3-abdd-70461a16e332.marks:
Content and Organisation (24 marks):
Top band (19–24) Compelling, convincing communication with varied structural features and extensive vocabulary.
Upper-mid band (13–18) Clearly communicated with effective structural features.
Lower-mid band (7–12) Some success in communication with some structural features.
Lower band (1–6) Simple communication.

Technical Accuracy (16 marks):
Top band (13–16) Highly accurate spelling, punctuation, and grammar throughout.
Upper-mid band (9–12) Mostly accurate with good range.
Lower-mid band (5–8) Some accuracy.
Lower band (1–4) Limited accuracy.

f1dad116-49d3-44b3-abdd-70461a16e332.text: How does the 19th-century writer structure their argument to build towards a climax? Refer to the opening, development, and conclusion of the text.
f1dad116-49d3-44b3-abdd-70461a16e332.marks:
Upper band (3-4): Clear explanation of how structure builds the argument. References specific parts of the text with relevant evidence.
Lower band (1-2): Some awareness of structure with limited comment.

991dcc70-9bf0-4845-9286-6926f15b1eee.text: Identify two things the writer tells you about the condition of the school building. Use evidence from lines 3 to 10.
991dcc70-9bf0-4845-9286-6926f15b1eee.marks: 1 mark per valid point, up to 2 marks. Must be drawn from the specified lines. Accept quotation or paraphrase.

991dcc70-9bf0-4845-9286-6926f15b1eee.text: Explain how the writer uses language in lines 12 to 20 to show their disappointment with the government's response to the flood.
991dcc70-9bf0-4845-9286-6926f15b1eee.marks:
Upper band (3-4): Clear explanation with relevant evidence. Comments on specific word choices and their effect, using appropriate terminology.
Lower band (1-2): Some identification of relevant language with limited comment.

991dcc70-9bf0-4845-9286-6926f15b1eee.text: Analyse how the 19th-century writer uses language to convey the excitement of their first railway journey. Use specific examples from the text.
991dcc70-9bf0-4845-9286-6926f15b1eee.marks:
Top band (7-8): Perceptive analysis with well-chosen evidence and precise terminology. Detailed exploration of effects.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Clear analysis with relevant evidence.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Some relevant comments with limited analysis.
Lower band (1-2): Simple identification with no analysis.

991dcc70-9bf0-4845-9286-6926f15b1eee.text: Compare how both writers convey their attitudes towards technological change. Use evidence from both texts.
991dcc70-9bf0-4845-9286-6926f15b1eee.marks:
Top band (10-12): Perceptive comparison with well-integrated evidence from both texts. Analyses methods used to convey attitudes.
Upper-mid band (7-9): Clear comparison with relevant evidence.
Lower-mid band (4-6): Some comparison with some evidence.
Lower band (1-3): Simple statements with limited evidence.

991dcc70-9bf0-4845-9286-6926f15b1eee.text: Write a speech for your school assembly in which you persuade students to volunteer for a local community project.
991dcc70-9bf0-4845-9286-6926f15b1eee.marks:
Content and Organisation (24 marks):
Top band (19–24) Compelling, convincing communication with varied structural features.
Upper-mid band (13–18) Clearly communicated with effective structure.
Lower-mid band (7–12) Communicates with some success.
Lower band (1–6) Simple communication.

Technical Accuracy (16 marks):
Top band (13–16) Highly accurate throughout.
Upper-mid band (9–12) Mostly accurate.
Lower-mid band (5–8) Some accuracy.
Lower band (1–4) Limited accuracy.

991dcc70-9bf0-4845-9286-6926f15b1eee.text: What does the writer implicitly suggest about the character of the explorer in lines 1 to 8? Support your answer with evidence.
991dcc70-9bf0-4845-9286-6926f15b1eee.marks:
Upper band (3-4): Clear inference supported by well-chosen evidence. Explains what the language suggests about the character.
Lower band (1-2): Simple inference with limited evidence.

7cd184d1-d2d5-4466-b36a-d5f48dedfc7e.text: Identify two structural features the writer uses in the opening paragraph of the 19th-century text.
7cd184d1-d2d5-4466-b36a-d5f48dedfc7e.marks: 1 mark per valid structural feature identified, up to 2 marks. Accept features such as: rhetorical question, short opening sentence, direct address, anecdote.

7cd184d1-d2d5-4466-b36a-d5f48dedfc7e.text: Explain how the writer uses sentence structure in lines 10 to 18 to build tension. Use specific examples from the text.
7cd184d1-d2d5-4466-b36a-d5f48dedfc7e.marks:
Upper band (3-4): Clear explanation of how sentence structures (e.g. short sentences, listing, sentence length variation) create tension. Uses specific examples.
Lower band (1-2): Some identification of sentence features with limited comment.

7cd184d1-d2d5-4466-b36a-d5f48dedfc7e.text: Analyse how the writer uses both language and structure to present their argument in the modern text. Refer to the whole text in your answer.
7cd184d1-d2d5-4466-b36a-d5f48dedfc7e.marks:
Top band (7-8): Perceptive analysis covering both language and structure. Well-chosen evidence with precise terminology.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Clear analysis covering language and/or structure.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Some relevant comments.
Lower band (1-2): Simple identification.

7cd184d1-d2d5-4466-b36a-d5f48dedfc7e.text: Compare how both writers structure their texts to engage the reader. Consider openings, development, and conclusions.
7cd184d1-d2d5-4466-b36a-d5f48dedfc7e.marks:
Top band (10-12): Perceptive comparison of structural choices with detailed analysis of effects.
Upper-mid band (7-9): Clear comparison with relevant evidence.
Lower-mid band (4-6): Some comparison.
Lower band (1-3): Simple statements.

7cd184d1-d2d5-4466-b36a-d5f48dedfc7e.text: Write a letter to a newspaper in which you argue for or against the introduction of a four-day school week.
7cd184d1-d2d5-4466-b36a-d5f48dedfc7e.marks:
Content and Organisation (24 marks):
Top band (19–24) Compelling communication with varied structural features.

078171fd-2d57-416e-bc99-262ba2d63fe8.text:
Read the following extract from Stave 4:

“A churchyard. Here, then; the wretched man whose name he had now to learn, lay underneath the ground. It was a worthy place. Walled in by houses; overrun by grass and weeds, the growth of vegetation’s death, not life; choked up with too much burying; fat with repleted appetite. A worthy place!”

Starting with this extract, explore how Dickens uses setting to convey ideas about death and moral failure.
078171fd-2d57-416e-bc99-262ba2d63fe8.marks:
Top band (7-8): Perceptive analysis of language, structure, and context. Explores ‘vegetation’s death, not life’ as an oxymoron reflecting spiritual emptiness. ‘Choked up’ and ‘fat with repleted appetite’ personify the graveyard as overfed on death — mirroring how Scrooge has consumed wealth without giving back. The ironic repetition of ‘worthy place’ highlights how Scrooge’s life has led to a worthless end. Links to Victorian context: neglected graves for the unmourned.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Clear analysis with some language exploration and contextual links.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Supported comments on the extract with some relevant points.
Lower band (1-2): Simple comments with limited textual reference.

078171fd-2d57-416e-bc99-262ba2d63fe8.text:
Read the following extract from Stave 4:

“The ways were foul and narrow; the shops and houses wretched; the people half-naked, drunken, slipshod, ugly.”

Starting with this extract, explore how Dickens presents the effects of poverty in A Christmas Carol.
078171fd-2d57-416e-bc99-262ba2d63fe8.marks:
Top band (7-8): Perceptive analysis connecting extract to wider novel. Explores the list of adjectives ‘foul’, ‘wretched’, ‘drunken’ as creating a catalogue of degradation. Links to Ignorance and Want from Stave 3 — these are the consequences Dickens warned about. Discusses how Old Joe’s customers are driven to crime by want, not inherent wickedness. References Dickens’s social purpose: making Victorian readers confront poverty they preferred to ignore.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Clear analysis with some language features and links to the wider text.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Supported comments with some relevant references.
Lower band (1-2): Simple identification of poverty with minimal analysis.

078171fd-2d57-416e-bc99-262ba2d63fe8.text: How does Dickens use the juxtaposition of Scrooge’s death and Tiny Tim’s death in Stave 4 to present his message about social responsibility?

Analyses specific language: businessmen’s indifference vs Bob’s grief. Links to Dickens’s message: wealth without compassion leads to spiritual death; generosity even in poverty creates meaning. References Victorian context — Malthusian attitudes, the Poor Law, Dickens’s social reform agenda. Discusses structural purpose: juxtaposition as the final push toward Scrooge’s transformation.
Upper band (21-25): Thoughtful, developed response with well-chosen references and clear analysis of language, form and structure.
Upper-mid band (16-20): Clear, explained analysis with relevant textual references and some contextual links.

Lower-mid band (6-10): Supported comments with some analysis of language or structure.

078171fd-2d57-416e-bc99-262ba2d63fe8.text:
Starting with the extract below, explore how Dickens presents fear and its power to change people in A Christmas Carol.

“Scrooge crept towards it, trembling as he went; and following the finger, read upon the stone of the neglected grave his own name, Ebenezer Scrooge. ‘Am I that man who lay upon the bed?’ he cried, upon his knees.”

Write about:
• how Dickens presents fear in this extract
• how Dickens presents fear and its effects in the novella as a whole.
[30 marks]
078171fd-2d57-416e-bc99-262ba2d63fe8.marks:
Top band (26-30) Convincing, critical, exploratory response. Analyses ‘crept’ and ‘trembling’ as showing Scrooge’s physical terror. Explores ‘neglected grave’ as reflecting his neglected moral life. Discusses the progression of fear across staves: unease (Marley), discomfort (Past), guilt (Present), terror (Yet to Come). Links to Gothic conventions and Dickens’s moral purpose. Argues fear is redemptive — without it, Scrooge could not change. References Victorian context: the novella as a warning to wealthy readers.
Upper band (21-25) Thoughtful, developed response with clear analysis and contextual understanding.
Top band (16-20): Clear understanding with explained comments and relevant references.
Upper-mid band (11-15): Some explained comments with appropriate references.
Lower-mid band (6-10): Supported comments with some relevant textual reference.

2a817043-5794-4c6b-9574-f1775f3ad65e.text: Read the following quotation: 'the air was heavy with the smell of blood, which had been unknown there since the expulsion of Jones.' How does Orwell use language to convey the horror of the purges in this quotation?

2a817043-5794-4c6b-9574-f1775f3ad65e.text: Starting with this quotation, where Squealer announces that Snowball 'was in league with Jones from the very start,' explore how Orwell presents the use of propaganda in Animal Farm. The repetition of 'categorically' mimics the relentless, bullying tone of Soviet propaganda. Boxer's capitulation ('If Comrade Napoleon says it, it must be right') shows how loyalty can be weaponised. Squealer's 'ugly look at Boxer' foreshadows Boxer's eventual fate. 2a817043-5794-4c6b-9574-f1775f3ad65e.text: How does Orwell use the character of Squealer to explore ideas about truth and lies in Animal Farm? Write about: what Squealer says and does, and how Orwell uses the character of Squealer to explore ideas about truth and lies.
2a817043-5794-4c6b-9574-f1775f3ad65e.marks:
Top band (26–30 marks + up to 4 spelling/grammar)Critical, exploratory response. Squealer represents the propaganda machine of a totalitarian state — paralleling Pravda, the Soviet state newspaper. His earliest lie (justifying the milk and apples) is relatively small, but his deceptions escalate with each chapter: rewriting the Battle of the Cowshed, claiming Snowball was 'Jones's agent from the very start', justifying the purges. Orwell emphasises Squealer's physical mannerisms ('making little nervous skips', 'frisking from side to side') to suggest his discomfort with his own lies, creating dark comedy. The phrase 'could turn black into white' foreshadows his role. His constant accompaniment by 'two or three dogs' reveals that propaganda is always backed by force. Squealer's lies become the animals' reality because they lack the literacy and confidence to challenge them — Orwell's warning about the importance of education and a free press.

2a817043-5794-4c6b-9574-f1775f3ad65e.text: How does Orwell present the importance of Clover's moment of reflection after the executions in Chapter Seven?
2a817043-5794-4c6b-9574-f1775f3ad65e.marks:
Top band (11-12) Critical, exploratory response. Clover's reflection is one of the most emotionally powerful moments in the novel. She thinks that 'these scenes of terror and slaughter were not what they had looked forward to on that night when Old Major first stirred them to rebellion.' This is a rare moment of genuine insight from one of the common animals — she sees the truth clearly. However, Orwell's devastating point is that these were Clover's thoughts 'though she lacked the words to express them.' Her lack of education and articulation means she cannot challenge the pigs. This is Orwell's central warning: without education and the ability to express dissent, ordinary people are powerless against tyranny. The banning of 'Beasts of England' immediately afterwards shows the pigs suppressing any remaining channel for the animals' feelings.

2a817043-5794-4c6b-9574-f1775f3ad65e.text: How does Orwell use the banning of 'Beasts of England' and its replacement to explore the theme of revolution and betrayal in Animal Farm?

Banning it is an act of ideological suppression: the pigs cannot allow the animals to remember what was promised. Orwell suggests that the first sign of a revolution's failure is when its leaders suppress the symbols that inspired it.

The windmill is Orwell's central symbol of exploited labour — it represents how totalitarian leaders channel workers' hopes into projects that serve the ruling class. Napoleon's adoption of Snowball's plans shows how dictators steal ideas. The repeated destruction and rebuilding mirrors the futility of the Five-Year Plans. Boxer's dedication to the windmill makes his betrayal more devastating. The finished windmill is used for milling corn to sell for profit — not for the three-day week Snowball promised.

3a5ac98e-d0c0-48a2-b627-ac38f1560fe9.text: How far does Orwell present Boxer as a sympathetic character in Animal Farm? Write about: what Boxer says and does, and how far Orwell presents Boxer as a sympathetic character.
3a5ac98e-d0c0-48a2-b627-ac38f1560fe9.marks:
Top band (26–30 marks + up to 4 spelling/grammar)Critical, exploratory response. Boxer's mottos ('I will work harder' / 'Napoleon is always right') combine admirable determination with dangerous naivety. Orwell creates sympathy through Boxer's physical sacrifices and his genuine belief in Animalism's ideals. The image of 'his hoofs clawing at the ground' generates pathos. However, Orwell also implies criticism — Boxer's refusal to think for himself enables the pigs' tyranny. His loyalty to Napoleon despite mounting evidence of corruption makes him complicit. Context: parallels Stakhanovite workers and the broader proletariat under Stalin. The reader's sympathy is deepened by dramatic irony — we understand Boxer is being exploited even when he cannot see it himself. His death at the knacker's (Chapter 9) is the ultimate betrayal.

3a5ac98e-d0c0-48a2-b627-ac38f1560fe9.text: How does Orwell use the character of Mr Whymper and the farm's engagement with humans to present the betrayal of the revolution in Animal Farm?
3a5ac98e-d0c0-48a2-b627-ac38f1560fe9.marks:

His introduction directly contradicts the original principles of Animalism. Squealer's euphemism ('not of course for any commercial purpose') exposes the gap between rhetoric and reality. The pigs' trade with Frederick and Pilkington mirrors the USSR's diplomatic dealings with capitalist nations. This engagement marks a turning point: the pigs are no longer pretending to be different from humans.

b8e74bc1-70e8-44fa-8774-d9ad427e05aa.text: Read the following quotation: 'Father of All Animals, Terror of Mankind, Protector of the Sheep-fold, Ducklings' Friend.' How does Orwell use language to satirise Napoleon's cult of personality?
b8e74bc1-70e8-44fa-8774-d9ad427e05aa.marks:
Upper band (3-4): Detailed analysis of language choices. E.g. The epithets are deliberately contradictory — 'Terror of Mankind' suggests fear and power, while 'Ducklings' Friend' suggests warmth and gentleness. The juxtaposition is absurd, and Orwell uses this absurdity to satirise how dictators construct a false, all-encompassing image. 'Father of All Animals' echoes Stalin's title 'Father of Nations', explicitly linking Napoleon to the Soviet dictator. The accumulation of titles mimics the excessive praise typical of totalitarian propaganda.
Lower band (1-2): Basic comments. E.g. Napoleon has lots of different titles which makes him seem important.

b8e74bc1-70e8-44fa-8774-d9ad427e05aa.text: Starting with this quotation from the poem 'Comrade Napoleon' ('Friend of fatherless! Fountain of happiness! Lord of the swill-bucket!'), explore how Orwell uses language to present propaganda in Animal Farm. Write about: how Orwell presents propaganda in this quotation, and how Orwell presents propaganda in the novel as a whole.
b8e74bc1-70e8-44fa-8774-d9ad427e05aa.marks:
Top band (7-8): Perceptive analysis. The poem uses religious register ('Thou art the giver') to deify Napoleon, making criticism feel like blasphemy. 'Lord of the swill-bucket' is bathetic — the grand religious language collapses into the mundane reality of pig-food, exposing the absurdity. 'His first squeak should be Comrade Napoleon' suggests totalitarian indoctrination from birth. The poem is inscribed opposite the Seven Commandments — Napoleon's image literally replaces the revolution's principles. Across the novel, propaganda evolves from Squealer's verbal arguments to this kind of cultural saturation. Context: parallels Pravda, Soviet art, and mandatory praise of Stalin.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Clear, relevant analysis.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Some relevant comments.

b8e74bc1-70e8-44fa-8774-d9ad427e05aa.text: How does Orwell use the character of Napoleon to explore ideas about power and control in Animal Farm? Write about: how Orwell presents the character of Napoleon, and how Orwell uses the character of Napoleon to present ideas about power and control in the novel.
b8e74bc1-70e8-44fa-8774-d9ad427e05aa.marks:
Top band (26–30 marks + up to 4 spelling/grammar)Critical, exploratory response. Napoleon's rise to power follows a clear trajectory: political manoeuvring (using the dogs to exile Snowball), consolidation through fear (the purges of Chapter Seven), and the creation of a cult of personality (Chapter Eight). Orwell shows that power corrupts absolutely — Napoleon begins as one pig among many and ends as an indistinguishable copy of Jones. His epithets ('Father of All Animals') parallel Stalin's self-glorification. The cult of personality makes him untouchable: criticism becomes impossible when the leader is presented as infallible. Napoleon's methods — propaganda (Squealer), violence (the dogs), and manipulation of history (changing the commandments) — are the three pillars of totalitarian control. The Battle of the Windmill shows his ability to turn failure into propaganda victory. The whisky episode reveals his hypocrisy: he punishes others for what he does himself. Context: Napoleon represents Stalin, but also any leader who uses power for self-enrichment rather than the public good.

b8e74bc1-70e8-44fa-8774-d9ad427e05aa.text: Starting with this quotation describing the Battle of the Windmill and its aftermath ('it did seem to them after all that they had won a great victory'), explore how Orwell presents the difference between reality and propaganda in Animal Farm. Write about: how Orwell presents this difference in this quotation, and how Orwell presents it in the novel as a whole.
b8e74bc1-70e8-44fa-8774-d9ad427e05aa.marks:
Top band (7-8): Perceptive analysis. The windmill — years of backbreaking labour — has been destroyed, yet Napoleon declares 'a great victory.' The 'Order of the Green Banner, which he had conferred upon himself' is darkly comic — Napoleon awards himself for a battle he directed 'from the rear.' 'In the general rejoicings the unfortunate affair of the banknotes was forgotten' shows how celebrations are used to distract from failures. The pattern across the novel: every disaster is reframed as success (windmill destroyed by storm = Snowball's sabotage; forged banknotes = a lesson learned). Context: Stalin reframed the devastating German invasion as the 'Great Patriotic War.'

b8e74bc1-70e8-44fa-8774-d9ad427e05aa.text: How does Orwell use humour and irony to criticise Napoleon's leadership in Animal Farm?
b8e74bc1-70e8-44fa-8774-d9ad427e05aa.marks:
Top band (11-12) Critical, exploratory response. Orwell's satire works on multiple levels. The image of Napoleon 'wearing an old bowler hat of Mr. Jones's' and galloping drunkenly round the yard is comic but devastating — it visually represents the pigs becoming the humans they overthrew. 'Lord of the swill-bucket' deflates Napoleon's grandeur with bathos. The Fifth Commandment being changed to 'No animal shall drink alcohol to excess' is ironic because the pigs define 'excess' to suit themselves. The hens crediting Napoleon for their egg production is absurd comedy that exposes how cults of personality function. Orwell uses humour to make his political critique accessible — the reader laughs, then realises the horror beneath.

b8e74bc1-70e8-44fa-8774-d9ad427e05aa.text: How does Orwell use the changing of the commandments throughout Animal Farm to present the corruption of the revolution?
b8e74bc1-70e8-44fa-8774-d9ad427e05aa.marks:
Top band (11-12) Critical, exploratory response. The commandments function as a barometer of corruption. Each change is small enough to go unnoticed: 'with sheets' (Ch.6), 'without cause' (Ch.8), 'to excess' (Ch.8). This gradual erosion mirrors how totalitarian regimes dismantle rights incrementally. The animals' inability to remember the originals highlights Orwell's warning about the importance of literacy and education. Clover checks the wall but cannot be certain it has changed. By Chapter Ten, all commandments are replaced by a single paradox: 'All animals are equal but some animals are more equal than others.' The revolution's foundational principles have been completely inverted. Context: parallels Stalin's systematic dismantling of Marxist principles while claiming to uphold them.

477594ea-62bd-4816-994f-477ba31599f3.text: How does Shakespeare use money and debt to drive the plot of The Merchant of Venice?

The bond (financial contract with a human penalty) blurs the line between money and flesh. The casket test equates moral choice with material choice. Money creates power imbalances that drive prejudice, love, and conflict.

No love is purely idealised. The ring trick exposes romantic love’s fragility. Shakespeare suggests all love is compromised by self-interest, prejudice, or social structure.

Shakespeare structures the play so that comedy and tragedy coexist, refusing a simple genre classification.

Upper band (3-4): Detailed explanation. The entailment means Longbourn passes to Mr Collins, not the Bennet daughters. This creates urgency: the girls must marry well or face poverty. It motivates Mrs Bennet’s matchmaking, justifies Charlotte’s pragmatic marriage to Collins, and makes Elizabeth’s refusal of Collins a high-stakes gamble. The entailment symbolises how the legal system trapped women in financial dependence on men.
Lower band (1-2): Basic identification with limited explanation.

65fece77-1755-4524-aec4-f656561e3dbe.marks: A word that imitates the natural sound of the thing it describes (1 mark). Accept examples such as 'crash,' 'hiss,' 'buzz' if accompanied by a brief definition.

65fece77-1755-4524-aec4-f656561e3dbe.text: Describe two ways a writer could use the sense of sound to create atmosphere in a descriptive piece.
65fece77-1755-4524-aec4-f656561e3dbe.marks: One mark for each way described, up to 2 marks. For example: • Use onomatopoeia such as 'crash' or 'hiss' to make the reader hear the sound directly (1 mark). • Use a contrast between silence and sudden noise to create tension or surprise (1 mark). • Use repetition of sounds (e.g. 'yip yip yip') to convey a relentless or overwhelming atmosphere (1 mark). Accept any two valid methods with brief explanation.

65fece77-1755-4524-aec4-f656561e3dbe.text: Explain how the 'zooming in' technique can help a student organise a descriptive writing response effectively.
65fece77-1755-4524-aec4-f656561e3dbe.marks: Award up to 4 marks for a clear explanation that covers: • Definition: zooming in means moving from a wide overview of a scene to a small, specific detail (1 mark). • Effect on reader: it mimics how the human eye works, creating a sense of discovery as focus narrows (1 mark). • Structural benefit: it provides a logical, deliberate organisation rather than random listing of details (1 mark). • Link to assessment: strong answers show 'varied and inventive use of structural features' at the highest band for content and organisation (1 mark). Accept reverse zoom (close to wide) if clearly explained.

65fece77-1755-4524-aec4-f656561e3dbe.text: Explain how Peter Fleming uses personification to describe the train crash in Source A. Use specific examples from the text to support your answer.
65fece77-1755-4524-aec4-f656561e3dbe.marks:
Award up to 6 marks across two levels:
Upper band (4-6): Clear, detailed explanation with specific examples and analysis of effect. For example:
• The train 'sprawled foolishly' — the adverb 'foolishly' gives the train a human quality of embarrassment or stupidity, creating dark humour from the wreckage (up to 2 marks).
• The carriages are 'disposed in attitudes' and the last one remains 'primly, on the rails' — 'primly' suggests prim, proper behaviour, as if the carriage is morally superior to the others, adding absurdist comedy (up to 2 marks).
• The engine has 'a defiant and naughty look' and is 'definitely conscious of indiscretion' — it is presented as a mischievous child who knows it has done wrong, which undercuts the danger of the crash with comic tone (up to 2 marks).
Lower band (1-3): Some relevant examples identified with simple or partial explanation of effect.

65fece77-1755-4524-aec4-f656561e3dbe.text:
Read the following student response to a descriptive writing task:

'The beach was nice. The sea was blue and the sand was golden. There were some seagulls flying around. The sun was warm and it felt relaxing. I could hear the waves.'

Evaluate this response against the Level 4 descriptors for content and organisation. To what extent does it meet the standard? What specific improvements would you recommend?
65fece77-1755-4524-aec4-f656561e3dbe.marks:
Award up to 9 marks using a three-level structure:
Top band (7-9): Perceptive evaluation that identifies specific weaknesses and offers detailed, practical improvements. The response should note:
• The writing tells rather than shows — 'The beach was nice' is a statement, not a description. Level 4 requires 'convincing and compelling' communication.
• Vocabulary is generic ('nice,' 'blue,' 'golden,' 'warm') — Level 4 requires 'extensive and ambitious vocabulary.'
• Only two senses are used (sight and touch/hearing briefly) and none are developed with figurative language.
• No structural variety — every sentence follows the same subject-verb-complement pattern.
• Improvements: use specific sensory detail ('the gritty warmth of sand between my toes'), figurative language ('waves exhaling against the shore'), varied sentence forms, and a deliberate structure (e.g. zooming in).
Mid band (4-6): Clear identification of some weaknesses with some useful suggestions.
Lower band (1-3): Simple or limited comments, may identify it as 'not very good' without specific analysis.

65fece77-1755-4524-aec4-f656561e3dbe.text:
You are going to enter a creative writing competition. Your entry will be judged by a panel of English teachers.

Write a description suggested by this task: 'Describe a place where everything has stopped.'

(24 marks for content and organisation, 16 marks for technical accuracy)

Plan and write your response. You should aim to use precise sensory detail, varied sentence structures, and at least one example of the 'zooming in' technique.
65fece77-1755-4524-aec4-f656561e3dbe.marks:
Content and Organisation (24 marks):
Top band (19–24) Communication is convincing and compelling. Tone, style and register assuredly matched to purpose. Extensive and ambitious vocabulary with sustained crafting of linguistic devices. Varied and inventive structural features. Fluently linked paragraphs.
Upper-mid band (13–18) Communication is consistently clear. Increasingly sophisticated vocabulary chosen for effect. Effective structural features. Coherent paragraphs with integrated discourse markers.
Lower-mid band (7–12) Communicates with some success. Conscious use of vocabulary. Some structural features. Some use of paragraphs.
Lower band (1–6) Simple communication. Simple vocabulary. Limited structural features.

Technical Accuracy (16 marks):
Top band (13–16) Consistently secure sentence demarcation. Wide range of punctuation with high accuracy. Full range of sentence forms for effect. High-level spelling including ambitious vocabulary.
Upper-mid band (9–12) Mostly secure demarcation. Variety of sentence forms. Generally accurate spelling.
Lower-mid band (5–8) Mostly secure demarcation, sometimes accurate. Some control of punctuation range. Attempts variety of sentence forms.
Lower band (1–4) Occasional sentence demarcation. Simple sentence forms. Accurate basic spelling.

Indicative content: Students should demonstrate careful observation of a still or frozen scene using multiple senses. Strong responses will use zooming in/out, figurative language (simile, metaphor, personification), varied sentence lengths for pace control, and ambitious vocabulary. The 'stopped' prompt lends itself to contrasts between stillness and implied movement, silence and implied sound.

70facceb-ef6a-4607-a9f8-421f7d55a387.marks: A simile is a figure of speech that compares two different things using 'like' or 'as' (1 mark).

70facceb-ef6a-4607-a9f8-421f7d55a387.text: Describe two ways a writer can make a simile effective in creative writing.
70facceb-ef6a-4607-a9f8-421f7d55a387.marks:
1 marks for each valid way, up to 2 marks. Possible answers:
• By making the comparison unexpected or original, so it creates a vivid image (1)
• By matching the simile to the mood or atmosphere of the piece (1)
• By using the simile to reveal something about the character or narrator’s feelings (1)
• By extending the comparison across several sentences to create a sustained effect (1)

70facceb-ef6a-4607-a9f8-421f7d55a387.text: Explain why using clichéd similes (such as 'cold as ice' or 'quiet as a mouse') is likely to lower a student's mark in Paper 1 Section B.
70facceb-ef6a-4607-a9f8-421f7d55a387.marks:
Award up to 4 marks for a clear explanation. Possible points:
• Clichés are overused expressions that have lost their impact — they do not create a vivid or original image in the reader’s mind (1)
• The mark scheme rewards ‘ambitious vocabulary’ and ‘crafting of linguistic devices’ — clichés demonstrate neither (1)
• Clichés suggest the writer is not thinking carefully about their word choices, which signals Level 1 or 2 writing (1)
• They fail to convey a specific mood or perspective because they are so generic (1)
• Examiners read thousands of responses — original language stands out, clichés do not (1)

70facceb-ef6a-4607-a9f8-421f7d55a387.text: Explain how an extended metaphor can help a student achieve Level 4 in the AQA Paper 1 creative writing task. You should refer to specific features of the Level 4 mark scheme descriptors in your answer.
70facceb-ef6a-4607-a9f8-421f7d55a387.marks:
Award up to 6 marks. Possible points:
• Level 4 requires ‘sustained crafting of linguistic devices’ — an extended metaphor that runs across a paragraph or whole response demonstrates sustained, deliberate crafting (1–2)
• Level 4 requires ‘extensive and ambitious vocabulary’ — an extended metaphor naturally generates a semantic field of related vocabulary, showing range and ambition (1–2)
• Level 4 requires ‘compelling, convincing communication’ — a well-developed extended metaphor creates a strong, immersive atmosphere that draws the reader in (1–2)
• Reference to how structure supports the device: an extended metaphor can unify a paragraph and give it coherence, linking to ‘varied and inventive use of structural features’ (1)
• Example: comparing a storm to an argument across multiple sentences (thunder as shouting, lightning as accusations, silence as a truce) shows control and ambition (1)

70facceb-ef6a-4607-a9f8-421f7d55a387.text:
Read the following student's opening paragraph:

'The forest was dark. The trees were tall. The wind blew through the branches like a cold breeze. It was scary. I walked slowly.'

Evaluate this paragraph's use of figurative language and suggest how it could be improved to reach Level 3 or above.
70facceb-ef6a-4607-a9f8-421f7d55a387.marks:
Award up to 9 marks using a best-fit approach.
Top band (7-9): Clear, detailed evaluation. Identifies that the simile ‘like a cold breeze’ is weak because wind already IS a breeze, so no real comparison is being made. Notes the reliance on simple adjectives (‘dark’, ‘tall’, ‘scary’) with no figurative language to create atmosphere. Offers specific, practical improvements, e.g. replacing ‘like a cold breeze’ with an original simile (‘the wind moved through the branches like fingers searching for something lost’), using personification for the trees, or adding a metaphor that conveys the narrator’s fear.
Mid band (4-6): Some valid points about the weakness of the simile and the lack of vivid language. Suggestions for improvement are general rather than specific.
Lower band (1-3): Simple identification that the writing is ‘boring’ or ‘needs more description’ without explaining why or offering concrete alternatives.

70facceb-ef6a-4607-a9f8-421f7d55a387.text:
You are going to enter a creative writing competition. Your entry will be judged by a panel of experienced writers.

Write a description suggested by this picture: a lone figure standing at the edge of a cliff, looking out over a stormy sea.

You should use figurative language, including at least one original simile and one example of personification, to create a vivid atmosphere.

(24 marks for content and organisation
16 marks for technical accuracy)
70facceb-ef6a-4607-a9f8-421f7d55a387.marks:
Content and Organisation (AO5, 24 marks):
Top band (19–24) Communication is convincing and compelling. Tone, style and register assuredly matched to purpose. Extensive and ambitious vocabulary with sustained crafting of linguistic devices (simile, personification, metaphor). Varied and inventive structural features. Fluently linked paragraphs.
Upper-mid band (13–18) Communication is consistently clear. Increasingly sophisticated vocabulary chosen for effect with a range of successful linguistic devices. Effective use of structural features. Coherent paragraphs with integrated discourse markers.
Lower-mid band (7–12) Communicates with some success. Conscious use of vocabulary with some use of linguistic devices. Some use of structural features and paragraphs.
Lower band (1–6) Simple communication. Simple vocabulary and simple linguistic devices. Random paragraph structure.

Technical Accuracy (AO6, 16 marks):
Top band (13–16) Consistently secure sentence demarcation. Wide range of punctuation with high accuracy. Full range of sentence forms. High level of spelling accuracy.
Upper-mid band (9–12) Mostly secure demarcation. Range of punctuation mostly successful. Variety of sentence forms. Generally accurate spelling.
Lower-mid band (5–8) Mostly secure demarcation, sometimes accurate. Some control of punctuation. Attempts variety of sentence forms.
Lower band (1–4) Occasional sentence demarcation. Simple range of sentence forms. Accurate basic spelling.

d96fa366-519f-4c25-b09e-3ccb72b0676c.marks:
1 mark(s) for a clear definition, e.g.:
• Language that appeals to one or more of the five senses (sight, sound, smell, taste, touch) to help the reader experience a scene.

d96fa366-519f-4c25-b09e-3ccb72b0676c.text: Describe two ways a writer could use 'show don't tell' to convey a character's fear.
d96fa366-519f-4c25-b09e-3ccb72b0676c.marks:
1 marks for each valid way, up to 2 marks. Possible answers:
• Describe physical reactions such as trembling hands, shallow breathing, a racing heart or cold sweat (1 mark)
• Describe the character's actions, such as backing away, freezing, or gripping something tightly (1 mark)
• Use sensory details that create a threatening atmosphere, such as sounds, shadows, or cold air (1 mark)
• Use a powerful verb that implies fear without naming it, e.g. 'stumbled' or 'recoiled' (1 mark)

d96fa366-519f-4c25-b09e-3ccb72b0676c.text: Explain how Peter Fleming uses the verb 'cannonaded' to describe the impact of the suitcase during the train crash in Source A (Paper 2, 2026 sample). You should comment on the effect this has on the reader.
d96fa366-519f-4c25-b09e-3ccb72b0676c.marks:
Award up to 4 marks. Indicative content:
• The verb 'cannonaded' is a metaphor that compares the falling suitcase to a cannon being fired (1 mark)
• This creates the impression of a violent military attack, suggesting the impact was extremely forceful (1 mark)
• It turns an ordinary object (a suitcase) into a weapon, making the writer seem like a victim under bombardment (1 mark)
• The hyperbolic effect exaggerates the incident for humorous or dramatic purposes, fitting the writer's sardonic tone (1 mark)

d96fa366-519f-4c25-b09e-3ccb72b0676c.text: Explain how Yann Martel uses sensory language and powerful verbs to create tension in the Life of Pi extract (Paper 1, 2026 sample). You should refer to specific examples from the text in your answer.
d96fa366-519f-4c25-b09e-3ccb72b0676c.marks:
Award up to 6 marks using a best-fit approach.

Indicative content:
• Onomatopoeic repetition of 'yip yip yip yip yip' appeals to the sense of sound and conveys the relentless, manic energy of the hyena (1–2 marks)
• The sensory detail 'the beating of its legs against the benches made the whole boat shake' uses touch/physical sensation to convey the hyena's power and proximity (1–2 marks)
• 'Its claws were loudly clicking on their surface' uses sound to emphasise the predatory threat (1 mark)
• Dynamic verbs such as 'leapt', 'ran', 'racing' create pace and energy, making the reader feel the hyena's frantic movement (1–2 marks)
• Pi's passive verbs ('could only watch', 'was seized by fear') contrast with the hyena's active verbs, showing his helplessness (1–2 marks)
• 'I pushed myself away on the oar till only the tips of my feet were holding on to the boat' is an example of 'show don't tell' — we understand Pi's terror through his physical actions (1–2 marks)

d96fa366-519f-4c25-b09e-3ccb72b0676c.text:
Evaluate the effectiveness of the following student's creative writing opening. To what extent does it successfully use sensory language, powerful verbs and 'show don't tell'?

'The house was old and creepy. I walked up the path and the door was open. I felt nervous. It was dark inside and I could hear a noise. I went in.'

In your response, you should identify strengths and weaknesses and suggest specific improvements.
d96fa366-519f-4c25-b09e-3ccb72b0676c.marks:
Top band (7-9): Perceptive evaluation that identifies specific weaknesses (generic verbs 'walked', 'went'; directly stating emotion 'I felt nervous'; lack of sensory detail beyond sight; adjectives 'old and creepy' are telling not showing) and offers precise, well-explained improvements demonstrating understanding of all three techniques.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Clear evaluation that identifies several weaknesses and suggests relevant improvements. May not address all three techniques equally.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Some valid comments on the writing. May identify that it is 'too simple' but struggle to explain exactly why or offer specific alternatives.
Lower band (1-2): Simple comments, e.g. 'it could use more description.' Limited understanding of the specific techniques.
Indicative improvements students might suggest:
• Replace 'old and creepy' with sensory showing: describe peeling paint, a sagging roof, the smell of damp wood
• Replace 'walked' with a powerful verb like 'crept', 'edged' or 'stumbled'
• Replace 'I felt nervous' with a physical reaction: sweating palms, dry mouth, tightening stomach
• Add sound detail beyond 'a noise' — specify what the noise sounds like
• Replace 'It was dark inside' with a showing description using imagery

d96fa366-519f-4c25-b09e-3ccb72b0676c.text:
Write a description of a busy market as suggested by the picture below.

[Imagine a picture of an outdoor market with colourful stalls, crowds and food.]

You should use sensory language appealing to at least three different senses, powerful verb choices, and 'show don't tell' techniques to create a vivid, immersive description.

(24 marks for content and organisation, 16 marks for technical accuracy)
d96fa366-519f-4c25-b09e-3ccb72b0676c.marks:
AO5 Content and Organisation (24 marks):
Top band (19–24) Compelling, convincing communication. Extensive and ambitious vocabulary with sustained crafting of linguistic devices. Sensory language appeals to multiple senses throughout. Powerful, precise verb choices. Emotion and atmosphere conveyed through showing, not telling. Varied and inventive structural features.

Upper-mid band (13–18) Consistent, clear communication. Increasingly sophisticated vocabulary chosen for effect. Sensory language present across most of the piece. Some powerful verb choices. Mostly shows rather than tells. Effective structural features.

Lower-mid band (7–12) Some successful communication. Some sensory language, possibly limited to one or two senses. Some attempt at verb variety. May lapse into telling. Some structural features.

Lower band (1–6) Simple, limited communication. Little or no sensory language. Generic verb choices. Relies on telling. Limited structural features.

AO6 Technical Accuracy (16 marks):
Top band (13–16) Consistently secure sentence demarcation. Wide range of punctuation used accurately. Full range of sentence forms for effect. High level of spelling accuracy. Extensive vocabulary.
Upper-mid band (9–12) Mostly secure demarcation. Range of punctuation mostly successful. Variety of sentence forms. Generally accurate spelling.
Lower-mid band (5–8) Mostly secure demarcation, sometimes accurate. Some control of punctuation. Attempts variety of sentence forms.
Lower band (1–4) Occasional sentence demarcation. Simple range of sentence forms. Accurate basic spelling.

9cea9234-9798-4fae-9700-4b759b353743.marks:
One mark for a clear definition, e.g.:
• The art of using language to persuade an audience (1 mark)
• Effective or persuasive use of language (1 mark)

9cea9234-9798-4fae-9700-4b759b353743.text: Describe two ways a writer can build ethos in a piece of persuasive writing.
9cea9234-9798-4fae-9700-4b759b353743.marks:
One mark for each valid way described, e.g.:
• Acknowledging the opposing viewpoint to appear fair and balanced (1)
• Using a formal, confident tone that matches the audience (1)
• Referencing facts, authorities, or personal experience to build credibility (1)
• Avoiding hedging language to sound assured (1)

9cea9234-9798-4fae-9700-4b759b353743.text: Explain how a writer could use logos to argue that public transport should be made cheaper.
9cea9234-9798-4fae-9700-4b759b353743.marks:
Upper band (3-4): Clear explanation of how logos works with specific examples. E.g.: A writer could use logos by including a statistic such as 'for every £1 invested in buses, the local economy gains £4' to provide concrete evidence that the policy makes financial sense. They could also use cause-and-effect reasoning: 'if fares are reduced, more people will use buses, reducing traffic congestion and lowering road maintenance costs.' This logical chain shows the audience that the argument is rational, not just emotional.
Lower band (1-2): Simple or general explanation. E.g.: They could use facts and statistics to prove their point, like saying how much money it would save.

9cea9234-9798-4fae-9700-4b759b353743.text: Explain why using all three rhetorical appeals (ethos, logos, pathos) together is more effective than relying on just one.
9cea9234-9798-4fae-9700-4b759b353743.marks:
Top band (5-6): Detailed explanation showing understanding of how the appeals complement each other, with examples. E.g.: Using all three appeals creates a more convincing and well-rounded argument. Logos provides the evidence that satisfies a sceptical reader's need for proof, while pathos engages the reader's emotions and makes them care about the issue on a personal level. Ethos underpins both by ensuring the reader trusts the writer enough to accept the evidence and respond to the emotional appeal. A response that relies only on pathos risks seeming manipulative, while one that uses only logos may feel cold and fail to motivate the reader to act.
Mid band (3-4): Some valid explanation but may lack examples or detail. E.g.: Using all three together makes the argument stronger because logos convinces the reader's brain, pathos convinces their heart, and ethos makes them trust the writer. If you only use emotion, the reader might not believe you.
Lower band (1-2): Simple awareness. E.g.: It is better to use all three because it makes your writing more persuasive and gets more marks.

9cea9234-9798-4fae-9700-4b759b353743.text:
Read the following extract from a student's response to the AQA 2026 sample question about public transport:

'Public transport is absolutely terrible! Buses are always late! Nobody likes getting the bus! Something needs to change right now!!!'

Evaluate the effectiveness of this student's use of rhetoric. In your response, you should identify which rhetorical appeals are present or absent and explain how the writing could be improved.
9cea9234-9798-4fae-9700-4b759b353743.marks:
Top band (7-9): Perceptive evaluation. The student relies almost entirely on pathos — emotive language and exclamation marks create a sense of outrage, but the response lacks logos (no evidence, statistics, or logical reasoning) and ethos (no acknowledgement of the audience, no credibility established, informal tone inappropriate for a council meeting). The overuse of exclamation marks and generalisations ('Nobody likes getting the bus') weakens the argument because it feels exaggerated rather than measured. To improve, the student could include a specific statistic to add logos, acknowledge the council's financial constraints to build ethos, and replace one emotional outburst with a specific anecdote to create more controlled pathos.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Clear evaluation identifying at least two appeals (present or missing) with some explanation of improvement. E.g.: The student uses lots of pathos with exclamation marks and emotive language but doesn't use logos or ethos. They could add a statistic and write in a more formal tone.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Some valid comment but limited. E.g.: The student is using emotion to persuade but it could be better if they used facts.
Lower band (1-2): Simple comment. E.g.: The student is quite persuasive because they use exclamation marks.

9cea9234-9798-4fae-9700-4b759b353743.text:
'Cars are convenient, comfortable and save time. However, we need to use them less by making public transport such as trains, trams and buses cheaper, more reliable and easier to access.'

Write a speech to be given at a meeting of your local council in which you argue your point of view on this statement.

(24 marks for content and organisation
16 marks for technical accuracy)

In your response, you should aim to use ethos, logos, and pathos effectively.
9cea9234-9798-4fae-9700-4b759b353743.marks:
AO5 Content and Organisation (24 marks):
Top band (19–24) Communication is convincing and compelling. Tone, style and register assuredly matched to a council meeting audience. Extensive vocabulary with sustained crafting of linguistic devices (including deliberate use of ethos, logos, and pathos). Varied structural features. Fluently linked paragraphs.
Upper-mid band (13–18) Consistently clear communication. Tone matched to audience. Range of successful linguistic devices. Effective use of structural features.
Lower-mid band (7–12) Some sustained success. Some attempt to match tone to audience. Some use of linguistic devices.
Lower band (1–6) Simple communication. Simple awareness of audience. Simple vocabulary and devices.

AO6 Technical Accuracy (16 marks):
Top band (13–16) Consistently secure sentence demarcation. Wide range of punctuation. Full range of sentence forms. Secure Standard English. High-level spelling accuracy. Extensive vocabulary.
Upper-mid band (9–12) Mostly secure demarcation. Range of punctuation mostly successful. Variety of sentence forms. Generally accurate spelling.
Lower-mid band (5–8) Mostly secure demarcation. Some control of punctuation. Attempts variety of sentence forms. Some accurate spelling.
Lower band (1–4) Occasional sentence demarcation. Some conscious punctuation. Simple sentence forms. Accurate basic spelling.

d7b47993-f300-4e56-b2eb-10540d1bbade.marks: A word that imitates the natural sound of the thing it describes (1 mark). Accept examples such as 'crash,' 'hiss,' 'buzz' if accompanied by a brief definition.

d7b47993-f300-4e56-b2eb-10540d1bbade.text: Describe two ways a writer could use the sense of sound to create atmosphere in a descriptive piece.

For example: • Use onomatopoeia such as 'crash' or 'hiss' to make the reader hear the sound directly (1 mark). • Use a contrast between silence and sudden noise to create tension or surprise (1 mark). • Use repetition of sounds (e.g. 'yip yip yip') to convey a relentless or overwhelming atmosphere (1 mark). Accept any two valid methods with brief explanation.

d7b47993-f300-4e56-b2eb-10540d1bbade.marks: Award up to 4 marks for a clear explanation that covers: • Definition: zooming in means moving from a wide overview of a scene to a small, specific detail (1 mark). • Effect on reader: it mimics how the human eye works, creating a sense of discovery as focus narrows (1 mark). • Structural benefit: it provides a logical, deliberate organisation rather than random listing of details (1 mark). • Link to assessment: a deliberate structure earns credit for varied and inventive use of structural features (1 mark). Accept reverse zoom (close to wide) if clearly explained.

d7b47993-f300-4e56-b2eb-10540d1bbade.text: Explain how Peter Fleming uses personification to describe the train crash in the passage you have studied. Use specific examples from the text to support your answer.
d7b47993-f300-4e56-b2eb-10540d1bbade.marks:
Award up to 6 marks across two levels:
Upper band (4-6): Clear, detailed explanation with specific examples and analysis of effect. For example:
• The train 'sprawled foolishly' — the adverb 'foolishly' gives the train a human quality of embarrassment or stupidity, creating dark humour from the wreckage (up to 2 marks).
• The carriages are 'disposed in attitudes' and the last one remains 'primly, on the rails' — 'primly' suggests prim, proper behaviour, as if the carriage is morally superior to the others, adding absurdist comedy (up to 2 marks).

d7b47993-f300-4e56-b2eb-10540d1bbade.text:
Read the following student response to a descriptive writing task:

'The beach was nice. The sea was blue and the sand was golden. There were some seagulls flying around. The sun was warm and it felt relaxing. I could hear the waves.'

Evaluate this response in terms of content and organisation quality. To what extent does it meet a high standard? What specific improvements would you recommend?
d7b47993-f300-4e56-b2eb-10540d1bbade.marks:
Award up to 9 marks using a three-level structure:
Top band (7-9): Perceptive evaluation that identifies specific weaknesses and offers detailed, practical improvements. The response should note:
• The writing tells rather than shows — 'The beach was nice' is a statement, not a description. High-level responses require 'convincing and compelling' communication.
• Vocabulary is generic ('nice,' 'blue,' 'golden,' 'warm') — top-band responses require 'extensive and ambitious vocabulary.'
• Only two senses are used (sight and touch/hearing briefly) and none are developed with figurative language.
• No structural variety — every sentence follows the same subject-verb-complement pattern.
• Improvements: use specific sensory detail ('the gritty warmth of sand between my toes'), figurative language ('waves exhaling against the shore'), varied sentence forms, and a deliberate structure (e.g. zooming in).
Mid band (4-6): Clear identification of some weaknesses with some useful suggestions.
Lower band (1-3): Simple or limited comments, may identify it as 'not very good' without specific analysis.

d7b47993-f300-4e56-b2eb-10540d1bbade.text:
You are going to enter a creative writing competition. Your entry will be judged by a panel of English teachers.

Lower-mid band (7–12) Communicates with some success. Conscious use of vocabulary. Some structural features. Some use of paragraphs.
Lower band (1–6) Simple communication. Simple vocabulary. Limited structural features.

Lower-mid band (5–8) Mostly secure demarcation, sometimes accurate. Some control of punctuation range. Attempts variety of sentence forms.

Indicative content: Students should demonstrate careful observation of a still or frozen scene using multiple senses. Strong responses will use zooming in/out, figurative language (simile, metaphor, personification), varied sentence lengths for pace control, and ambitious vocabulary. The 'stopped' prompt lends itself to contrasts between stillness and implied movement, silence and implied sound.
